(4) Let $\delta_n = (b - a)/n$ and $\chi_n$ be $0$ on $[a, a + \delta_n/2]$, $1$ on $[a + \delta_n, b]$, and linear
between. Then $f\chi_n$, extended by $0$ at $a$, lies in $C[a, b]$. For $m > n$, $0 \leq \chi_n \leq \chi_m \leq 1$ and
$\chi_m - \chi_n$ vanishes on $[a + \delta_n, b]$, so $\|f\chi_m - f\chi_n\|_p^p \leq \int_a^{a + \delta_n}|f|^p \to 0$
by the convergence of the improper integral (@def-improper-integral). So $(f\chi_n)$ is Cauchy and converges to an
element $[f]$. Its norm is $\lim\|f\chi_n\|_p$, and $\int_{a + \delta_n}^b|f|^p \leq \|f\chi_n\|_p^p \leq \int_{a +
\delta_n/2}^b|f|^p$, both of which tend to $\int_a^b|f|^p$. On $\mathbb{R}$ use $\chi_R = 1$ on $[-R, R]$, $0$ outside
$[-R - 1, R + 1]$ and linear between, and the tails $\int_{|x| > R}|f|^p \to 0$.

(5) Let $h_n$ be the tent of height $1$ at $x_0$ supported in $[x_0 - \tfrac1n, x_0 + \tfrac1n]$, cut off at $a$ and $b$.
Then $h_n(x_0) = 1$ and $\|h_n\|_p \leq (2/n)^{1/p} \to 0$. A continuous linear extension $E$ of the evaluation would
give $1 = h_n(x_0) = E(ih_n) \to E(0) = 0$, a contradiction. $\square$

This is the construction of @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Sec. I.3], who complete $C[a, b]$ in $\|\cdot\|_1$ and only then
realise the completion as a space of functions, with a theory of integration that this tutorial does not develop.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The sequences $1/n^\alpha$ are the test cases of the sequence spaces: whether they belong to $\ell^p$ is decided by the
$p$-series. The first example records the result.

::: {#exm-fan-power-sequences}
#### Power sequences

$a_n = n^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha > 0$ lies in $\ell^p$ exactly when $\alpha p > 1$ (@thm-convergence-tests, @sec-series),
and always in $\ell^\infty$. So $1/n$ lies in every $\ell^p$ with $p > 1$ but not in $\ell^1$, and $1/\sqrt n$ lies in
$\ell^p$ for $p > 2$ only. The left panel of the figure shows $\|1/n\|_p$ decreasing in $p$ and blowing up as $p \to 1$.
:::

The unit sequences have norm one in every $\ell^p$ but are far apart, and their distances depend on $p$. The second
example computes them and the inclusions between the spaces.

::: {#exm-fan-ellp-unit-vectors}
#### Unit sequences and inclusions

$\|\delta^{(n)}\|_p = 1$ and $\|\delta^{(n)} - \delta^{(m)}\|_p = 2^{1/p}$ for $n \neq m$, which is $2$ in $\ell^1$,
$\sqrt2$ in $\ell^2$ and $1$ in $\ell^\infty$. If $\|a\|_p = 1$ then every $|a_n| \leq 1$, so $|a_n|^q \leq |a_n|^p$ for
$q > p$ and $\|a\|_q \leq \|a\|_p$: hence $\ell^1 \subset \ell^2 \subset \ell^\infty$, with $(1/n) \in \ell^2 \setminus
\ell^1$ and $(1, 1, \dots) \in \ell^\infty \setminus \ell^2$.
:::

A step function is not continuous, but it defines an element of every $L^p[0, 1]$ by part (3), and the figure shows
how continuous ramps approach it. The third example computes the distances.

![Left: the step function $\Theta(x - \tfrac12)$ on $[0, 1]$ and continuous ramps $g_n$, equal to $0$ up to $\tfrac12 -
\tfrac1n$ and to $1$ from $\tfrac12$ on, for $n = 3, 6, 12$. Right: $\|g_n - \Theta(\cdot - \tfrac12)\|_p = (n(p +
1))^{-1/p}$ for $p = 1, 2, 4$, all tending to $0$.](figures/fa2-lp-step.svg){#fig-fa2-lp-step width=95%}

::: {#exm-fan-step-in-lp}
#### The step function in $L^p[0, 1]$

$\Theta(x - \tfrac12)$, $0$ for $x < \tfrac12$ and $1$ for $x \geq \tfrac12$, lies in $PC[0, 1]$. The ramps of the
figure differ from it only on $[\tfrac12 - \tfrac1n, \tfrac12)$, where $|g_n - \Theta| = n(x - \tfrac12) + 1$ rises from
$0$ to $1$, so $\|g_n - \Theta\|_p^p = \frac{1}{n(p + 1)}$. By part (3), $[\Theta] = \lim g_n$ in every $L^p[0, 1]$,
with $\|[\Theta]\| = 2^{-1/p}$. Changing the value at $\tfrac12$ to $0$ or $\tfrac12$ gives the same element.
:::

Power functions with a singularity define elements of $L^p$ through part (4), and the condition depends on whether the
singularity is at zero or the decay is at infinity. The fourth example compares the two ends.

::: {#exm-fan-power-functions}
#### Power functions

On $(0, 1]$, $\int_0^1x^{-\alpha p}dx$ converges exactly when $\alpha p < 1$ (@def-improper-integral (3)), so
$x^{-\alpha}$ defines an element of $L^p[0, 1]$ for $p < 1/\alpha$; thus $x^{-1/4}$ gives one for $p < 4$ (right panel
of the figure). On the line, $f(x) = (1 + |x|)^{-1}$ has $\int|f|^2 = 2$, so it defines an element of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$,
but its cut-offs are not Cauchy in $\|\cdot\|_1$: $\|f\chi_S - f\chi_R\|_1 \geq 2\int_{R + 1}^S\frac{dx}{1 + x} \to
\infty$ as $S \to \infty$.
:::

The Gaussian lies in every $L^p(\mathbb{R})$, and its norms can be computed in closed form. The fifth example does so
for the ground state of the oscillator.

::: {#exm-fan-gaussian-lp}
#### The Gaussian in $L^p(\mathbb{R})$

For $g(x) = e^{-x^2/2}$, $\int_{\mathbb{R}}|g|^p = \int e^{-px^2/2}dx = \sqrt{2\pi/p}$, so by part (4) $g$ defines an
element of $L^p(\mathbb{R})$ with $\|g\|_p = (2\pi/p)^{1/(2p)}$ for $1 \leq p < \infty$. In particular $\|g\|_1 =
\sqrt{2\pi}$ and $\|g\|_2 = \pi^{1/4}$, and $\|g\|_p \to 1 = \max g$ as $p \to \infty$, as in @exm-fan-p-norm-limit.
:::

A spectral line has a Lorentzian profile, which decays only like $x^{-2}$ but still lies in $L^1$ and $L^2$. The sixth
example computes its norms.

::: {#exm-fan-lorentzian}
#### The Lorentzian line shape

$L(x) = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}$, the profile of a line of unit half-width, is continuous with $\int_{\mathbb{R}}L = \pi$ and
$\int L^2 = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2t\,dt = \frac\pi2$ (substitute $x = \tan t$), so by part (4) it defines elements of $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ and
$L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with $\|L\|_1 = \pi$ and $\|L\|_2 = \sqrt{\pi/2}$. The Gaussian of the same height and the same
$\|\cdot\|_1$, $e^{-x^2/\pi}$, has much thinner tails.
:::

The normal modes of a string are continuous functions on an interval, hence elements of every $L^p[0, 1]$. The seventh
example measures them.

::: {#exm-fan-lp-sine-modes}
#### Modes of a string

$u_n(x) = \sin(n\pi x)$ on $[0, 1]$ has $\|u_n\|_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and $\|u_n\|_1 = \frac2\pi$ for every $n \geq 1$,
and $\|u_n - u_m\|_2 = 1$ for $n \neq m$, because $\int_0^1u_nu_m = 0$. So the modes are a bounded sequence in
$L^2[0, 1]$ with no convergent subsequence, as in @exr-fan-riesz-lemma, even though each is a smooth function.
:::

An element of $L^p$ does not have a value at a point, and convergence in $L^p$ says nothing about values. The eighth
example shows both failures.

::: {#exm-fan-lp-no-point-values}
#### No values at points

The functions $x^n$ tend to $0$ in every $L^p[0, 1]$, since $\|x^n\|_p = (np + 1)^{-1/p}$, while their values at $1$
stay $1$. And $\Theta(x - \tfrac12)$, $\Theta(x - \tfrac12) - \delta_{x, 1/2}$ (value $0$ at $\tfrac12$) and any other
modification at finitely many points define the same element of $L^p[0, 1]$ by part (3); so "the value of $[\Theta]$ at
$\tfrac12$" has no meaning, in agreement with part (5).
:::

The inclusions of the sequence spaces are strict, and the ninth example gives sequences in the gaps. They also show that
$\ell^p$ with $p < q$ is not closed in $\ell^q$.

::: {#exm-fan-ellp-strict}
#### Strict inclusions

$(1/n)$ lies in $\ell^2$ but not in $\ell^1$, and $(n^{-1/3})$ lies in $\ell^4$ but not in $\ell^2$. The truncations of
$(1/n)$ lie in $\ell^1$ and converge to $(1/n)$ in $\ell^2$, since $\|(1/n) - a^{(N)}\|_2^2 = \sum_{n > N}n^{-2} \to 0$;
so $\ell^1$ is not closed in $\ell^2$, and with the norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ it is not complete.
:::

On a bounded interval the spaces $L^p$ are ordered, but on the line no inclusion holds in either direction. The tenth
example exhibits the two functions that show it.

::: {#exm-fan-lp-line-incomparable}
#### No inclusion on the line

On $[0, 1]$, $\|f\|_1 \leq \|f\|_2$ for continuous $f$ (@exr-fan-power-means), so the identity of $C[0, 1]$ extends to a
map $L^2[0, 1] \to L^1[0, 1]$ of norm at most $1$ (@thm-completion (2)). On $\mathbb{R}$ there is no such bound in
either direction. The cut-off $\chi_R$ has $\|\chi_R\|_1 = 2R + 1$ and $\|\chi_R\|_2^2 = 2R + \tfrac23$, so the ratio
$\|\chi_R\|_1/\|\chi_R\|_2$ is unbounded. The tents $h_n(x) = n\max(0, 1 - n|x|)$ have $\|h_n\|_1 = 1$ and $\|h_n\|_2^2
= \tfrac{2n}{3}$, so $\|h_n\|_2/\|h_n\|_1$ is unbounded too.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The inclusions between the sequence spaces and between the spaces on an interval go in opposite directions. The first
exercise proves both and finds elements in the gaps.

::: {#exr-fan-lp-inclusions}
#### Inclusions

Show that $\|a\|_q \leq \|a\|_p$ for sequences and $1 \leq p < q \leq \infty$, so that $\ell^p \subset \ell^q$. On
$[0, 1]$ show $\|f\|_p \leq \|f\|_q$ for continuous $f$, so that the identity extends to a map $L^q[0, 1] \to L^p[0,
1]$ of norm at most $1$. Find a sequence in $\ell^4$ that is not in $\ell^2$, and show that the cut-offs of $x^{-1/3}$,
which define an element of $L^2[0, 1]$, are not Cauchy in $\|\cdot\|_4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $\|a\|_p = 1$ then $|a_n| \leq 1$ and $\sum|a_n|^q \leq \sum|a_n|^p = 1$; homogeneity gives the general case, and
$q = \infty$ is $|a_n| \leq \|a\|_p$. On $[0, 1]$, $\|f\|_p \leq \|f\|_q$ is @exr-fan-power-means with $b - a = 1$, and
@thm-completion (2) extends the identity of $C[0, 1]$. The sequence $n^{-1/3}$ has $\sum n^{-4/3} < \infty$ and $\sum
n^{-2/3} = \infty$. For $f = x^{-1/3}$, $\int_0^1x^{-2/3} = 3$, so part (4) of @def-lp-space gives an element of $L^2$;
but $\int_\varepsilon^1x^{-4/3}dx = 3(\varepsilon^{-1/3} - 1) \to \infty$, and with the cut-offs of the definition
$\|f\chi_m - f\chi_n\|_4^4 \geq \int_{\delta_m}^{\delta_n/2}x^{-4/3}dx$ for $\delta_m < \delta_n/2$, which is unbounded
as $m \to \infty$.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates the partial sums and the integral that diverge.

```{.python .sage}
x, eps = var('x eps'); assume(eps > 0, eps < 1)
print("sum n^(-4/3) up to 10^5 = %.4f, sum n^(-2/3) up to 10^5 = %.1f" % (sum(n^(-4/3.) for n in range(1, 10^5 + 1)), sum(n^(-2/3.) for n in range(1, 10^5 + 1))))
print("int_0^1 x^(-2/3) =", integrate(x^(-2/3), x, 0, 1), "; int_eps^1 x^(-4/3) =", integrate(x^(-4/3), x, eps, 1).simplify_full())
forget()
```

```{.text .sage-output}
sum n^(-4/3) up to 10^5 = 3.5363, sum n^(-2/3) up to 10^5 = 136.8
int_0^1 x^(-2/3) = 3 ; int_eps^1 x^(-4/3) = -3*(eps^(1/3) - 1)/eps^(1/3)
```
::::
:::

Truncations converge in $\ell^p$ for $p < \infty$, at a rate given by the tail of the series. The second exercise
computes it for $(1/n)$ in $\ell^2$, where the truncations do not converge in $\ell^1$.

::: {#exr-fan-ellp-complete}
#### Truncations in $\ell^2$

Let $a = (1/n)$ and $a^{(m)} = (1, \tfrac12, \dots, \tfrac1m, 0, \dots)$. Show $\|a - a^{(m)}\|_2^2 = \sum_{n > m}n^{-2}$,
bound it between $\frac{1}{m + 1}$ and $\frac1m$, and show that $(a^{(m)})$ is not Cauchy in $\|\cdot\|_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The difference $a - a^{(m)}$ has entries $1/n$ for $n > m$ and $0$ before. The integral test (@def-improper-integral
(4)) with $f(x) = x^{-2}$ gives $\int_{m + 1}^\infty x^{-2}dx \leq \sum_{n > m}n^{-2} \leq \int_m^\infty x^{-2}dx$, that
is $\frac{1}{m + 1} \leq \|a - a^{(m)}\|_2^2 \leq \frac1m$. In $\|\cdot\|_1$, $\|a^{(2m)} - a^{(m)}\|_1 = \sum_{m < n
\leq 2m}\frac1n \geq m\cdot\frac{1}{2m} = \frac12$, so the truncations are not Cauchy.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates the squared tail and the two bounds for $m = 10, 100$.

```{.python .sage}
for m in (10, 100):
    t = (zeta(2) - sum(QQ(1) / n^2 for n in range(1, m + 1))).n()
    print("m = %3d: tail %.6f in [%.6f, %.6f];  |a^(2m) - a^(m)|_1 = %.4f" % (m, t, 1 / (m + 1.), 1. / m, sum(1. / n for n in range(m + 1, 2 * m + 1))))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
m =  10: tail 0.095166 in [0.090909, 0.100000];  |a^(2m) - a^(m)|_1 = 0.6688
m = 100: tail 0.009950 in [0.009901, 0.010000];  |a^(2m) - a^(m)|_1 = 0.6907
```
::::
:::

The integrals and series of the examples can be evaluated in closed form, which makes the membership criteria
quantitative. The third exercise treats a few borderline cases.

::: {#exr-fan-lp-borderline}
#### Borderline memberships

Compute $\|(1/n)\|_p^p = \zeta(p)$ for $p = 2, 4$, the integral $\int_0^1x^{-p/4}dx$ as a function of $p < 4$, and the
Gaussian norms $\|e^{-x^2/2}\|_p$ for $p = 1, 2, 3$. For which $p$ does $\log(1/x)$, continuous on $(0, 1]$, define an
element of $L^p[0, 1]$ by part (4) of @def-lp-space?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$ and $\zeta(4) = \pi^4/90$ (@exr-fs-zeta4), $\int_0^1x^{-p/4} = 4/(4 - p)$ by
@def-improper-integral (3), and the Gaussian norms follow @exm-fan-gaussian-lp: $\sqrt{2\pi}$, $\pi^{1/4}$ and
$(2\pi/3)^{1/6}$. With $x = e^{-t}$, $\int_\varepsilon^1\log(1/x)^pdx = \int_0^{\log(1/\varepsilon)}t^pe^{-t}dt$, which
converges as $\varepsilon \to 0$ to $\Gamma(p + 1) < \infty$, so $\log(1/x)$ defines an element of every $L^p[0, 1]$,
$1 \leq p < \infty$, although it is unbounded.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates the zeta values, the integrals and the Gaussian norms, and the moments of $\log(1/x)$ numerically.

```{.python .sage}
x, p = var('x p'); assume(p > 0, p < 4)
print("zeta(2), zeta(4) =", zeta(2), zeta(4))
print("int_0^1 x^(-p/4) dx =", integrate(x^(-p / 4), x, 0, 1))
forget()
for q in (1, 2, 3):
    print("|exp(-x^2/2)|_%d =" % q, (integrate(exp(-q * x^2 / 2), x, -oo, oo))^(1 / q))
for q in (1, 2, 5):
    print("int_0^1 log(1/x)^%s dx = %.6f (Gamma(%s) = %s)" % (q, numerical_integral(lambda u: log(1 / u)^q, 0, 1)[0], q + 1, gamma(q + 1)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
zeta(2), zeta(4) = 1/6*pi^2 1/90*pi^4
int_0^1 x^(-p/4) dx = -4/(p - 4)
|exp(-x^2/2)|_1 = sqrt(2)*sqrt(pi)
|exp(-x^2/2)|_2 = pi^(1/4)
|exp(-x^2/2)|_3 = (1/3)^(1/3)*(sqrt(3)*sqrt(2)*sqrt(pi))^(1/3)
int_0^1 log(1/x)^1 dx = 1.000000 (Gamma(2) = 1)
int_0^1 log(1/x)^2 dx = 2.000000 (Gamma(3) = 2)
int_0^1 log(1/x)^5 dx = 120.000000 (Gamma(6) = 120)
```
::::
:::

Distances between elements given by piecewise continuous functions are integrals, by part (3). The fourth exercise
computes the distance from the step function to the identity function.

::: {#exr-fan-lp-step-distance}
#### A distance in $L^p[0, 1]$

Compute $\|[\Theta(\cdot - \tfrac12)] - x\|$ in $L^1[0, 1]$ and in $L^2[0, 1]$, and find the constant $c$ minimising
$\|[\Theta(\cdot - \tfrac12)] - c\|$ in $L^2[0, 1]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By part (3), the distance is $\|\Theta - x\|_p$ computed with the Riemann integral. For $p = 1$: $\int_0^{1/2}x\,dx +
\int_{1/2}^1(1 - x)\,dx = \tfrac18 + \tfrac18 = \tfrac14$. For $p = 2$: $\int_0^{1/2}x^2 + \int_{1/2}^1(1 - x)^2 =
\tfrac1{24} + \tfrac1{24} = \tfrac1{12}$, so the distance is $1/\sqrt{12}$. For a constant, $\|\Theta - c\|_2^2 =
\tfrac12c^2 + \tfrac12(1 - c)^2$, minimal at $c = \tfrac12$, with value $\tfrac14$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the integrals piecewise.

```{.python .sage}
x, c = var('x c')
d1 = integrate(x, x, 0, 1/2) + integrate(1 - x, x, 1/2, 1)
d2 = integrate(x^2, x, 0, 1/2) + integrate((1 - x)^2, x, 1/2, 1)
F = c^2 / 2 + (1 - c)^2 / 2
print("L^1 distance:", d1, " L^2 distance:", sqrt(d2), " best constant:", solve(diff(F, c) == 0, c), " min:", F.subs(c=1/2))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
L^1 distance: 1/4  L^2 distance: 1/2*sqrt(1/3)  best constant: [
c == (1/2)
]  min: 1/4
```
::::
:::

The continuous approximants of part (3) can be written down explicitly for a jump. The fifth exercise does this for the
sign function on $[-1, 1]$ and computes the rate.

::: {#exr-fan-lp-pc-approx}
#### Approximating the sign function

For $f = \operatorname{sgn}x$ on $[-1, 1]$, let $g_\eta$ be as in the proof of part (3) of @def-lp-space: $f$ outside
$[-\eta, \eta]$ and linear inside. Compute $\|f - g_\eta\|_p$ and compare with the bound $(2B)^p\cdot 2r\eta$ of the
proof.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$g_\eta(x) = x/\eta$ on $[-\eta, \eta]$, so $|f - g_\eta| = 1 - |x|/\eta$ there and $\|f - g_\eta\|_p^p =
2\int_0^\eta(1 - x/\eta)^pdx = \frac{2\eta}{p + 1}$. The bound of the proof, with $B = 1$ and $r = 1$, is $2^p\cdot
2\eta$, larger by the factor $2^p(p + 1)$, because it uses only $|f - g_\eta| \leq 2B$. Both tend to $0$ like $\eta$.

## SageMath

Sage computes $\|f - g_\eta\|_p^p$ symbolically for $p = 1, 2, 3$.

```{.python .sage}
x, eta = var('x eta'); assume(eta > 0)
for p in (1, 2, 3):
    print("p = %d: |f - g|_p^p =" % p, (2 * integrate((1 - x / eta)^p, x, 0, eta)).simplify_full(), " bound:", 2^p * 2 * eta)
forget()
```

```{.text .sage-output}
p = 1: |f - g|_p^p = eta  bound: 4*eta
p = 2: |f - g|_p^p = 2/3*eta  bound: 8*eta
p = 3: |f - g|_p^p = 1/2*eta  bound: 16*eta
```
::::
:::

The finitely supported sequences are dense in $\ell^p$ for $p < \infty$ but not in $\ell^\infty$. The sixth exercise
proves the failure and finds the closure of $c_{00}$ in $\ell^\infty$.

::: {#exr-fan-ellp-dense-fails}
#### $c_{00}$ in $\ell^\infty$

Show that $\operatorname{dist}(a, c_{00}) = \limsup_n|a_n|$ in $\ell^\infty$, so that the closure of $c_{00}$ in
$\ell^\infty$ is $c_0$. Compute the distance for $a_n = (-1)^n + 1/n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For $b \in c_{00}$ with $b_n = 0$ for $n > N$, $\|a - b\|_\infty \geq \sup_{n > N}|a_n| \geq \limsup|a_n|$. Conversely
the truncation $b$ at $N$ gives $\|a - b\|_\infty = \sup_{n > N}|a_n|$, which decreases to $\limsup|a_n|$. So the
distance is $\limsup|a_n|$, which is $0$ exactly when $a \in c_0$. For $a_n = (-1)^n + 1/n$, $|a_n| \to 1$, so the
distance is $1$.

## SageMath

Sage computes $\sup_{n > N}|a_n|$ for several $N$, over a long stretch of indices.

```{.python .sage}
a = lambda n: (-1)^n + QQ(1) / n
for N in (1, 10, 100, 1000):
    print("N = %4d: sup_{n > N} |a_n| = %s" % (N, max(abs(a(n)) for n in range(N + 1, N + 2001))))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
N =    1: sup_{n > N} |a_n| = 3/2
N =   10: sup_{n > N} |a_n| = 13/12
N =  100: sup_{n > N} |a_n| = 103/102
N = 1000: sup_{n > N} |a_n| = 1003/1002
```
::::
:::

Hölder's inequality shows that products of sequences in conjugate spaces are summable. The seventh exercise applies it
to a weighted sequence and computes the bound.

::: {#exr-fan-ellp-holder-membership}
#### Products of sequences

Show that $a \in \ell^p$ and $b \in \ell^q$ with conjugate $p$, $q$ give $(a_nb_n) \in \ell^1$, and that $a \in \ell^2$
gives $(a_n/n) \in \ell^1$. For $a_n = n^{-0.6}$, which lies in $\ell^2$ but not in $\ell^1$, compute $\sum a_n/n$
and the bound $\|a\|_2\,\pi/\sqrt6$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

@thm-holder-inequality (2) gives $\sum|a_nb_n| \leq \|a\|_p\|b\|_q$. With $b_n = 1/n \in \ell^2$, $\|b\|_2 = \pi/\sqrt6$.
For $a_n = n^{-0.6}$: $\sum n^{-1.2} < \infty$ (exponent $1.2 > 1$) and $\sum n^{-0.6} = \infty$. The sum is $\sum
n^{-1.6} = \zeta(1.6) \approx 2.2858$ and the bound is $\zeta(1.2)^{1/2}\pi/\sqrt6 \approx 2.3647\cdot 1.2825 \approx
3.033$.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates both sides with zeta values.

```{.python .sage}
print("sum a_n/n = zeta(1.6) = %.4f" % zeta(1.6), "  bound = %.4f" % (sqrt(zeta(1.2)) * pi.n() / sqrt(6.)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
sum a_n/n = zeta(1.6) = 2.2858   bound = 3.0328
```
::::
:::

Integration is a continuous functional on $L^1[0, 1]$, while evaluation at a point is not. The eighth exercise extends
the integral and computes it on an element given by a singular function.

::: {#exr-fan-lp-integral-functional}
#### The integral on $L^1[0, 1]$

Show that $f \mapsto \int_0^1f$ extends from $C[0, 1]$ to a linear map $I$ on $L^1[0, 1]$ with $|I(F)| \leq \|F\|$. Show
that $I([f]) = \int_0^1f$ for $f \in PC[0, 1]$ and for $f$ as in part (4) of @def-lp-space, and compute $I([x^{-1/2}])$
and $\|[x^{-1/2}]\|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$|\int f| \leq \|f\|_1$ (@def-riemann-integral (4)), so @thm-completion (2) gives $I$. For $f \in PC[0, 1]$ and
continuous $g_n$ with $\|f - g_n\|_1 \to 0$, $|\int f - \int g_n| \leq \|f - g_n\|_1 \to 0$, so $I([f]) = \lim\int g_n
= \int f$. For $f$ continuous on $(0, 1]$ with $\int_0^1|f| < \infty$, $|\int_0^1f - \int_0^1f\chi_n| \leq
\int_0^{\delta_n}|f| \to 0$, so $I([f]) = \int_0^1f$. For $x^{-1/2}$, $f \geq 0$ and both numbers equal $\int_0^1x^{-1/2}dx
= 2$.

## SageMath

Sage computes $\int_0^1x^{-1/2}\chi_n$ for the cut-offs of the definition.

```{.python .sage}
x = var('x')
for n in (10, 100, 1000):
    d = QQ(1) / n
    val = integrate(x^(-1/2) * (x - d / 2) / (d / 2), x, d / 2, d) + integrate(x^(-1/2), x, d, 1)
    print("n = %4d: int f chi_n = %.6f" % (n, val.n()))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
n =   10: int f chi_n = 1.454868
n =  100: int f chi_n = 1.827614
n = 1000: int f chi_n = 1.945487
```
::::
:::

Rescaling the variable changes the $L^p$ norm by a power of the scale, and the right power makes it an isometry. The
ninth exercise extends the rescaling to $L^p(\mathbb{R})$ and applies it to the Gaussian, the ground state of oscillators
of different frequencies.

::: {#exr-fan-lp-dilation}
#### Dilations of $L^p(\mathbb{R})$

For $\lambda > 0$ let $(D_\lambda f)(x) = \lambda^{1/p}f(\lambda x)$ on $C_c(\mathbb{R})$. Show $\|D_\lambda f\|_p =
\|f\|_p$, that $D_\lambda$ extends to a linear isometry of $L^p(\mathbb{R})$ onto itself, and compute $D_\lambda$ of the
Gaussian $e^{-x^2/2}$ for $p = 2$: it is the ground state of the oscillator of frequency $\lambda^2\omega$ when $e^{-x^2/2}$
is that of frequency $\omega$ (with $m = \hbar = 1$, $\omega = 1$).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

With $y = \lambda x$, $\int|\lambda^{1/p}f(\lambda x)|^pdx = \int|f(y)|^pdy$. $D_\lambda$ maps $C_c$ onto $C_c$ with inverse
$D_{1/\lambda}$, so by @thm-completion (2) it extends to an isometry of $L^p(\mathbb{R})$, and $D_{1/\lambda}$ extends to
its inverse by uniqueness of extensions (both composites extend the identity). For $p = 2$, $D_\lambda e^{-x^2/2} =
\sqrt\lambda\,e^{-\lambda^2x^2/2}$, whose norm is $\pi^{1/4}$ for every $\lambda$; $e^{-\omega' x^2/2}$ is the ground
state of frequency $\omega' = \lambda^2$.

## SageMath

Sage checks that the $L^2$ norm of $\sqrt\lambda e^{-\lambda^2x^2/2}$ does not depend on $\lambda$.

```{.python .sage}
x, lam = var('x lam'); assume(lam > 0)
print("|D_lam g|_2^2 =", integrate((sqrt(lam) * exp(-lam^2 * x^2 / 2))^2, x, -oo, oo), " |g|_2^2 =", integrate(exp(-x^2), x, -oo, oo))
forget()
```

```{.text .sage-output}
|D_lam g|_2^2 = sqrt(pi)  |g|_2^2 = sqrt(pi)
```
::::
:::

Translations act continuously on $L^p(\mathbb{R})$, a fact proved on continuous functions and carried to the
completion by density. The tenth exercise combines uniform continuity with @thm-completion.

::: {#exr-fan-lp-translation}
#### Continuity of translations

For $f \in C_c(\mathbb{R})$ and $(\tau_hf)(x) = f(x - h)$, show $\|\tau_hf - f\|_p \to 0$ as $h \to 0$. Deduce that
$\tau_h$ extends to an isometry of $L^p(\mathbb{R})$ with $\|\tau_hF - F\| \to 0$ for every $F$. Compute $\|\tau_h\chi_0 -
\chi_0\|_1$ for the tent $\chi_0 = \max(0, 1 - |x|)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $f$ vanish outside $[-R, R]$. For $|h| \leq 1$, $\tau_hf - f$ vanishes outside $[-R - 1, R + 1]$, and $f$ is
uniformly continuous there (proof of @def-riemann-integral (3)), so $\|\tau_hf - f\|_\infty \to 0$ and $\|\tau_hf -
f\|_p \leq (2R + 2)^{1/p}\|\tau_hf - f\|_\infty \to 0$. Translation preserves $\|\cdot\|_p$ on $C_c$, so it extends to an
isometry (@thm-completion (2)). For $F \in L^p(\mathbb{R})$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ choose $f \in C_c$ with $\|F - f\| <
\varepsilon$; then $\|\tau_hF - F\| \leq \|\tau_h(F - f)\| + \|\tau_hf - f\| + \|f - F\| < 3\varepsilon$ for small $h$.
For the tent and $0 < h \leq 1$, split at $-1, h - 1, 0, h, 1, 1 + h$: on $[-1, h - 1]$ the difference is $1 + x$, on
$[h - 1, 0]$ and on $[h, 1]$ it has modulus $h$, on $[0, h]$ it is $|2x - h|$, and on $[1, 1 + h]$ it is $1 + h - x$. The
integrals are $\tfrac{h^2}2$, $h(1 - h)$, $h(1 - h)$, $\tfrac{h^2}{2}$, $\tfrac{h^2}{2}$, so $\|\tau_h\chi_0 - \chi_0\|_1 = 2h -
\tfrac{h^2}{2}$.

## SageMath

Sage integrates $|\chi_0(x - h) - \chi_0(x)|$ numerically for a few $h$ and compares with $2h - h^2/2$.

```{.python .sage}
chi = lambda t: max(0.0, 1 - abs(t))
for h in (0.1, 0.5, 1.0):
    v = numerical_integral(lambda t: abs(chi(t - h) - chi(t)), -2, 3, max_points=400)[0]
    print("h = %.1f: %.6f vs 2h - h^2/2 = %.6f" % (h, v, 2 * h - h^2 / 2))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
h = 0.1: 0.195000 vs 2h - h^2/2 = 0.195000
h = 0.5: 0.875000 vs 2h - h^2/2 = 0.875000
h = 1.0: 1.500000 vs 2h - h^2/2 = 1.500000
```
::::
:::
::::

### Bounded linear maps

A linear map between normed spaces is continuous exactly when it stretches vectors by a bounded factor. The figure
shows the factor for one matrix and three norms on the plane: the image of each unit ball and the smallest ball of the
same norm that contains it.

![The image of the unit ball of $\|\cdot\|_1$ (left), $\|\cdot\|_2$ (centre) and $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ (right) under
$\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, inside the ball of radius $\|\mathbf A\|$ of the same norm,
which is $3$, $1 + \sqrt2$ and $3$. The dots mark images of vectors where the norm is attained.](figures/fa2-operator-norms.svg){#fig-fa2-operator-norms width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-bounded-linear-map}
#### Bounded linear map

A linear map $T : X \to Y$ between normed spaces (@def-linear-map) is **bounded** if $\|Tx\| \leq C\|x\|$ for some
constant $C$ and all $x$; the **operator norm** $\|T\| = \sup_{\|x\| \leq 1}\|Tx\|$ is the smallest such constant. The
bounded linear maps form the space $\mathcal{B}(X, Y)$, and $\mathcal B(X) = \mathcal B(X, X)$. Then:

1. $T$ is bounded if and only if it is continuous, if and only if it is continuous at $0$; a bounded $T$ is Lipschitz,
   $\|Tx - Ty\| \leq \|T\|\,\|x - y\|$;
2. the operator norm is a norm on $\mathcal{B}(X, Y)$, which is a Banach space when $Y$ is;
3. if $T \in \mathcal B(X, Y)$ and $S \in \mathcal B(Y, Z)$, then $ST \in \mathcal B(X, Z)$ and $\|ST\| \leq \|S\|\,\|T\|$;
4. if $X$ is finite-dimensional, every linear map $T : X \to Y$ is bounded.
:::
::::

*Proof.* For $x \neq 0$, $x/\|x\|$ has norm $1$, so $\|Tx\| \leq \|T\|\,\|x\|$, and any $C$ with $\|Tx\| \leq C\|x\|$
satisfies $C \geq \|T\|$; so $\|T\|$ is the smallest constant.

(1) If $T$ is bounded, $\|Tx - Ty\| = \|T(x - y)\| \leq \|T\|\,\|x - y\|$, so $T$ is Lipschitz, hence continuous, hence
continuous at $0$. If $T$ is continuous at $0$, there is $\delta > 0$ with $\|Tx\| \leq 1$ for $\|x\| \leq \delta$; for
$x \neq 0$, $\|Tx\| = \frac{\|x\|}{\delta}\|T(\delta x/\|x\|)\| \leq \|x\|/\delta$, so $T$ is bounded with $\|T\| \leq
1/\delta$.

(2) $\|(S + T)x\| \leq \|Sx\| + \|Tx\|$ and $\|(\lambda T)x\| = |\lambda|\,\|Tx\|$ give the triangle inequality and
homogeneity, and $\|T\| = 0$ forces $Tx = 0$ for all $x$. Let $Y$ be complete and $(T_n)$ Cauchy. Since $\|T_nx -
T_mx\| \leq \|T_n - T_m\|\,\|x\|$, each $(T_nx)$ is Cauchy and converges, to $Tx$ say, and $T$ is linear by the limit
rules. Given $\varepsilon$, choose $N$ with $\|T_n - T_m\| \leq \varepsilon$ for $n, m \geq N$; for $\|x\| \leq 1$,
$\|T_nx - T_mx\| \leq \varepsilon$, and letting $m \to \infty$, $\|T_nx - Tx\| \leq \varepsilon$. So $T - T_N$ is
bounded, hence so is $T$, and $\|T_n - T\| \leq \varepsilon$ for $n \geq N$.

(3) $\|STx\| \leq \|S\|\,\|Tx\| \leq \|S\|\,\|T\|\,\|x\|$.

(4) This is @exr-fan-finite-dim-linear-continuous: in a basis, $\|Tx\| \leq (\max_k\|Te_k\|)\|x\|_1 \leq C\|x\|$ by
@thm-norm-equivalence. $\square$

These are @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.6, Exercise 3.4] and @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Thm. I.6]; @picard2020primer [Lemma
B.4.3] treats the case of inner-product norms.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Multiplication by a scalar is the simplest bounded map, and its norm is the modulus of the scalar. The first example
records it.

::: {#exm-fan-bounded-scalar}
#### Multiples of the identity

On any normed space $X \neq \{0\}$, $T = \lambda\,\mathrm{id}$ has $\|Tx\| = |\lambda|\,\|x\|$, so $\|T\| = |\lambda|$,
and the norm is attained at every $x$. In particular $\|\mathrm{id}\| = 1$ and $\|0\| = 0$, and in $\mathcal B(X)$ the
identity has norm $1$ whatever the norm of $X$.
:::

On $\mathbb{C}^n$ with the norms $\|\cdot\|_1$ and $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ the operator norm of a matrix has a closed form.
The second example derives the two formulas drawn in the figure.

::: {#exm-fan-matrix-norms}
#### Column and row sums

For a matrix $\mathbf A$ on $(\mathbb{C}^n, \|\cdot\|_1)$, $\|\mathbf A\mathbf x\|_1 \leq
\sum_j|x_j|\sum_i|A_{ij}| \leq (\max_j\sum_i|A_{ij}|)\|\mathbf x\|_1$, with equality at the basis vector of the
largest column: $\|\mathbf A\|_{1 \to 1}$ is the largest column sum. On $(\mathbb{C}^n, \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ the same
argument gives the largest row sum, attained at $x_j = (\operatorname{sgn}A_{ij})^*$ for the largest row $i$. For the
matrix of the figure both are $3$.
:::

The Euclidean operator norm of a matrix is its largest singular value. The third example computes it for the matrix of
the figure.

::: {#exm-fan-operator-norm-euclid}
#### The Euclidean norm of a matrix

$\|\mathbf A\mathbf x\|_2^2 = \mathbf x^\top\mathbf A^\top\mathbf A\mathbf x$, and by the singular value decomposition
(@thm-svd) the largest value on the unit sphere is the largest eigenvalue of $\mathbf A^\top\mathbf A$. For $\mathbf A =
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf A^\top\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{pmatrix}$ has
eigenvalues $3 \pm 2\sqrt2 = (1 \pm \sqrt2)^2$, so $\|\mathbf A\|_{2 \to 2} = 1 + \sqrt2$, the radius of the dashed
circle in the figure.
:::

Multiplication by a fixed function is the simplest operator on a function space, and its norm is the size of the
multiplier. The fourth example computes it on $L^p[a, b]$, and the same for diagonal operators on $\ell^p$
@arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.11].

::: {#exm-fan-multiplication-lp}
#### Multiplication and diagonal operators

For $g \in C[a, b]$, $M_gf = gf$ satisfies $\|gf\|_p \leq \|g\|_\infty\|f\|_p$ on $C[a, b]$, so it extends to $L^p[a,
b]$ with $\|M_g\| \leq \|g\|_\infty$ (@thm-completion (2)). The bound is sharp: if $|g(x_0)| = \|g\|_\infty$, the tents
$h_n$ at $x_0$ have $\|gh_n\|_p/\|h_n\|_p \to |g(x_0)|$, because $|g| \geq |g(x_0)| - \varepsilon$ on their supports for
large $n$. So $\|M_g\| = \|g\|_\infty$. In the same way a bounded sequence $d$ defines $(Da)_n = d_na_n$ on $\ell^p$, $1
\leq p \leq \infty$, with $\|D\| = \sup_n|d_n|$: the bound is clear, and $\|D\delta^{(n)}\|_p = |d_n|$.
:::

An integral operator with a bounded kernel is bounded on $C[0, 1]$. The fifth example computes the norm of the Volterra
operator, which integrates a function from $0$.

::: {#exm-fan-volterra-norm}
#### The Volterra operator on $C[0, 1\rbrack$

$(Vf)(x) = \int_0^xf(t)\,dt$ is continuous in $x$ and satisfies $|Vf(x)| \leq x\|f\|_\infty$, so $\|V\| \leq 1$ on
$(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_\infty)$, with equality at $f = 1$, where $Vf(x) = x$. Its powers are $(V^nf)(x) = \int_0^x\frac{(x
- t)^{n - 1}}{(n - 1)!}f(t)\,dt$, with $\|V^n\| = \frac1{n!}$, attained again at $f = 1$; so $\|V^n\| < \|V\|^n$ for $n
\geq 2$.
:::

The shifts of sequences are the basic operators of infinite dimension, and they show that a one-sided inverse need not
be an inverse. The sixth example computes their norms on $\ell^p$.

::: {#exm-fan-shift-operators}
#### Shifts

On $\ell^p$, the right shift $S(a_1, a_2, \dots) = (0, a_1, a_2, \dots)$ preserves norms, so $\|S\| = 1$, and the left
shift $L(a_1, a_2, \dots) = (a_2, a_3, \dots)$ has $\|La\|_p \leq \|a\|_p$, with equality when $a_1 = 0$, so $\|L\| =
1$. Then $LS = \mathrm{id}$ but $SL\delta^{(1)} = 0$: $S$ is injective and not onto, $L$ onto and not injective, which
cannot happen for square matrices.
:::

The Pauli matrices act on spin states, and their operator norm in $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the largest modulus of an eigenvalue.
The seventh example computes it for spin operators.

::: {#exm-fan-pauli-operator-norm}
#### Spin operators

$\sigma_a$ is Hermitian with eigenvalues $\pm1$, and $\sigma_a^\dagger\sigma_a = \mathbf I_2$, so $\|\sigma_a\mathbf
z\|_2 = \|\mathbf z\|_2$ and $\|\sigma_a\|_{2 \to 2} = 1$. For a unit vector $\mathbf n$, $(\mathbf
n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)^2 = \mathbf I_2$ gives $\|\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma\|_{2 \to 2} = 1$, so the spin
component $\tfrac12\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$ along any axis has norm $\tfrac12$, the largest value it can be
measured to have. The Frobenius norm of the same matrix is $\sqrt2/2$, a different number.
:::

The flow of the oscillator preserves energy, so it is an isometry in the energy norm, while its Euclidean norm depends
on the frequency. The eighth example compares the two norms of the flow of @exm-fan-oscillator-propagator.

::: {#exm-fan-oscillator-flow-norm}
#### Norms of the oscillator flow

$e^{t\mathbf A}$ preserves $H$, so $\|e^{t\mathbf A}\|_{E \to E} = 1$ in the energy norm of @exm-fan-oscillator-energy-norm.
In the Euclidean norm, for $\omega = 2$ and $t = \pi/4$, $e^{t\mathbf A} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \tfrac12 \\ -2 &
0\end{pmatrix}$, whose largest singular value is $2$: the flow stretches some phase-space vectors by $2$, although it
conserves the energy. The two norms are equivalent (@exm-fan-oscillator-equivalence), so the Euclidean norm of the
flow stays bounded in $t$.
:::

Differentiation is the standard unbounded operator of analysis. The ninth example records why it is not bounded on
the continuous functions with the supremum norm.

::: {#exm-fan-derivative-unbounded}
#### Differentiation is unbounded

On the polynomials with $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ on $[0, 1]$, $D = d/dx$ is linear but $\|Dx^n\|_\infty = n$ while
$\|x^n\|_\infty = 1$, so $D$ is not bounded, and by part (1) not continuous: $x^n/n \to 0$ but $D(x^n/n) = x^{n - 1}$
does not tend to $0$. With the norm of $C^1$ on the domain it is bounded with norm at most $1$ (@exr-fan-ck-derivative).
:::

The supremum in the operator norm need not be attained in infinite dimension, even for a diagonal operator. The tenth
example gives one.

::: {#exm-fan-norm-not-attained}
#### A norm that is not attained

On $\ell^2$, $D = \operatorname{diag}(1 - \tfrac1n)$ has $\|D\| = \sup_n(1 - \tfrac1n) = 1$ by @exm-fan-multiplication-lp.
For $a \neq 0$, $\|Da\|_2^2 = \sum_n(1 - \tfrac1n)^2|a_n|^2 < \sum_n|a_n|^2$, so $\|Da\|_2 < \|a\|_2$ for every
non-zero $a$: the norm is a supremum, not a maximum. In finite dimensions it is always attained, because the unit sphere
is compact (@thm-norm-equivalence).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A combination of a point value and an integral is bounded for the supremum norm, and its norm is attained at a
constant. The first exercise computes it and shows that the same map is not continuous for the integral norm.

::: {#exr-fan-bounded-continuous}
#### A value plus an integral

Show that $T(f) = f(0) + \int_0^1f$ on $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ is bounded with $\|T\| = 2$. Show that on $(C[0,
1], \|\cdot\|_1)$ it is not continuous at $0$, using $f_n = (1 - x)^n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$|T(f)| \leq |f(0)| + \int|f| \leq 2\|f\|_\infty$, and $T(1) = 2$ with $\|1\|_\infty = 1$, so $\|T\| = 2$. For $f_n$,
$\|f_n\|_1 = \frac1{n + 1} \to 0$ while $T(f_n) = 1 + \frac1{n + 1} \to 1 \neq 0$, so $T$ is not continuous at $0$ for
$\|\cdot\|_1$, hence unbounded there by @def-bounded-linear-map (1).

## SageMath

Sage evaluates $T(f_n)$ and $\|f_n\|_1$.

```{.python .sage}
x = var('x')
for n in (1, 10, 100):
    f = (1 - x)^n
    print("n = %3d: T(f_n) = %s, |f_n|_1 = %s" % (n, f.subs(x=0) + integrate(f, x, 0, 1), integrate(f, x, 0, 1)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
n =   1: T(f_n) = 3/2, |f_n|_1 = 1/2
n =  10: T(f_n) = 12/11, |f_n|_1 = 1/11
n = 100: T(f_n) = 102/101, |f_n|_1 = 1/101
```
::::
:::

If a Cauchy sequence of operators converges pointwise, the pointwise limit is also its norm limit. The second exercise
proves this @gasinski2014exercises [Problem 5.28], a refinement of part (2).

::: {#exr-fan-bounded-maps-complete}
#### Norm limits and pointwise limits

Let $Y$ be a Banach space, $(T_n)$ Cauchy in $\mathcal{B}(X, Y)$, and $T$ linear with $T_nx \to Tx$ for every $x$. Show
$\|T_n - T\| \to 0$. Check it on $T_n = \sum_{k \leq n}\mathbf A^k$ with $\mathbf A = \tfrac12\sigma_1$ of
@exr-fan-neumann-matrix.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By @def-bounded-linear-map (2), $T_n \to T'$ in operator norm for some $T'$, so $T_nx \to T'x$ for every $x$; limits in
$Y$ are unique, so $T' = T$ and $\|T_n - T\| \to 0$. For the matrices, $T_n \to (\mathbf I_2 - \mathbf A)^{-1}$
entrywise, and the operator norm of the difference is $\|\mathbf A^{n + 1}(\mathbf I_2 - \mathbf A)^{-1}\| = 2^{-n -
1}\|(\mathbf I_2 - \mathbf A)^{-1}\|_{2 \to 2} = 2^{-n - 1}\cdot 2 = 2^{-n}$, because $\mathbf A^{n + 1}$ is $2^{-n -
1}$ times $\mathbf I_2$ or $\sigma_1$, which preserve $\|\cdot\|_2$, and $(\mathbf I_2 - \mathbf A)^{-1}$ has
eigenvalues $2$ and $\tfrac23$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the Euclidean operator norms of $(\mathbf I_2 - \mathbf A)^{-1} - T_n$.

```{.python .sage}
A = matrix(QQ, [[0, 1], [1, 0]]) / 2
R = (1 - A).inverse()
for n in (1, 5, 10):
    Tn = sum(A^k for k in range(n + 1))
    print("n = %2d: |R - T_n| = %s, 2^(-n) = %s" % (n, max(abs(e) for e in (R - Tn).eigenvalues()), QQ(1) / 2^n))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
n =  1: |R - T_n| = 1/2, 2^(-n) = 1/2
n =  5: |R - T_n| = 1/32, 2^(-n) = 1/32
n = 10: |R - T_n| = 1/1024, 2^(-n) = 1/1024
```
::::
:::

The Euclidean operator norm of a small matrix can be computed exactly from its singular values. The third exercise does
so for the matrix of the figure and compares the three norms.

::: {#exr-fan-operator-norms-matrix}
#### Three norms of one matrix

For $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, compute $\|\mathbf A^{-1}\|_{2 \to 2}$, the norms
$\|\mathbf A\|_{1 \to 1}$ and $\|\mathbf A\|_{\infty \to \infty}$ of the figure, and show $\|\mathbf A\|_{2 \to 2}^2
\leq \|\mathbf A\|_{1 \to 1}\|\mathbf A\|_{\infty \to \infty}$ here.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By @exm-fan-operator-norm-euclid, $\|\mathbf A\|_{2 \to 2} = 1 + \sqrt2$. $\mathbf A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0
& 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $(\mathbf A^{-1})^\top\mathbf A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{pmatrix}$ has the same
eigenvalues $3 \pm 2\sqrt2$, so $\|\mathbf A^{-1}\|_{2 \to 2} = 1 + \sqrt2$ too. The column sums of $\mathbf A$ are $1$
and $3$, the row sums $3$ and $1$, so the other two norms are $3$. Then $(1 + \sqrt2)^2 = 3 + 2\sqrt2 \approx 5.83 \leq
9$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the three norms and the norm of the inverse.

```{.python .sage}
A = matrix(QQ, [[1, 2], [0, 1]])
n2 = sqrt(max((A.transpose() * A).eigenvalues()))
print("|A|_2 =", n2, "=", n2.n(digits=6))
print("|A|_1 =", max(sum(abs(A[i, j]) for i in range(2)) for j in range(2)), " |A|_inf =", max(sum(abs(A[i, j]) for j in range(2)) for i in range(2)))
Ai = A.inverse()
print("|A^-1|_2 =", sqrt(max((Ai.transpose() * Ai).eigenvalues())).n(digits=6))
print("|A|_2^2 <= 9:", bool(n2^2 <= 9), (n2^2).n(digits=5))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
|A|_2 = 2.414213562373095? = 2.41421
|A|_1 = 3  |A|_inf = 3
|A^-1|_2 = 2.41421
|A|_2^2 <= 9: True 5.8284
```
::::
:::

Completeness of the bounded maps and the series criterion together give a quick proof that operators close to the
identity are invertible. The fourth exercise carries it out on $\ell^p$.

::: {#exr-fan-banach-identity-perturbation}
#### Operators near the identity

Let $X$ be a Banach space and $T \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ with $\|T\| < 1$. Show that $\sum_kT^k$ converges in
$\mathcal{B}(X)$ to an inverse of $1 - T$, with $\|(1 - T)^{-1}\| \leq 1/(1 - \|T\|)$. Apply this on $\ell^p$ to $T =
\tfrac12S$, with $S$ the right shift, and compute $(1 - T)^{-1}\delta^{(1)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\|T^k\| \leq \|T\|^k$ by part (3), so $\sum\|T^k\| \leq 1/(1 - \|T\|)$ and the series converges in the Banach space
$\mathcal{B}(X)$ (parts (2) and @thm-absolute-series), with the stated bound. With $R_N = \sum_{k \leq N}T^k$, $(1 -
T)R_N = R_N(1 - T) = 1 - T^{N + 1} \to 1$ in norm, and multiplication is continuous by part (3), so the sum $R$
satisfies $(1 - T)R = R(1 - T) = 1$. For $T = \tfrac12S$, $\|T\| = \tfrac12$ on every $\ell^p$, and $(1 -
T)^{-1}\delta^{(1)} = \sum_k2^{-k}S^k\delta^{(1)} = (1, \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \dots)$, of $\ell^p$ norm $(1 - 2^{-p})^{-1/p}
\leq 2$.

## SageMath

Check on truncations of length $30$: Sage applies $1 - T$ to the computed vector and compares the norms with the bound
$2$.

```{.python .sage}
n = 30
v = vector(QQ, [QQ(1) / 2^k for k in range(n)])
w = vector(QQ, [v[0]] + [v[k] - v[k - 1] / 2 for k in range(1, n)])
print("(1 - T) v =", w[:5], "... all further entries zero:", all(t == 0 for t in w[1:]))
for p in (1, 2, 4):
    print("p = %d: |v|_p = %.6f, (1 - 2^-p)^(-1/p) = %.6f" % (p, v.change_ring(RDF).norm(p), (1 - 2.^-p)^(-1 / p)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
(1 - T) v = (1, 0, 0, 0, 0) ... all further entries zero: True
p = 1: |v|_p = 2.000000, (1 - 2^-p)^(-1/p) = 2.000000
p = 2: |v|_p = 1.154701, (1 - 2^-p)^(-1/p) = 1.154701
p = 4: |v|_p = 1.016265, (1 - 2^-p)^(-1/p) = 1.016265
```
::::
:::

The shift and the diagonal operators act on all the $\ell^p$ with the same norm. The fifth exercise computes norms of
the shift and of a diagonal operator, and of their finite truncations.

::: {#exr-fan-ellp-operators}
#### Operators on all the $\ell^p$

Show that the right shift $S$ and the diagonal operator $D = \operatorname{diag}(1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots)$ have
$\|S\| = \|D\| = 1$ on every $\ell^p$, that $\|D^k\| = 1$, and that $\|D - \tfrac12\| = \tfrac12$. Compute the $1 \to 1$
and $\infty \to \infty$ norms of the $6 \times 6$ truncation of $S + D$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$S$ preserves every $\ell^p$ norm, so $\|S\| = 1$. For a diagonal operator $\|D\| = \sup_n|d_n|$ on every $\ell^p$
(@exm-fan-multiplication-lp), giving $1$ for $D$ and $D^k = \operatorname{diag}(n^{-k})$, and $\sup_n|\tfrac1n -
\tfrac12| = \tfrac12$ for $D - \tfrac12$ (at $n = 1$, and as $n \to \infty$). The truncation of $S + D$ has $1/n$ on the
diagonal and $1$ below it. Its largest column sum is $1 + 1 = 2$ (first column) and its largest row sum is $1 +
\tfrac12 = \tfrac32$ (second row), so by @exm-fan-matrix-norms the two norms are $2$ and $\tfrac32$; the Euclidean norm
is at most $\sqrt{2\cdot\tfrac32} = \sqrt3$, as in @exr-fan-operator-norms-matrix.

## SageMath

Sage builds the truncation and computes its three norms.

```{.python .sage}
n = 6
M = matrix(QQ, n, n, lambda i, j: (QQ(1) / (i + 1) if i == j else 0) + (1 if i == j + 1 else 0))
print("column sums max:", max(sum(abs(M[i, j]) for i in range(n)) for j in range(n)), " row sums max:", max(sum(abs(M[i, j]) for j in range(n)) for i in range(n)))
print("Euclidean norm: %.5f <= sqrt(3) = %.5f" % (M.change_ring(RDF).norm(2), sqrt(3.)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
column sums max: 2  row sums max: 3/2
Euclidean norm: 1.50712 <= sqrt(3) = 1.73205
```
::::
:::

The operator norm is a supremum over the unit sphere, which need not be attained. The sixth exercise computes the norm
of the Volterra operator on the integral norm, where it is not attained.

::: {#exr-fan-volterra-l1}
#### The Volterra operator for $\|\cdot\|_1$

On $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_1)$ show $\|Vf\|_1 \leq \int_0^1(1 - t)|f(t)|\,dt$, so $\|V\| \leq 1$, that $\|Vf\|_1 < \|f\|_1$
for every $f \neq 0$, and that $\|V\| = 1$, using $f_n = (1 - x)^n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\|Vf\|_1 = \int_0^1|\int_0^xf| \,dx \leq \int_0^1\int_0^x|f(t)|\,dt\,dx = \int_0^1(1 - t)|f(t)|\,dt$, , where the last
equality is an integration by parts with $F(x) = \int_0^x|f|$: $\int_0^1F = [(x - 1)F(x)]_0^1 + \int_0^1(1 - x)F'(x)\,dx$,
and the bracket vanishes. Since $1 - t < 1$ on $(0, 1]$ and $|f| > 0$ on some interval if $f \neq 0$, $\int(1 -
t)|f| < \int|f|$. For $f_n = (1 - x)^n \geq 0$, $Vf_n = \frac{1 - (1 - x)^{n + 1}}{n + 1}$ and $\|Vf_n\|_1 = \frac{1}{n
+ 1}(1 - \frac1{n + 2})$, while $\|f_n\|_1 = \frac1{n + 1}$; the ratio $\frac{n + 1}{n + 2} \to 1$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the ratios $\|Vf_n\|_1/\|f_n\|_1$.

```{.python .sage}
x, t = var('x t')
for n in (1, 10, 100):
    f = (1 - t)^n
    Vf = integrate(f, t, 0, x)
    print("n = %3d: ratio = %s" % (n, integrate(Vf, x, 0, 1) / integrate(f, t, 0, 1)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
n =   1: ratio = 2/3
n =  10: ratio = 11/12
n = 100: ratio = 101/102
```
::::
:::

The kernel of a bounded map is closed, and for a scalar-valued linear map the converse holds. The seventh exercise
proves both @gasinski2014exercises [Problem 5.31].

::: {#exr-fan-kernel-closed}
#### Closed kernels

Show that $\ker T$ is closed for $T \in \mathcal{B}(X, Y)$. For a non-zero linear $\varphi : X \to \mathbb{C}$ with
closed kernel, pick $x_0$ with $\varphi(x_0) = 1$, let $d = \operatorname{dist}(x_0, \ker\varphi) > 0$, and show $|\varphi(x)|
\leq \|x\|/d$. Compute $d$ for $\varphi(\mathbf x) = x_1 + x_2$ on $(\mathbb{R}^2, \|\cdot\|_2)$ with $\mathbf x_0 =
\mathbf e_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\ker T = T^{-1}(\{0\})$ is the preimage of a closed set under a continuous map. For $\varphi$: $d > 0$ because the kernel
is closed and $x_0 \notin \ker\varphi$. For $\varphi(x) \neq 0$, $y = x_0 - x/\varphi(x) \in \ker\varphi$, so $\|x\|/|\varphi(x)| =
\|x_0 - y\| \geq d$, that is $|\varphi(x)| \leq \|x\|/d$; for $\varphi(x) = 0$ there is nothing to prove. For $\varphi = x_1 + x_2$, the kernel is the line $x_2 = -x_1$, and the distance from $\mathbf e_1$ to it is
$\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$; indeed $|x_1 + x_2| \leq \sqrt2\|\mathbf x\|_2$ is Cauchy-Schwarz, with the sharp constant $1/d =
\sqrt2$.

## SageMath

Sage minimises $\|\mathbf e_1 - t(1, -1)\|_2$ over $t$.

```{.python .sage}
t = var('t')
d2 = (1 - t)^2 + t^2
tm = solve(diff(d2, t) == 0, t)[0].rhs()
print("closest t:", tm, " d =", sqrt(d2.subs(t=tm)), " 1/d =", 1 / sqrt(d2.subs(t=tm)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
closest t: 1/2  d = sqrt(1/2)  1/d = 2*sqrt(1/2)
```
::::
:::

The norm of a multiplication operator is the maximum of the multiplier, approached by functions concentrated near the
maximum. The eighth exercise computes the approach for $g = x(1 - x)$ on $L^2[0, 1]$.

::: {#exr-fan-multiplication-sharp}
#### Approaching the norm of $M_g$

For $g(x) = x(1 - x)$ on $L^2[0, 1]$, $\|M_g\| = \tfrac14$. Compute $\|gh_n\|_2/\|h_n\|_2$ for the tents $h_n$ of height
$1$ at $\tfrac12$ supported in $[\tfrac12 - \tfrac1n, \tfrac12 + \tfrac1n]$, and show that the ratio tends to $\tfrac14$
from below.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By @exm-fan-multiplication-lp, $\|M_g\| = \max g = \tfrac14$. On the support of $h_n$, $\tfrac14 - \tfrac1{n^2} \leq
g \leq \tfrac14$, since $g = \tfrac14 - (x - \tfrac12)^2$. Hence $(\tfrac14 - \tfrac1{n^2})\|h_n\|_2 \leq \|gh_n\|_2 <
\tfrac14\|h_n\|_2$, and the ratio tends to $\tfrac14$ from below; it is never equal to $\tfrac14$, because $g <
\tfrac14$ away from $\tfrac12$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the ratio exactly for $n = 2, 10, 100$.

```{.python .sage}
x = var('x')
g = x * (1 - x)
for n in (2, 10, 100):
    h = 1 - n * abs(x - 1/2)
    num = 2 * integrate((g * (1 - n * (x - 1/2)))^2, x, 1/2, 1/2 + 1 / n)
    den = 2 * integrate((1 - n * (x - 1/2))^2, x, 1/2, 1/2 + 1 / n)
    print("n = %3d: ratio = %.6f" % (n, sqrt(num / den).n()))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
n =   2: ratio = 0.227565
n =  10: ratio = 0.249004
n = 100: ratio = 0.249990
```
::::
:::

The submultiplicative inequality $\|ST\| \leq \|S\|\,\|T\|$ can be strict, even with $ST = 0$. The ninth exercise gives
two instances with matrices.

::: {#exr-fan-composition-norm}
#### When $\|ST\| < \|S\|\,\|T\|$

Let $\mathbf P_1$, $\mathbf P_2$ be the orthogonal projections of $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto the two axes, and $\mathbf N =
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. Compute $\|\mathbf P_1\mathbf P_2\|$, $\|\mathbf N^2\|$ and the
products of the norms in $\|\cdot\|_{2 \to 2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathbf P_1 = \operatorname{diag}(1, 0)$ and $\mathbf P_2 = \operatorname{diag}(0, 1)$ have norm $1$ (they do not
increase lengths, and fix a unit vector), and $\mathbf P_1\mathbf P_2 = 0$. $\mathbf N\mathbf x = (x_2, 0)$ has
$\|\mathbf N\mathbf x\|_2 = |x_2| \leq \|\mathbf x\|_2$, with equality at $\mathbf e_2$, so $\|\mathbf N\| = 1$, while
$\mathbf N^2 = 0$. In both cases $0 = \|ST\| < \|S\|\,\|T\| = 1$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the norms.

```{.python .sage}
P1 = matrix(RDF, [[1, 0], [0, 0]]); P2 = matrix(RDF, [[0, 0], [0, 1]]); N = matrix(RDF, [[0, 1], [0, 0]])
print("|P1| = %s, |P2| = %s, |P1 P2| = %s" % (P1.norm(2), P2.norm(2), (P1 * P2).norm(2)))
print("|N| = %s, |N^2| = %s" % (N.norm(2), (N * N).norm(2)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
|P1| = 1.0, |P2| = 1.0, |P1 P2| = 0.0
|N| = 1.0, |N^2| = 0.0
```
::::
:::

Bessel's inequality says that the Fourier coefficient map is bounded from the mean-square norm to the sequence norm,
so it extends to the completion. The tenth exercise combines @def-fourier-coefficient with @thm-completion.

::: {#exr-fan-fourier-map-extension}
#### The Fourier coefficient map

Let $X$ be $C(S^1)$ with the mean-square norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ of @def-fourier-coefficient, and $\mathcal F f =
(c_n)_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$. Show that $\mathcal F : X \to \ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ is bounded with norm $1$, that it extends to
the completion $\tilde X$ with the same norm, and that the extension is isometric, using Parseval's identity
(@thm-parseval). Compute $\mathcal F$ of the element defined by the square wave in @exm-fan-completion-square-wave.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$, the square-summable sequences indexed by $\mathbb{Z}$, is a Banach space by the proof of
@def-lp-space (1). By Parseval's identity $\sum|c_n|^2 = \lVert f\rVert^2$ for continuous $f$, so $\mathcal F$ is
isometric, with norm $1$. By @thm-completion (2) it extends to an isometry of $\tilde X$. The square-wave element $\xi$
is the limit of $S_Nf$, whose coefficients are $c_n$ for $|n| \leq N$ and $0$ beyond; their images converge in
$\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ to the coefficient sequence $c_n = \frac{2}{i\pi n}$ ($n$ odd), $0$ otherwise. So $\mathcal F\xi$ is
that sequence, of norm $1 = \|\xi\|$.

## SageMath

Sage sums $|c_n|^2$ for the square wave up to $|n| \leq 2001$.

```{.python .sage}
print("sum |c_n|^2 over |n| <= 2001: %.6f" % (2 * sum(4 / (pi.n()^2 * n^2) for n in range(1, 2002, 2))))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
sum |c_n|^2 over |n| <= 2001: 0.999798
```
::::
:::
::::

### Dual spaces

The continuous linear functionals on a normed space form its dual, the space of all bounded ways of measuring a vector
by a number. The figure shows, for the norms $\|\cdot\|_3$ and $\|\cdot\|_{3/2}$ of the plane, the supporting line that
realises the norm of a vector as the value of a dual vector of norm one.

![The unit balls of $\|\cdot\|_3$ and of $\|\cdot\|_{3/2}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$, with $\mathbf x = (1, 2)/\|(1, 2)\|_3$ and
$\mathbf y = (1, 4)/\|(1, 4)\|_{3/2}$. The line $\varphi = 1$ of $\varphi(\mathbf z) = y_1z_1 + y_2z_2$ touches the
first ball at $\mathbf x$, so that $\|\varphi\| = 1 = \|\mathbf y\|_{3/2}$.](figures/fa2-dual-norms.svg){#fig-fa2-dual-norms width=60%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-continuous-dual}
#### Continuous dual space

The **dual space** of a normed space $X$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ is $X^* = \mathcal{B}(X,
\mathbb{K})$, the space of continuous linear functionals (@def-linear-functional) with the norm $\|\varphi\| =
\sup_{\|x\| \leq 1}|\varphi(x)|$. The dual of $X^*$ is the **bidual** $X^{**}$. Then:

1. $X^*$ is a Banach space, even when $X$ is not;
2. if $\dim X = n$, every linear functional is continuous, so $X^*$ is the algebraic dual of @def-dual-space, of
   dimension $n$;
3. on $(c_{00}, \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ the linear functional $\varphi(a) = \sum_nna_n$ is not continuous, so in infinite
   dimension $X^*$ can be a proper subspace of the algebraic dual;
4. each $x \in X$ defines $Jx \in X^{**}$ by $(Jx)(\varphi) = \varphi(x)$, and $J$ is linear with $\|Jx\| \leq \|x\|$;
5. if $D \subseteq X$ is a dense subspace and $\varphi : D \to \mathbb{K}$ is linear with $|\varphi(x)| \leq C\|x\|$,
   then $\varphi$ has a unique extension $\tilde\varphi \in X^*$, and $\|\tilde\varphi\| = \sup_{x \in D, \|x\| \leq
   1}|\varphi(x)|$.
:::
::::

*Proof.* (1) $\mathbb{K}$ is complete, so @def-bounded-linear-map (2) applies. (2) This is @def-bounded-linear-map (4).
(3) $\varphi$ is linear and finite on finitely supported sequences, but $\varphi(\delta^{(n)}) = n$ with
$\|\delta^{(n)}\|_\infty = 1$. (4) Linearity of $J$ and of each $Jx$ is clear, and $|(Jx)(\varphi)| = |\varphi(x)|
\leq \|\varphi\|\,\|x\|$. (5) For $x \in X$ choose $x_n \in D$ with $x_n \to x$. Then $|\varphi(x_n) - \varphi(x_m)|
\leq C\|x_n - x_m\|$, so $\varphi(x_n)$ converges; interlacing two such sequences shows that the limit does not depend on
the sequence, and it equals $\varphi(x)$ for $x \in D$. Define $\tilde\varphi(x)$ as the limit; it is linear by the limit
rules, and $|\tilde\varphi(x)| = \lim|\varphi(x_n)| \leq C'\lim\|x_n\| = C'\|x\|$ with $C' = \sup_{x \in D, \|x\| \leq
1}|\varphi(x)|$. Two continuous extensions agree on $D$, hence on its closure $X$. $\square$

The dual of a normed space is that of @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 3.2]; part (3) is @arcozzi2025 [Prop. 3.2] in its explicit
form, and part (5) is the B.L.T. theorem of @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Thm. I.7] for functionals.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The coordinates of a vector are the first functionals one meets. The first example computes their norms in the $p$-norms
of $\mathbb{C}^n$.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-coordinate}
#### Coordinate functionals

On $\mathbb{C}^n$ the coordinate functional $\varepsilon^k(\mathbf x) = x_k$ satisfies $|x_k| \leq \|\mathbf x\|_p$ for
every $p$, with equality at $\mathbf e_k$, so $\|\varepsilon^k\| = 1$ for all $1 \leq p \leq \infty$. The functionals
$\varepsilon^1, \dots, \varepsilon^n$ are the dual basis of the standard basis (@def-dual-basis), and by part (2) they
span $(\mathbb{C}^n)^*$.
:::

The dual of $\mathbb{C}^n$ with a $p$-norm is $\mathbb{C}^n$ with the conjugate norm, as the figure shows for $p = 3$.
The second example derives it from Hölder's inequality.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-cn}
#### Duals of $(\mathbb{C}^n, \|\cdot\|_p)$

Every functional on $\mathbb{C}^n$ is $\varphi_{\mathbf y}(\mathbf x) = \sum_ky_kx_k$. By Hölder,
$|\varphi_{\mathbf y}(\mathbf x)| \leq \|\mathbf y\|_q\|\mathbf x\|_p$, and the extremal vector of
@exr-fan-holder-equality (with the roles of $p$ and $q$ exchanged) gives equality, so $\|\varphi_{\mathbf y}\| =
\|\mathbf y\|_q$ with $\tfrac1p + \tfrac1q = 1$. The dual of $\|\cdot\|_1$ is $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ and conversely, and
$\|\cdot\|_2$ is its own dual.
:::

Evaluating a continuous function at a point is a functional on $C(K)$, and integrating against a continuous weight is
another. The third example computes the norms of these functionals.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-ck}
#### Point evaluations and integrals

On $C[0, 1]$, $\delta_a(f) = f(a)$ has $|\delta_a(f)| \leq \|f\|_\infty$ with equality at $f = 1$, so $\|\delta_a\| =
1$, and $\|\delta_a - \delta_b\| = 2$ for $a \neq b$: the bound $2$ is attained at a continuous $f$ with $f(a) = 1$,
$f(b) = -1$ and $|f| \leq 1$. The functional $\varphi_g(f) = \int_0^1gf$ with $g \in C[0, 1]$ has norm $\|g\|_1$: the
bound is clear, and $f_\varepsilon = g^*/(|g| + \varepsilon)$ has $|f_\varepsilon| \leq 1$ and $\varphi_g(f_\varepsilon)
= \int\frac{|g|^2}{|g| + \varepsilon} \geq \|g\|_1 - \varepsilon$.
:::

A bounded sequence defines a functional on the absolutely summable sequences by summing against it. The fourth example
computes its norm.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-ell1-elements}
#### Functionals on $\ell^1$ from bounded sequences

For $y \in \ell^\infty$, $\varphi_y(a) = \sum_ny_na_n$ converges absolutely on $\ell^1$ with $|\varphi_y(a)| \leq
\|y\|_\infty\|a\|_1$, and $|\varphi_y(\delta^{(n)})| = |y_n|$, so $\|\varphi_y\| = \|y\|_\infty$. For $y = (1, -1, 1,
\dots)$, $\varphi_y(a)$ is the alternating sum, of norm $1$; for $y_n = 1 - \tfrac1n$ the norm $1$ is not attained by any
$a$.
:::

The integral is a functional of norm one on the continuous functions with either norm, and by part (5) it extends from
there. The fifth example records the extension to $L^1[0, 1]$.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-integral-functional}
#### The integral

$I(f) = \int_0^1f$ satisfies $|I(f)| \leq \|f\|_1 \leq \|f\|_\infty$, with equality at $f = 1$, so $\|I\| = 1$ on
$(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ and on $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_1)$. By part (5) it extends to $L^1[0, 1]$, in which $C[0, 1]$
is dense (@def-lp-space (2)), with norm $1$, and the extension is the integral of piecewise continuous and of
integrable singular functions (@exr-fan-lp-integral-functional).
:::

A state of a quantum system assigns expectation values to observables, linearly, and the expectations are bounded by the
size of the observable. The sixth example computes the norm of an expectation functional on $2 \times 2$ matrices.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-expectation}
#### Expectation values

Give the complex $2 \times 2$ matrices the operator norm $\|\mathbf M\|_{2 \to 2}$, and let $\boldsymbol\rho = \sum_kp_k\mathbf z_k\mathbf
z_k^\dagger$ be a mixture of pure states, with unit vectors $\mathbf z_k$ and weights $p_k \geq 0$, $\sum p_k = 1$. Then $\varphi_{\boldsymbol\rho}(\mathbf
M) = \operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol\rho\mathbf M) = \sum_kp_k\mathbf z_k^\dagger\mathbf M\mathbf z_k$ has
$|\varphi_{\boldsymbol\rho}(\mathbf M)| \leq \sum_kp_k\|\mathbf z_k\|_2\|\mathbf M\mathbf z_k\|_2 \leq \|\mathbf M\|$ by Cauchy-Schwarz, and $\varphi_{\boldsymbol\rho}(\mathbf I_2) = 1$; so
$\|\varphi_{\boldsymbol\rho}\| = 1$ for every state.
:::

On the circle each Fourier coefficient is a functional on $C(S^1)$. The seventh example computes its norm.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-fourier-coefficient}
#### Fourier coefficients as functionals

$c_n(f) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(x)e^{-inx}dx$ satisfies $|c_n(f)| \leq \|f\|_\infty$, with equality at $f =
e^{inx}$, so $\|c_n\| = 1$ in $C(S^1)^*$. By @exm-fan-dual-ck with the weight $g = e^{-inx}/2\pi$, the same functional on
$C(S^1)$ with the norm $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|$ also has norm $1$.
:::

A functional may need a stronger norm on its space to be continuous. The eighth example evaluates a derivative, which
is continuous on $C^1[0, 1]$ but not on $C[0, 1]$.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-derivative-eval}
#### Evaluating a derivative

$\varphi(f) = f'(\tfrac12)$ satisfies $|\varphi(f)| \leq \|f'\|_\infty \leq \|f\|_{C^1}$, so $\varphi \in C^1[0,
1]^*$ with $\|\varphi\| \leq 1$; $f(x) = \sin(n(x - \tfrac12))/n$ gives $\varphi(f) = 1$ and $\|f\|_{C^1} \leq 1 +
\tfrac1n$, so $\|\varphi\| = 1$. On the $C^1$ functions with $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ the same $f$ have norm $\leq \tfrac1n$
and $\varphi(f) = 1$, so $\varphi$ is not continuous there.
:::

On an infinite-dimensional space a linear functional need not be continuous, as part (3) says. The ninth example
examines the functional of part (3) and shows that its kernel is dense @waterstraat2016 [Lemma 1.1.10].

::: {#exm-fan-unbounded-functional}
#### A discontinuous linear functional

On $(c_{00}, \|\cdot\|_\infty)$, $\varphi(a) = \sum_nna_n$ has $\varphi(\delta^{(n)}/n) = 1$ with $\|\delta^{(n)}/n\|_\infty
= \tfrac1n \to 0$. For any $a \in c_{00}$, $a - \varphi(a)\delta^{(N)}/N$ lies in $\ker\varphi$ and is at distance
$|\varphi(a)|/N$ from $a$, so $\ker\varphi$ is dense, while the kernel of a continuous functional is closed.
:::

The same linear functional can be continuous for one norm and not for another, so the dual depends on the norm. The
tenth example shows this with the sum of the entries on $c_{00}$.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-depends-norm-sum}
#### One functional, two norms

$\sigma(a) = \sum_na_n$ on $c_{00}$ satisfies $|\sigma(a)| \leq \|a\|_1$, with equality at $\delta^{(1)}$, so $\sigma \in
(c_{00}, \|\cdot\|_1)^*$ with norm $1$. For $\|\cdot\|_\infty$, $a^{(N)} = (1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots)$ has norm $1$ and
$\sigma(a^{(N)}) = N$, so $\sigma \notin (c_{00}, \|\cdot\|_\infty)^*$. The two norms are not equivalent
(@thm-norm-equivalence), and their duals differ.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The norm of a functional on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with a $p$-norm can be found by maximising over the unit sphere with a
Lagrange multiplier. The first exercise compares the result with the dual-norm formula on the example of the figure.

::: {#exr-fan-dual-norm-lagrange}
#### Dual norms by Lagrange multipliers

Maximise $\varphi(\mathbf x) = x_1 + 4x_2$ over $x_1^3 + x_2^3 = 1$, $x_k \geq 0$, the positive part of the unit
sphere of $\|\cdot\|_3$, with a Lagrange multiplier (@thm-lagrange-multipliers), and compare with $\|(1,
4)\|_{3/2}$. Find the maximiser and compare with the extremal vector of @exr-fan-holder-equality.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\|(1, 4)\|_{3/2} = (1 + 8)^{2/3} = 9^{2/3} \approx 4.327$. The Lagrange condition $(1, 4) = 3\mu(x_1^2, x_2^2)$ gives
$x_2^2/x_1^2 = 4$, so $x_2 = 2x_1$, and the constraint gives $\mathbf x = (1, 2)/9^{1/3}$, with $\varphi(\mathbf x) =
9/9^{1/3} = 9^{2/3}$. On the boundary points $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$, $\varphi$ is $1$ and $4$, smaller; the negative
quadrants give smaller values still, since $|\varphi(\mathbf x)| \leq \varphi(|x_1|, |x_2|)$. The maximiser is
proportional to $(1, 2) = (1^{1/2}, 4^{1/2})$, that is $|x_k|^3 \propto |y_k|^{3/2}$, the equality case of Hölder and
the point of contact in the figure.

## SageMath

Sage solves the Lagrange system and compares the maximum with $9^{2/3}$.

```{.python .sage}
x1, x2, mu = var('x1 x2 mu')
sols = solve([1 == 3 * mu * x1^2, 4 == 3 * mu * x2^2, x1^3 + x2^3 == 1], x1, x2, mu, solution_dict=True)
real = [s for s in sols if all(s[v] in RR and s[v] > 0 for v in (x1, x2))]
for s in real:
    print("maximiser: %.6f %.6f, ratio %.6f, value %.7f" % (s[x1], s[x2], s[x2] / s[x1], s[x1] + 4 * s[x2]))
print("9^(2/3) = %.7f" % (9^(2/3)).n())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
maximiser: 0.480750 0.961500, ratio 2.000000, value 4.3267488
9^(2/3) = 4.3267487
```
::::
:::

The limit of a convergent sequence is a functional on $c$ that no summable sequence represents. The second exercise shows
this @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.7].

::: {#exr-fan-limit-functional}
#### The limit functional

On the space $c$ of convergent sequences with $\|\cdot\|_\infty$, show that $L(a) = \lim_na_n$ is a functional of norm
$1$. Show that there is no $y \in \ell^1$ with $L(a) = \sum_ny_na_n$ for all $a \in c$, by testing on the $\delta^{(n)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$L$ is linear by the limit rules and $|\lim a_n| \leq \sup|a_n|$, with equality at $a = (1, 1, \dots)$, so $\|L\| = 1$.
If $L(a) = \sum y_na_n$, then $y_n = L(\delta^{(n)}) = 0$ for every $n$, so $L = 0$, contradicting $L(1, 1, \dots) = 1$.

## SageMath

Check on truncations: Sage evaluates $L$ and the candidate sums on $\delta^{(n)}$ and on a long constant sequence.

```{.python .sage}
L = lambda a: a[-1]  # the limit, read off a long eventually constant sequence
print("L(delta^(n)) for n = 1, 2, 3:", [L([1 if k == n else 0 for k in range(1, 1001)]) for n in (1, 2, 3)])
print("L(1, 1, ...):", L([1] * 1000), " while any y with all y_n = 0 gives sum 0")
```

```{.text .sage-output}
L(delta^(n)) for n = 1, 2, 3: [0, 0, 0]
L(1, 1, ...): 1  while any y with all y_n = 0 gives sum 0
```
::::
:::

The dual of a space depends on its norm, and different norms on the same functions give different duals. The third
exercise compares the continuous functions with two norms, and identifies part of the dual of the integral norm.

::: {#exr-fan-dual-depends-on-norm}
#### Duals depend on the norm

Show that $\delta_{1/2}$ is a bounded functional on $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ but not on $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_1)$.
Show that every continuous functional on $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_1)$ extends uniquely to $L^1[0, 1]$, and that $\varphi_g(f)
= \int_0^1gf$ with $g \in C[0, 1]$ has norm $\|g\|_\infty$ on $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$|f(\tfrac12)| \leq \|f\|_\infty$. In $\|\cdot\|_1$, the tent $h_n$ of height $1$ on $[\tfrac12 - \tfrac1n, \tfrac12 +
\tfrac1n]$ has $\|h_n\|_1 = \tfrac1n$ and $\delta_{1/2}(h_n) = 1$, so $\delta_{1/2}$ is unbounded. $C[0, 1]$ is dense in
its completion $L^1[0, 1]$, so @def-continuous-dual (5) extends each functional. For $\varphi_g$, $|\int gf| \leq
\|g\|_\infty\|f\|_1$. Let $|g(x_0)| = \|g\|_\infty > 0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$; on an interval $J$ around $x_0$, $|g -
g(x_0)| < \varepsilon$. A tent $h \geq 0$ supported in $J$, multiplied by the constant $g(x_0)^*/|g(x_0)|$, gives $f$
with $\|f\|_1 = \|h\|_1$ and $|\int gf| \geq (|g(x_0)| - \varepsilon)\|h\|_1$. So $\|\varphi_g\| = \|g\|_\infty$.

## SageMath

Check on $g(x) = x$: Sage computes $\int_0^1g h_n/\|h_n\|_1$ for tents $h_n$ at $x_0 = 1$ and compares with
$\|g\|_\infty = 1$.

```{.python .sage}
x = var('x')
for n in (2, 10, 100):
    h = 1 - n * (1 - x)  # the half tent at 1, supported in [1 - 1/n, 1]
    print("n = %3d: ratio = %s" % (n, integrate(x * h, x, 1 - 1 / n, 1) / integrate(h, x, 1 - 1 / n, 1)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
n =   2: ratio = 5/6
n =  10: ratio = 29/30
n = 100: ratio = 299/300
```
::::
:::

The dual of an incomplete space is complete, as part (1) says, and the finitely supported sequences give an explicit
case. The fourth exercise identifies the dual of $(c_{00}, \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ with $\ell^1$.

::: {#exr-fan-dual-c00}
#### The dual of $(c_{00}, \|\cdot\|_\infty)$

For $\varphi \in (c_{00}, \|\cdot\|_\infty)^*$ put $y_n = \varphi(\delta^{(n)})$. Show that $\sum_n|y_n| = \|\varphi\|$,
using $a = ((\operatorname{sgn}y_1)^*, \dots, (\operatorname{sgn}y_N)^*, 0, \dots)$, and that $y \mapsto \varphi_y$ is an
isometry from $\ell^1$ onto the dual. Compute $\|\varphi\|$ for $\varphi(a) = \sum_n(-2)^{-n}a_n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Every $a \in c_{00}$ is $\sum_{n \leq N}a_n\delta^{(n)}$, so $\varphi(a) = \sum_ny_na_n$. The vector $a$ given has
$\|a\|_\infty \leq 1$ and $\varphi(a) = \sum_{n \leq N}|y_n|$, so $\sum_{n \leq N}|y_n| \leq \|\varphi\|$ for all $N$
and $y \in \ell^1$. Conversely $|\sum y_na_n| \leq \|y\|_1\|a\|_\infty$. So $\|\varphi\| = \|y\|_1$, and every $y \in
\ell^1$ defines such a functional; the map is an isometry onto. For $y_n = (-2)^{-n}$, $\|\varphi\| = \sum2^{-n} = 1$.

## SageMath

Check on $y_n = (-2)^{-n}$: Sage evaluates $\varphi$ on the sign vectors of length $N$.

```{.python .sage}
y = lambda n: QQ(-2)^(-n)
for N in (1, 5, 20):
    print("N = %2d: phi(sign vector) = %s" % (N, sum(y(n) * sign(y(n)) for n in range(1, N + 1))))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
N =  1: phi(sign vector) = 1/2
N =  5: phi(sign vector) = 31/32
N = 20: phi(sign vector) = 1048575/1048576
```
::::
:::

In finite dimension every functional is continuous, but its norm still depends on the norm of the space. The fifth
exercise computes the norms of the coordinate functionals for the hexagonal norm.

::: {#exr-fan-dual-hexagon}
#### Dual norms for the hexagon

For $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{hex}}$ of @exm-fan-hexagon-norm, compute the norms of $\varepsilon^1(\mathbf x) = x_1$ and
$\varepsilon^2(\mathbf x) = x_2$ by evaluating them at the six vertices of the unit ball.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A linear function on a convex polygon attains its maximum at a vertex, because each point of the polygon is a convex
combination of the vertices. The vertices are $(\pm1, 0)$ and $(\pm\tfrac12, \pm\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2})$. So $\|\varepsilon^1\| =
\max|x_1| = 1$ and $\|\varepsilon^2\| = \max|x_2| = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, which is the constant of
@exr-fan-coordinate-continuity.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates the two coordinates at the vertices.

```{.python .sage}
r3 = sqrt(3)
verts = [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (1/2, r3 / 2), (-1/2, r3 / 2), (1/2, -r3 / 2), (-1/2, -r3 / 2)]
print("|eps^1| =", max(abs(v[0]) for v in verts), " |eps^2| =", max(abs(v[1]) for v in verts))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
|eps^1| = 1  |eps^2| = 1/2*sqrt(3)
```
::::
:::

A functional bounded on a dense subspace extends with the same norm, by part (5). The sixth exercise extends a weighted
sum from the finitely supported sequences to $\ell^2$.

::: {#exr-fan-dual-extension-dense}
#### Extending a weighted sum

Show that $\varphi(a) = \sum_na_n/n$ on $(c_{00}, \|\cdot\|_2)$ satisfies $|\varphi(a)| \leq \frac{\pi}{\sqrt6}\|a\|_2$,
and that its extension to $\ell^2$ has norm exactly $\frac{\pi}{\sqrt6}$. Compute the value of the extension on $a =
(1/n)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Cauchy-Schwarz (@thm-holder-inequality (2)) with $b_n = 1/n$ gives the bound, and $c_{00}$ is dense in $\ell^2$
(@def-lp-space (1)), so part (5) extends $\varphi$. The truncations $a^{(N)}$ of $(1/n)$ give $\varphi(a^{(N)}) =
\sum_{n \leq N}n^{-2} = \|a^{(N)}\|_2^2$, so $\varphi(a^{(N)})/\|a^{(N)}\|_2 = \|a^{(N)}\|_2 \to \frac{\pi}{\sqrt6}$, and the
norm is $\frac{\pi}{\sqrt6}$. On $(1/n)$ the extension is $\lim\varphi(a^{(N)}) = \frac{\pi^2}{6}$.

## SageMath

Sage computes $\varphi(a^{(N)})/\|a^{(N)}\|_2$ for growing $N$.

```{.python .sage}
for N in (10, 1000, 100000):
    s = sum(1.0 / n^2 for n in range(1, N + 1))
    print("N = %6d: ratio %.6f" % (N, sqrt(s)))
print("pi/sqrt(6) = %.6f, pi^2/6 = %.6f" % ((pi / sqrt(6)).n(), (pi^2 / 6).n()))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
N =     10: ratio 1.244897
N =   1000: ratio 1.282160
N = 100000: ratio 1.282546
pi/sqrt(6) = 1.282550, pi^2/6 = 1.644934
```
::::
:::

The kernel of a discontinuous functional is dense, which is the dichotomy behind part (3). The seventh exercise proves
it in general @gasinski2014exercises [Problem 5.33].

::: {#exr-fan-dual-kernel-dense}
#### Kernels are closed or dense

Let $\varphi : X \to \mathbb{K}$ be linear and not bounded. Show that there are $x_n$ with $\varphi(x_n) = 1$ and $\|x_n\|
\to 0$, and that $\ker\varphi$ is dense. Conclude, with @exr-fan-kernel-closed, that the kernel of a linear functional is
either closed or dense.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Since $\varphi$ is unbounded, for each $n$ there is $u_n$ with $|\varphi(u_n)| > n\|u_n\|$; then $x_n =
u_n/\varphi(u_n)$ has $\varphi(x_n) = 1$ and $\|x_n\| < 1/n$. For any $x$, $x - \varphi(x)x_n \in \ker\varphi$ and $\|x
- (x - \varphi(x)x_n)\| \leq |\varphi(x)|/n \to 0$. If $\varphi$ is bounded its kernel is closed; otherwise it is dense,
by what was just shown, and then it is not closed unless it is all of $X$, that is unless $\varphi = 0$.

## SageMath

Check on $\varphi(a) = \sum na_n$ of part (3): Sage computes the distance from $a = \delta^{(1)}$ to the kernel element
$a - \varphi(a)\delta^{(N)}/N$.

```{.python .sage}
phi = lambda a: sum((n + 1) * t for n, t in enumerate(a))
for N in (10, 100, 1000):
    a = [1] + [0] * (N - 1)
    k = [t - phi(a) * (1 if i == N - 1 else 0) / N for i, t in enumerate(a)]
    print("N = %4d: phi(k) = %s, distance = %s" % (N, phi(k), max(abs(u - v) for u, v in zip(a, k))))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
N =   10: phi(k) = 0, distance = 1/10
N =  100: phi(k) = 0, distance = 1/100
N = 1000: phi(k) = 0, distance = 1/1000
```
::::
:::

On $\ell^p$ the map $J$ into the bidual is isometric, because the extremal vectors of Hölder's inequality supply norming
functionals. The eighth exercise proves it without any duality theorem.

::: {#exr-fan-bidual-isometry-ellp}
#### $J$ is isometric on $\ell^p$

For $1 < p < \infty$ and $a \in \ell^p$, $a \neq 0$, let $y_n = (\operatorname{sgn}a_n)^*|a_n|^{p - 1}/\|a\|_p^{p -
1}$. Show that $y \in \ell^q$ with $\|y\|_q = 1$, that $\varphi_y(b) = \sum y_nb_n$ is a functional of norm at most $1$
on $\ell^p$, and that $\varphi_y(a) = \|a\|_p$. Deduce $\|Ja\| = \|a\|_p$. Compute $y$ for $a_n = 2^{-n}$, $p = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\sum|y_n|^q = \sum|a_n|^{(p - 1)q}/\|a\|_p^{(p - 1)q} = \sum|a_n|^p/\|a\|_p^p = 1$. By Hölder (@thm-holder-inequality
(2)), $|\varphi_y(b)| \leq \|y\|_q\|b\|_p = \|b\|_p$, and $\varphi_y(a) = \sum|a_n|^p/\|a\|_p^{p - 1} = \|a\|_p$, as in
@exr-fan-holder-equality. Hence $\|Ja\| \geq |(Ja)(\varphi_y)| = \|a\|_p$, and $\|Ja\| \leq \|a\|_p$ by
@def-continuous-dual (4). For $a_n = 2^{-n}$, $\|a\|_2 = (\sum4^{-n})^{1/2} = 3^{-1/2}$ and $y = a/\|a\|_2 = (\sqrt3\,2^{-n})$.

## SageMath

Sage checks $\|y\|_2 = 1$ and $\varphi_y(a) = \|a\|_2$ on a long truncation.

```{.python .sage}
N = 60
a = vector(RDF, [2.0^(-n) for n in range(1, N + 1)])
y = a / a.norm(2)
print("|a|_2 = %.10f (1/sqrt 3 = %.10f), |y|_2 = %.10f, phi_y(a) = %.10f" % (a.norm(2), 1 / sqrt(3.), y.norm(2), y * a))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
|a|_2 = 0.5773502692 (1/sqrt 3 = 0.5773502692), |y|_2 = 1.0000000000, phi_y(a) = 0.5773502692
```
::::
:::

Point evaluations are far apart in the dual of $C[0, 1]$, but close in the dual of $C^1[0, 1]$, because the stronger
norm controls differences. The ninth exercise compares the two.

::: {#exr-fan-dual-delta-difference}
#### Nearby point evaluations

Show $\|\delta_a - \delta_b\| = 2$ in $C[0, 1]^*$ for $a \neq b$, and $\|\delta_a - \delta_b\| \leq |a - b|$ in $C^1[0,
1]^*$ with the norm $\|f\|_{C^1}$ for real-valued $f$. Check the second bound on $f(x) = \sin 5x$ with $a = 0.3$, $b =
0.31$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$|f(a) - f(b)| \leq 2\|f\|_\infty$, and a piecewise linear $f$ with $f(a) = 1$, $f(b) = -1$, $|f| \leq 1$ attains
$2$. On $C^1$, the mean value theorem (@thm-mean-value) gives $|f(a) - f(b)| \leq |a - b|\,\|f'\|_\infty \leq |a -
b|\,\|f\|_{C^1}$. For $\sin 5x$, $|f(0.3) - f(0.31)| \approx 0.0023$ while $|a - b|\,\|f\|_{C^1} = 0.01\cdot 6 =
0.06$.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates both sides for $\sin 5x$.

```{.python .sage}
f = lambda t: sin(5 * t)
print("|f(a) - f(b)| = %.5f, |a - b| |f|_C1 = %.5f" % (abs(f(0.3) - f(0.31)), 0.01 * (1 + 5)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
|f(a) - f(b)| = 0.00229, |a - b| |f|_C1 = 0.06000
```
::::
:::

An expectation functional on matrices has norm one in the operator norm, and a different norm in the Frobenius norm. The
tenth exercise computes both for a mixed spin state, combining @exm-fan-dual-expectation with Cauchy-Schwarz.

::: {#exr-fan-dual-expectation-norm}
#### The norm of a state

For $\boldsymbol\rho = \operatorname{diag}(\tfrac34, \tfrac14)$, show that $\varphi(\mathbf M) =
\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol\rho\mathbf M)$ has norm $1$ for the operator norm and norm $\|\boldsymbol\rho\|_F =
\tfrac{\sqrt{10}}{4}$ for the Frobenius norm on $2 \times 2$ matrices, and find matrices attaining both.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For the operator norm this is @exm-fan-dual-expectation, attained at $\mathbf M = \mathbf I_2$. With the Frobenius norm,
$\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol\rho\mathbf M) = \sum_{i, j}\rho_{ji}M_{ij}$ is the pairing of $\mathbb{C}^4$, so its norm
is the Euclidean norm of the entries of $\boldsymbol\rho$ (@exm-fan-dual-cn with $p = 2$): $(\tfrac9{16} +
\tfrac1{16})^{1/2} = \tfrac{\sqrt{10}}{4} \approx 0.791$, attained at $\mathbf M = \boldsymbol\rho/\|\boldsymbol\rho\|_F$.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates the two attaining matrices.

```{.python .sage}
rho = matrix(QQ, [[3/4, 0], [0, 1/4]])
fro = sqrt(sum(t^2 for t in rho.list()))
print("tr(rho I) =", (rho * identity_matrix(2)).trace(), " |rho|_F =", fro, " tr(rho rho/|rho|_F) =", ((rho * rho).trace() / fro).simplify_full())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
tr(rho I) = 1  |rho|_F = 1/2*sqrt(5/2)  tr(rho rho/|rho|_F) = 1/4*sqrt(5)*sqrt(2)
```
::::
:::
::::

For $1 \leq p < \infty$ the dual of $\ell^p$ is $\ell^q$, which is the infinite-dimensional version of @exm-fan-dual-cn.
The theorem below proves it, together with the dual of $c_0$. For the spaces $L^p[a, b]$ it proves what the completion
allows without a theory of integration: the integral $\int fg$ extends to a pairing between $L^p$ and $L^q$, the norm of
an element is computed by pairing it with continuous functions, and every element of $L^q$ defines a functional on
$L^p$ of the same norm.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-lp-duality}
#### Duality of $\ell^p$ and $L^p$ spaces

Let $1 \leq p < \infty$ and $\tfrac1p + \tfrac1q = 1$.

1. For $y \in \ell^q$, $\varphi_y(a) = \sum_ny_na_n$ defines $\varphi_y \in (\ell^p)^*$ with $\|\varphi_y\| =
   \|y\|_q$, and every $\varphi \in (\ell^p)^*$ is $\varphi_y$ for a unique $y$, namely $y_n = \varphi(\delta^{(n)})$. So
   $y \mapsto \varphi_y$ is an isometric isomorphism $\ell^q \to (\ell^p)^*$.
2. In the same way $y \mapsto \varphi_y$ is an isometric isomorphism $\ell^1 \to c_0^*$.
3. On $[a, b]$, the pairing $\langle f, g\rangle = \int_a^bfg$ of continuous functions extends to a bilinear map on
   $L^p[a, b] \times L^q[a, b]$ if $p > 1$, and on $L^1[a, b] \times C[a, b]$ if $p = 1$, with $|\langle F, G\rangle| \leq
   \|F\|\,\|G\|$ (the supremum norm on $C[a, b]$ if $p = 1$). For every $F \in L^p[a, b]$,
   $$
   \|F\| = \sup\{|\langle F, g\rangle| : g \in C[a, b],\ \|g\|_q \leq 1\} \qquad (\|g\|_\infty \leq 1 \text{ if } p = 1).
   $$
   Hence $G \mapsto \langle\cdot, G\rangle$ is a linear isometry $L^q[a, b] \to (L^p[a, b])^*$ for $1 < p < \infty$, and
   $g \mapsto \langle\cdot, g\rangle$ is a linear isometry $(C[a, b], \|\cdot\|_\infty) \to (L^1[a, b])^*$.

Part (3) does not say that every functional on $L^p[a, b]$ is of this form; that question is not decided in this
chapter.
:::
::::

*Proof.* (1) By Hölder (@thm-holder-inequality (2)), $\varphi_y$ is defined and $|\varphi_y(a)| \leq
\|y\|_q\|a\|_p$. For the lower bound when $q < \infty$ and $y \neq 0$, take $a^{(N)}_n = (\operatorname{sgn}y_n)^*|y_n|^{q
