- 1}$ for $n \leq N$ and $0$ beyond. Then $\varphi_y(a^{(N)}) = S_N := \sum_{n \leq N}|y_n|^q$ and $\|a^{(N)}\|_p =
S_N^{1/p}$, since $(q - 1)p = q$; so $\|\varphi_y\| \geq S_N^{1 - 1/p} = S_N^{1/q} \to \|y\|_q$. When $q = \infty$
($p = 1$), $|\varphi_y(\delta^{(n)})| = |y_n|$ gives $\|\varphi_y\| \geq \|y\|_\infty$. Now let $\varphi \in
(\ell^p)^*$ and $y_n = \varphi(\delta^{(n)})$. For $q < \infty$, the same vectors give $S_N = \varphi(a^{(N)}) \leq
\|\varphi\|S_N^{1/p}$, so $S_N^{1/q} \leq \|\varphi\|$ for all $N$ and $y \in \ell^q$; for $q = \infty$, $|y_n| \leq
\|\varphi\|$. The functionals $\varphi$ and $\varphi_y$ agree on each $\delta^{(n)}$, hence on $c_{00}$, which is dense
in $\ell^p$ (@def-lp-space (1)); being continuous, they agree everywhere. Uniqueness of $y$ is clear from $y_n =
\varphi(\delta^{(n)})$, and the map is linear.

(2) For $y \in \ell^1$, $|\sum y_na_n| \leq \|y\|_1\|a\|_\infty$. For $\varphi \in c_0^*$ and $y_n =
\varphi(\delta^{(n)})$, the vector $a^{(N)} = ((\operatorname{sgn}y_1)^*, \dots, (\operatorname{sgn}y_N)^*, 0, \dots) \in
c_0$ has $\|a^{(N)}\|_\infty \leq 1$ and $\varphi(a^{(N)}) = \sum_{n \leq N}|y_n|$, so $\|y\|_1 \leq \|\varphi\|$; and
$\varphi = \varphi_y$ on the dense subspace $c_{00}$ (@exm-fan-completion-c00-sup), hence on $c_0$. So the map is onto
and $\|\varphi_y\| = \|y\|_1$.

(3) *The pairing.* For fixed $g \in C[a, b]$, $|\int fg| \leq \|f\|_p\|g\|_q$ by @thm-holder-inequality (3) ($\|g\|_\infty$
if $p = 1$), so $f \mapsto \langle f, g\rangle$ extends to $L^p[a, b]$ (@thm-completion (2)), with $|\langle F, g\rangle|
\leq \|F\|\,\|g\|_q$. For $p > 1$, @exr-fan-bilinear-extension extends it further to $L^p \times L^q$, with the bound
$\|F\|\,\|G\|$ and $\langle F, G\rangle = \lim\langle f_n, g_n\rangle$ for continuous $f_n \to F$, $g_n \to G$.

*The norm formula.* The supremum is at most $\|F\|$ by the bound. For the reverse, let $F \neq 0$, $\varepsilon \in (0,
\|F\|)$, and $f \in C[a, b]$ with $\|F - f\| < \varepsilon$, so $f \neq 0$. If $p > 1$, put $g = f^*|f|^{p - 2}/\|f\|_p^{p
- 1}$ where $f \neq 0$ and $g = 0$ where $f = 0$. Since $|g| = |f|^{p - 1}/\|f\|_p^{p - 1}$ and $p - 1 > 0$, $g$ is
continuous, also at the zeros of $f$; and $\|g\|_q = 1$, $\langle f, g\rangle = \|f\|_p$, as in @exr-fan-holder-equality.
If $p = 1$, put $g_\delta = f^*/(|f| + \delta)$ for $\delta > 0$: it is continuous, $|g_\delta| \leq 1$, and $\langle
f, g_\delta\rangle = \int\frac{|f|^2}{|f| + \delta} \geq \int(|f| - \delta) = \|f\|_1 - \delta(b - a)$. In both cases
$|\langle F, g\rangle| \geq |\langle f, g\rangle| - |\langle F - f, g\rangle| \geq \|f\| - \varepsilon - \delta(b - a)
\geq \|F\| - 2\varepsilon - \delta(b - a)$ (with $\delta = 0$ if $p > 1$), and $\varepsilon$, $\delta$ are arbitrary.

*The isometries.* For $G \in L^q[a, b]$, $1 < p < \infty$, $\varphi_G = \langle\cdot, G\rangle$ is linear with
$\|\varphi_G\| \leq \|G\|$. The norm formula, applied in $L^q$ with the exponent $p$ (which is conjugate to $q$, $1 < q <
\infty$), gives continuous $f$ with $\|f\|_p \leq 1$ and $|\langle f, G\rangle|$ arbitrarily close to $\|G\|$; so
$\|\varphi_G\| = \|G\|$. For $p = 1$ and $g \in C[a, b]$, $\|\varphi_g\| \leq \|g\|_\infty$, and equality is
@exr-fan-dual-depends-on-norm, whose functionals are restrictions of $\varphi_g$ to $C[a, b]$. $\square$

The sequence case is @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 3.2, Exercise 3.7]; the function case follows @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Problem
II.1] in extending the pairing from continuous functions.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The duality pairs the sequence spaces of the figure of @fig-fa2-lp-norms in a fixed way. The first example lists the
pairs that recur in this chapter.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-pairs}
#### Dual pairs

$(\ell^2)^* = \ell^2$, $(\ell^{3/2})^* = \ell^3$, $(\ell^1)^* = \ell^\infty$ and $c_0^* = \ell^1$, each through
$y \mapsto \varphi_y$. On $[0, 1]$, $x^{-1/4}$ defines an element $G$ of $L^p[0, 1]$ for $p < 4$ (@exm-fan-power-functions),
so $\langle\cdot, G\rangle$ is a functional on $L^q[0, 1]$ for $q > \tfrac43$, of norm $\|G\| = (\int_0^1x^{-p/4})^{1/p} =
(\frac{4}{4 - p})^{1/p}$ with $p = q/(q - 1)$.
:::

On $\ell^2$ a functional and the sequence representing it have the same norm. The second example computes it for the
sequence $1/n$.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-ell2-self}
#### A functional on $\ell^2$

$y = (1/n) \in \ell^2$ gives $\varphi_y(a) = \sum a_n/n$, of norm $\|y\|_2 = \pi/\sqrt6$ by part (1), the extension
computed in @exr-fan-dual-extension-dense. The norm is attained at $a = y/\|y\|_2$, the extremal vector of
@exr-fan-bidual-isometry-ellp, with $\varphi_y(a) = \|y\|_2$.
:::

The coordinate functionals of $\ell^p$ correspond to the unit sequences of $\ell^q$. The third example records this.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-coordinates-ellp}
#### Coordinates of $\ell^p$

$a \mapsto a_n$ is $\varphi_{\delta^{(n)}}$, of norm $\|\delta^{(n)}\|_q = 1$ on every $\ell^p$. A finite combination
$\sum_{n \leq N}y_na_n$ has norm $\|(y_1, \dots, y_N)\|_q$, as in @exm-fan-dual-cn: the duality of $\mathbb{C}^N$ is
the truncation of the duality of $\ell^p$.
:::

The bidual of $c_0$ is $\ell^\infty$, which is larger than $c_0$, so the map $J$ into the bidual need not be onto. The
fourth example computes this by applying the theorem twice.

::: {#exm-fan-bidual-c0}
#### The bidual of $c_0$

$c_0^* = \ell^1$ by part (2) and $(\ell^1)^* = \ell^\infty$ by part (1), so $c_0^{**} = \ell^\infty$, and the canonical
map $J : a \mapsto Ja$ of @def-continuous-dual is the inclusion $c_0 \subset \ell^\infty$: $(Ja)(\varphi_y) =
\sum y_na_n$. The constant sequence $(1, 1, \dots)$ is an element of the bidual that does not come from $c_0$.
:::

For $1 < p < \infty$ the theorem applied twice returns to $\ell^p$, and $J$ is onto. The fifth example checks it.

::: {#exm-fan-ellp-bidual}
#### The bidual of $\ell^p$

For $1 < p < \infty$, $(\ell^p)^* = \ell^q$ and $(\ell^q)^* = \ell^p$ by part (1), so every element of $(\ell^p)^{**}$ is
$\varphi_y \mapsto \sum y_na_n$ for some $a \in \ell^p$, which is $Ja$. With @exr-fan-bidual-isometry-ellp, $J :
\ell^p \to (\ell^p)^{**}$ is an isometric isomorphism. For $p = 1$ the second step is not available: the
theorem does not describe $(\ell^\infty)^*$.
:::

The pairing of part (3) gives a concrete meaning to integrals against elements of $L^p$ defined by piecewise continuous
functions. The sixth example pairs the step function with continuous functions.

::: {#exm-fan-lp-pairing-step}
#### Pairing with the step function

For $[\Theta] = [\Theta(\cdot - \tfrac12)] \in L^p[0, 1]$ and $g \in C[0, 1]$, the ramps $g_n \to [\Theta]$ give $\langle
[\Theta], g\rangle = \lim\int g_ng = \int_{1/2}^1g$, since $|\int(g_n - \Theta)g| \leq \|g\|_\infty/n$. For $g = 1$ this
is $\tfrac12 = \|[\Theta]\|_1$, the supremum of part (3) for $p = 1$, attained.
:::

A particle in a box has continuous stationary states, and their amplitudes are the functionals of part (3) with $p = q
= 2$. The seventh example computes the amplitude of a simple state in the ground state.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-box-amplitude}
#### Amplitudes in a box

On $[0, 1]$ the ground state $\psi_1 = \sqrt2\sin\pi x$ has $\|\psi_1\|_2 = 1$, so $F \mapsto \langle F, \psi_1\rangle$ is
a functional of norm $1$ on $L^2[0, 1]$. For the state $f = \sqrt{30}\,x(1 - x)$, also of norm $1$, the amplitude is
$\langle f, \psi_1\rangle = \sqrt{60}\int_0^1x(1 - x)\sin\pi x\,dx = \sqrt{60}\cdot\frac{4}{\pi^3} \approx 0.9993$,
close to $1$ because $f$ is close to $\psi_1$.
:::

On the circle the Fourier coefficients are integrals against bounded continuous weights, so part (3) with $p = 1$
applies. The eighth example computes their norms on $L^1[0, 2\pi]$.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-circle-coefficients}
#### Fourier coefficients on $L^1$

$c_n(F) = \langle F, g_n\rangle$ with $g_n = e^{-inx}/2\pi \in C[0, 2\pi]$ is a functional on $L^1[0, 2\pi]$ of norm
$\|g_n\|_\infty = \frac{1}{2\pi}$ by part (3). So the coefficients of every element of $L^1[0, 2\pi]$ are defined and
bounded by $\frac{1}{2\pi}\|F\|$, which is the inequality $|c_n| \leq \frac1{2\pi}\int|f|$ of @exm-fan-holder-circle carried
to the completion.
:::

For $p = 1$ the norm of $\varphi_g$ need not be attained, even when $g$ is a polynomial. The ninth example shows this.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-p1-not-attained}
#### A norm that is not attained

On $L^1[0, 1]$, $\varphi_g$ with $g(x) = x$ has norm $\|g\|_\infty = 1$ by part (3). For continuous $f \neq 0$,
$|\int xf| \leq \int x|f| < \int|f|$, because $x < 1$ on $[0, 1)$ and $|f| > 0$ on an interval. The supremum $1$ is
approached by functions concentrated near $x = 1$, such as $(n + 1)x^n$, and attained by no continuous $f$.
:::

The theorem leaves the dual of $\ell^\infty$ and of $c$ alone, and the space $c$ shows why the pattern of part (2) cannot
be copied. The tenth example combines the theorem with the limit functional of @exr-fan-limit-functional.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-c-limit}
#### The dual of the convergent sequences

Each $y \in \ell^1$ gives $\varphi_y \in c^*$ with $\|\varphi_y\| = \|y\|_1$, by the proof of part (2), which only used
sequences of $c_{00}$ and sign vectors. But the limit functional $L$ is not of this form (@exr-fan-limit-functional), so
$y \mapsto \varphi_y$ is an isometry of $\ell^1$ into $c^*$ that is not onto; $c_{00}$ is not dense in $c$, and that is
exactly where the proof of part (2) breaks down.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The norm of a functional on $\ell^1$ is the supremum of its values on the unit sequences. The first exercise proves
$(\ell^1)^* = \ell^\infty$ by this observation @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.7], the case $p = 1$ of the theorem.

::: {#exr-fan-dual-ell1}
#### The dual of $\ell^1$

For $\varphi \in (\ell^1)^*$ set $y_n = \varphi(\delta^{(n)})$. Show $|y_n| \leq \|\varphi\|$, that $\varphi(a) =
\sum_ny_na_n$ for every $a \in \ell^1$, and that $\|\varphi\| = \|y\|_\infty$. Compute $\|\varphi\|$ for $\varphi(a) =
\sum_n\frac{n}{n + 1}a_n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$|y_n| = |\varphi(\delta^{(n)})| \leq \|\varphi\|\,\|\delta^{(n)}\|_1 = \|\varphi\|$. For $a \in \ell^1$ the partial
sums $\sum_{n \leq N}a_n\delta^{(n)}$ converge to $a$ in $\ell^1$, so by continuity $\varphi(a) = \lim\sum_{n \leq
N}a_ny_n$. Then $|\varphi(a)| \leq \|y\|_\infty\|a\|_1$, so $\|\varphi\| \leq \|y\|_\infty \leq \|\varphi\|$. For $y_n =
\frac{n}{n + 1}$, $\|\varphi\| = \sup_n\frac{n}{n + 1} = 1$, not attained (@exm-fan-dual-ell1-elements).

## SageMath

Sage evaluates $\varphi(\delta^{(n)})$ for large $n$.

```{.python .sage}
print("phi(delta^(n)) for n = 1, 10, 1000:", [QQ(n) / (n + 1) for n in (1, 10, 1000)], " sup = 1, not attained")
```

```{.text .sage-output}
phi(delta^(n)) for n = 1, 10, 1000: [1/2, 10/11, 1000/1001]  sup = 1, not attained
```
::::
:::

The proof of the theorem for $1 < p < \infty$ tests the functional on the extremal vector of a truncation. The second
exercise carries it out on a concrete functional.

::: {#exr-fan-ellp-dual-proof}
#### The dual of $\ell^p$ on an example

For $p = 3$, $q = \tfrac32$ and $\varphi(a) = \sum_na_n/n$, compute $y$, the truncated test vectors $a^{(N)}$ of the
proof, and the ratios $\varphi(a^{(N)})/\|a^{(N)}\|_3$ for $N = 10, 100$, and compare with $\|y\|_{3/2} =
\zeta(\tfrac32)^{2/3}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$y_n = \varphi(\delta^{(n)}) = 1/n$. The test vectors are $a^{(N)}_n = |y_n|^{q - 1} = n^{-1/2}$ for $n \leq N$. Then
$\varphi(a^{(N)}) = \sum_{n \leq N}n^{-3/2} = S_N$ and $\|a^{(N)}\|_3 = S_N^{1/3}$, so the ratio is $S_N^{2/3}$, which
increases to $\zeta(\tfrac32)^{2/3} \approx 1.896$, the norm of $\varphi$ by part (1).

## SageMath

Sage computes the ratios and the limit.

```{.python .sage}
for N in (10, 100, 10000):
    S = sum(n^(-1.5) for n in range(1, N + 1))
    print("N = %5d: ratio %.5f" % (N, S^(2/3)))
print("zeta(3/2)^(2/3) = %.5f" % (zeta(1.5)^(2/3)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
N =    10: ratio 1.58493
N =   100: ratio 1.79897
N = 10000: ratio 1.88712
zeta(3/2)^(2/3) = 1.89681
```
::::
:::

The norm of an integral functional on $L^2[0, 1]$ given by a singular weight can be computed exactly with part (3). The
third exercise does so and tests the bound on two functions.

::: {#exr-fan-lp-functional-norm}
#### The norm of an integral functional

For $G = [x^{-1/4}] \in L^2[0, 1]$ (@def-lp-space (4)), compute the norm of $\varphi_G(F) = \langle F, G\rangle$ on
$L^2[0, 1]$, and check $|\varphi_G(f)| \leq \|\varphi_G\|\,\|f\|_2$ on $f = 1$ and $f = x$, where $\varphi_G(f) =
\int_0^1x^{-1/4}f(x)\,dx$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By part (3), $\|\varphi_G\| = \|G\| = (\int_0^1x^{-1/2})^{1/2} = \sqrt2$. For continuous $f$, $\varphi_G(f) = \lim\langle
f, x^{-1/4}\chi_n\rangle = \int_0^1x^{-1/4}f$, the improper integral, since the difference is at most
$\|f\|_\infty\int_0^{\delta_n}x^{-1/4}$. For $f = 1$, $\varphi_G(1) = \tfrac43 \leq \sqrt2$; for $f = x$, $\varphi_G(x) =
\tfrac47$ and $\|x\|_2 = 1/\sqrt3$, with $\tfrac47 \approx 0.571 \leq \sqrt2/\sqrt3 \approx 0.816$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the norm and the two test values.

```{.python .sage}
x = var('x'); assume(x > 0)
g = x^(-1 / 4)
nrm = sqrt(integrate(g^2, x, 0, 1))
print("|G| =", nrm)
for f in (1, x):
    print("f = %s: phi(f) = %s, |phi| |f|_2 = %.5f" % (f, integrate(g * f, x, 0, 1), (nrm * sqrt(integrate(f^2, x, 0, 1))).n()))
forget()
```

```{.text .sage-output}
|G| = sqrt(2)
f = 1: phi(f) = 4/3, |phi| |f|_2 = 1.41421
f = x: phi(f) = 4/7, |phi| |f|_2 = 0.81650
```
::::
:::

The sequences summable in absolute value give functionals on the bounded sequences, isometrically. The fourth exercise
proves this and contrasts the separability of $\ell^1$ with that of its dual.

::: {#exr-fan-ell1-not-dual-of-ellinfty}
#### $\ell^1$ inside $(\ell^\infty)^*$, and a non-separable dual

Show that $y \mapsto \varphi_y$, $\varphi_y(a) = \sum y_na_n$, is a linear isometry $\ell^1 \to (\ell^\infty)^*$. Show
that $\ell^1$ is separable while its dual $(\ell^1)^* = \ell^\infty$ is not (@exr-fan-separability), so that a separable
space can have a non-separable dual.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$|\sum y_na_n| \leq \|y\|_1\|a\|_\infty$, and the bounded sequence $a_n = (\operatorname{sgn}y_n)^*$ gives $\varphi_y(a)
= \|y\|_1$ with $\|a\|_\infty \leq 1$; so $\|\varphi_y\| = \|y\|_1$. The finitely supported sequences with rational
entries are countable and dense in $\ell^1$ (@def-lp-space (1)), so $\ell^1$ is separable; by part (1),
$(\ell^1)^* = \ell^\infty$, which is not separable by @exr-fan-separability.

## SageMath

Check on $y_n = (-1)^n/n^2$: Sage evaluates $\varphi_y$ on the sign sequence and compares with $\|y\|_1 = \pi^2/6$.

```{.python .sage}
N = 10^5
s = sum(((-1)^n / n^2.) * sign((-1)^n) for n in range(1, N + 1))
print("phi_y(sign y) = %.6f, |y|_1 = pi^2/6 = %.6f (truncated at 10^5)" % (s, (pi^2 / 6).n()))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
phi_y(sign y) = 1.644924, |y|_1 = pi^2/6 = 1.644934 (truncated at 10^5)
```
::::
:::

A summable sequence acts on the null sequences, and its value on a given one can be summed in closed form. The fifth
exercise computes such a value.

::: {#exr-fan-c0-dual-compute}
#### A functional on $c_0$

For $y_n = 2^{-n}$, compute $\|\varphi_y\|$ on $c_0$, the value $\varphi_y((1/n))$, and a sequence $a \in c_0$ with
$\|a\|_\infty \leq 1$ and $\varphi_y(a) > 0.99$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By part (2), $\|\varphi_y\| = \|y\|_1 = 1$. Then $\varphi_y((1/n)) = \sum_n\frac{2^{-n}}{n} = -\log(1 - \tfrac12) = \log 2$,
from the power series of $-\log(1 - x)$ at $x = \tfrac12$, inside its radius of convergence. The sign vectors of the
proof, here $a = (1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots)$ with $N$ ones, give $\varphi_y(a) = 1 - 2^{-N}$, larger than $0.99$ for $N
\geq 7$.

## SageMath

Sage sums the series and finds the smallest $N$.

```{.python .sage}
n = var('n')
print("sum 2^-n/n =", sum(2^(-n) / n, n, 1, oo))
print("smallest N with 1 - 2^-N > 0.99:", min(N for N in range(1, 30) if 1 - 2.^(-N) > 0.99))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
sum 2^-n/n = log(2)
smallest N with 1 - 2^-N > 0.99: 7
```
::::
:::

On a bounded interval the identity of the continuous functions extends to a map $L^q \to L^p$ for $q > p$, and part (3)
shows that it loses nothing. The sixth exercise proves that the map is injective, so that $L^q[0, 1]$ may be regarded as
a subspace of $L^p[0, 1]$.

::: {#exr-fan-lp-inclusion-injective}
#### The inclusion $L^q[0, 1] \to L^p[0, 1]$ is injective

Let $1 \leq p < q < \infty$ and $j : L^q[0, 1] \to L^p[0, 1]$ the extension of the identity of $C[0, 1]$
(@exr-fan-lp-inclusions). Show that $\langle jF, g\rangle = \langle F, g\rangle$ for $F \in L^q$ and $g \in C[0, 1]$,
and deduce from the norm formula of part (3) in $L^q$ that $jF = 0$ implies $F = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For continuous $f_n \to F$ in $L^q$, $jf_n = f_n \to jF$ in $L^p$, and for fixed continuous $g$ both pairings are
continuous: $\langle jF, g\rangle = \lim\int f_ng = \langle F, g\rangle$. If $jF = 0$, then $\langle F, g\rangle = 0$ for
every continuous $g$, and the norm formula of part (3) in $L^q[0, 1]$ gives $\|F\| = \sup_g|\langle F, g\rangle| = 0$.
So $j$ is injective, and with $\|jF\| \leq \|F\|$ it embeds $L^q[0, 1]$ into $L^p[0, 1]$ continuously.

## SageMath

Check on $F = [x^{-1/3}] \in L^2[0, 1]$: Sage pairs it with $g = 1, x, x^2$ in $L^2$ and, through the cut-offs, in
$L^1$; the values agree.

```{.python .sage}
x = var('x'); assume(x > 0)
for g in (1, x, x^2):
    print("g = %s: int x^(-1/3) g = %s" % (g, integrate(x^(-1/3) * g, x, 0, 1)))
forget()
```

```{.text .sage-output}
g = 1: int x^(-1/3) g = 3/2
g = x: int x^(-1/3) g = 3/5
g = x^2: int x^(-1/3) g = 3/8
```
::::
:::

The supremum of part (3) is approached by continuous functions close to the extremal function, which may itself be
singular. The seventh exercise computes the approach for $F = [x^{-1/3}]$ in $L^2[0, 1]$.

::: {#exr-fan-lp-norming-compute}
#### Approaching the norm with continuous functions

For $F = [x^{-1/3}] \in L^2[0, 1]$, $\|F\| = \sqrt3$. Using the cut-offs $f_n = x^{-1/3}\chi_n$ of @def-lp-space (4),
compute $\langle F, f_n\rangle/\|f_n\|_2$ for $n = 10, 100, 1000$, and show that it tends to $\sqrt3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\|F\|^2 = \int_0^1x^{-2/3} = 3$. By part (3), $\langle F, f_n\rangle = \lim_m\int f_mf_n$. For $m$ with $\delta_m \leq \delta_n/2$, $\chi_m = 1$ wherever
$\chi_n \neq 0$, so $\int f_mf_n = \int_0^1x^{-2/3}\chi_n$, and this is $\langle F, f_n\rangle$. Also $\|f_n\|_2^2 =
\int x^{-2/3}\chi_n^2$. Both lie between $\int_{\delta_n}^1x^{-2/3}$ and $3$, so they tend to $3$, and the ratio tends to
$3/\sqrt3 = \sqrt3$; by the bound of part (3) it never exceeds $\|F\|$.

## SageMath

Sage integrates with the cut-offs exactly.

```{.python .sage}
x = var('x')
for n in (10, 100, 1000):
    d = QQ(1) / n
    chi = (x - d / 2) / (d / 2)
    pair = integrate(x^(-2/3) * chi, x, d / 2, d) + integrate(x^(-2/3), x, d, 1)
    nf2 = integrate(x^(-2/3) * chi^2, x, d / 2, d) + integrate(x^(-2/3), x, d, 1)
    print("n = %4d: ratio %.6f" % (n, (pair / sqrt(nf2)).n()))
print("sqrt(3) = %.6f" % sqrt(3.))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
n =   10: ratio 1.337528
n =  100: ratio 1.561243
n = 1000: ratio 1.654946
sqrt(3) = 1.732051
```
::::
:::

The space $c$ of convergent sequences differs from $c_0$ by one dimension, and so does its dual. The eighth exercise
describes every functional on $c$, combining part (2) with @exr-fan-limit-functional.

::: {#exr-fan-dual-c}
#### Every functional on $c$

For $\varphi \in c^*$ put $y_n = \varphi(\delta^{(n)})$ and $\lambda = \varphi(\mathbf 1) - \sum_ny_n$ with $\mathbf 1 =
(1, 1, \dots)$. Show that $y \in \ell^1$ and $\varphi(a) = \sum_ny_na_n + \lambda\lim_na_n$ for all $a \in c$. Compute
$y$ and $\lambda$ for $\varphi(a) = a_1 + 2\lim a_n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Restricted to $c_0$, $\varphi$ is $\varphi_y$ with $y \in \ell^1$ by part (2). Every $a \in c$ is $a = (a - L(a)\mathbf 1)
+ L(a)\mathbf 1$ with $L(a) = \lim a_n$ and $a - L(a)\mathbf 1 \in c_0$, so $\varphi(a) = \sum y_n(a_n - L(a)) +
L(a)\varphi(\mathbf 1) = \sum y_na_n + L(a)(\varphi(\mathbf 1) - \sum y_n)$, where the sums converge because $y \in
\ell^1$. For $\varphi(a) = a_1 + 2\lim a_n$: $y = \delta^{(1)}$, $\varphi(\mathbf 1) = 3$, $\lambda = 3 - 1 = 2$.

## SageMath

Check on $a_n = 1 + 1/n$: Sage evaluates $\varphi$ directly and through the formula.

```{.python .sage}
a1 = 2; lim = 1
print("phi(a) directly:", a1 + 2 * lim, " formula sum y_n a_n + lambda lim:", 1 * a1 + 2 * lim)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
phi(a) directly: 4  formula sum y_n a_n + lambda lim: 4
```
::::
:::

A sequence defines a bounded functional on $\ell^p$ only if it lies in $\ell^q$, and a sequence outside it produces a
divergent sum. The ninth exercise exhibits one for $p = 4$.

::: {#exr-fan-dual-unbounded-pairing}
#### A sequence that is not a functional

Let $y_n = n^{-1/2}$. Show $y \notin \ell^{4/3}$, and that $a_n = n^{-1/2}/\log(n + 1)$ lies in $\ell^4$ while
$\sum_ny_na_n$ diverges. Conclude that no functional on $\ell^4$ has $\varphi(\delta^{(n)}) = n^{-1/2}$ for all $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\sum|y_n|^{4/3} = \sum n^{-2/3} = \infty$. $\sum a_n^4 = \sum\frac{1}{n^2\log^4(n + 1)} \leq \sum\frac{1}{n^2\log^42}$
converges, while $\sum y_na_n = \sum\frac{1}{n\log(n + 1)}$ diverges by the condensation test (@thm-convergence-tests). If
$\varphi \in (\ell^4)^*$ had $\varphi(\delta^{(n)}) = y_n$, part (1) would give $y \in \ell^{4/3}$, a contradiction.

## SageMath

Sage shows the partial sums of $\sum y_na_n$ growing like $\log\log N$ and those of $\sum a_n^4$ settling.

```{.python .sage}
for N in (10^2, 10^4, 10^6):
    s1 = sum(1.0 / (n * log(n + 1.0)) for n in range(1, N + 1))
    s4 = sum(1.0 / (n^2 * log(n + 1.0)^4) for n in range(1, N + 1))
    print("N = %8d: sum y a = %.4f, sum a^4 = %.6f, log log N = %.4f" % (N, s1, s4, log(log(N * 1.0))))
```

```{.text .sage-output}

N =    10000: sum y a = 4.0619, sum a^4 = 4.552581, log log N = 2.2203
N =  1000000: sum y a = 4.4673, sum a^4 = 4.552581, log log N = 2.6258
```
