```{.python .sage}
b = lambda x, y: (x.conjugate() * B * y)
q = lambda x: b(x, x)
pol = sum(I^(-k) * q(u + I^k * v) for k in range(4)) / 4
print("polarisation - b(u, v) =", (pol - b(u, v)).expand())
print("q(e1 + e2) =", q(vector(SR, [1, 1])))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
polarisation - b(u, v) = 0
q(e1 + e2) = 2*I + 4
```
::::
:::

The two shifts of @def-bounded-operator (4) give two forms on $\ell^2$ that differ by exchanging the slots. The third exercise identifies
their operators and norms.

::: {#exr-sf-shift-form}
#### Forms of the shifts

On $\ell^2$ let $b_1(a, c) = \sum_na_n^*c_{n+1}$ and $b_2(a, c) = \sum_na_{n+1}^*c_n$. Show that they are bounded, find their operators,
and compute $\|b_1\|$ and $\|b_2\|$. Is $b_1$ hermitian?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$b_1(a, c) = \sum_na_n^*(Lc)_n = \langle a, Lc\rangle$ and $b_2(a, c) = \sum_{n \geq 2}a_n^*c_{n-1} = \langle a, Sc\rangle$, the series
converging absolutely by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in $\ell^2$ (@def-hilbert-space (3)). By part (2), the operators are $L$ and $S$, and
$\|b_1\| = \|L\| = 1$, $\|b_2\| = \|S\| = 1$ (@def-bounded-operator (4)). Since $b_1(c, a)^* = \sum_nc_na_{n+1}^* = b_2(a, c)$, $b_1$ is
hermitian only if $b_1 = b_2$, which fails: $b_1(\delta^{(1)}, \delta^{(2)}) = 1$ and $b_2(\delta^{(1)}, \delta^{(2)}) = 0$.

## SageMath

The code evaluates $b_1$ and $b_2$ on truncated vectors and the ratio $|b_1(a, c)|/(\|a\|\,\|c\|)$ for $a = (1, \dots, 1)$, $c = (0, 1,
\dots, 1)$.

```{.python .sage}
b1 = lambda a, c: sum(conjugate(a[n]) * c[n + 1] for n in range(len(a) - 1))
b2 = lambda a, c: sum(conjugate(a[n + 1]) * c[n] for n in range(len(a) - 1))
d = lambda n, N: [1 if k == n else 0 for k in range(N)]
print("b1(d1, d2) =", b1(d(0, 5), d(1, 5)), "; b2(d1, d2) =", b2(d(0, 5), d(1, 5)))
for N in [5, 50, 500]:
    a = [1] * N; c = [0] + [1] * (N - 1)
    print("N =", N, ": |b1(a, c)|/(||a|| ||c||) = %.6f" % (abs(b1(a, c)) / sqrt(N * (N - 1))).n())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
b1(d1, d2) = 1 ; b2(d1, d2) = 0
N = 5 : |b1(a, c)|/(||a|| ||c||) = 0.894427
N = 50 : |b1(a, c)|/(||a|| ||c||) = 0.989949
N = 500 : |b1(a, c)|/(||a|| ||c||) = 0.998999
```
::::
:::

A hermitian form with non-negative quadratic form satisfies the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, with the same proof as for the inner product.
The fourth exercise asks for it; it will give estimates for positive operators.

::: {#exr-sf-cauchy-schwarz-form}
#### Cauchy-Schwarz for a positive form

Let $b$ be a hermitian sesquilinear form with $q(u) \geq 0$ for all $u$. Show that $|b(u, v)|^2 \leq q(u)q(v)$ for all $u, v$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Choose $\theta$ real with $e^{i\theta}b(u, v) = |b(u, v)|$ and put $w = e^{i\theta}v$, so $b(u, w) = |b(u, v)|$ and $q(w) = q(v)$. For real
$t$, since $b$ is hermitian,
$$
0 \leq q(u + tw) = q(u) + 2t\operatorname{Re}b(u, w) + t^2q(w) = q(u) + 2t|b(u, v)| + t^2q(v) .
$$
If $q(v) = 0$, letting $t \to -\infty$ forces $|b(u, v)| = 0$. Otherwise the quadratic polynomial in $t$ has no two real roots, so its
discriminant is $\leq 0$: $4|b(u, v)|^2 \leq 4q(u)q(v)$.

## SageMath

Check on $b(\mathbf u, \mathbf v) = \mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf B\mathbf v$ with the positive $\mathbf B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & i \\ -i &
1\end{pmatrix}$: the code tests the inequality on random integer vectors, exactly.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(1)
K.<j> = QuadraticField(-1)
B = matrix(K, [[2, j], [-j, 1]])
conj = lambda w: vector(K, [x.conjugate() for x in w])
b = lambda x, y: conj(x) * B * y
ok = True
for _ in range(200):
    u = vector(K, [ZZ.random_element(-5, 6) + j * ZZ.random_element(-5, 6) for _ in range(2)])
    v = vector(K, [ZZ.random_element(-5, 6) + j * ZZ.random_element(-5, 6) for _ in range(2)])
    ok = ok and (QQ(b(u, v) * b(u, v).conjugate()) <= QQ(b(u, u) * b(v, v)))
print("B hermitian:", B == B.conjugate_transpose(), "; det B =", B.det(), "; inequality on 200 random pairs:", ok)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
B hermitian: True ; det B = 1 ; inequality on 200 random pairs: True
```
::::
:::

The second difference matrix plus the identity gives a coercive form, and part (4) bounds the norm of its inverse without computing the
inverse. The fifth exercise derives the coercivity from a summation by parts.

::: {#exr-sf-lax-milgram-discrete}
#### A discrete boundary value problem

Let $\mathbf D_n$ be the $n \times n$ tridiagonal matrix with $2$ on the diagonal and $-1$ next to it, and $\mathbf B = \mathbf D_n +
\mathbf I_n$. Show that $\mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf D_n\mathbf u = |u_1|^2 + \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}|u_{k+1} - u_k|^2 + |u_n|^2$, deduce that the
form of $\mathbf B$ is coercive with $c = 1$, and conclude $\|\mathbf B^{-1}\| \leq 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf D_n\mathbf u = 2\sum_k|u_k|^2 - \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(u_k^*u_{k+1} + u_{k+1}^*u_k)$, and $|u_{k+1} - u_k|^2 =
|u_k|^2 + |u_{k+1}|^2 - u_k^*u_{k+1} - u_{k+1}^*u_k$. Summing the last identity over $k = 1, \dots, n - 1$ counts each $|u_k|^2$ twice except
$|u_1|^2$ and $|u_n|^2$, which gives the formula. So $\mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf B\mathbf u \geq \|\mathbf u\|^2$, real, and part (4) gives
$\|\mathbf B^{-1}\| \leq 1$.

## SageMath

Check on $n = 6$: the code verifies the summation by parts symbolically and computes $\|\mathbf B^{-1}\|$.

```{.python .sage}
n = 6
D = matrix(SR, n, n, lambda j, k: 2 if j == k else (-1 if abs(j - k) == 1 else 0))
xs = var(" ".join("x%d" % k for k in range(n))); ys = var(" ".join("y%d" % k for k in range(n)))
for t in xs + ys: assume(t, "real")
u = vector([xs[k] + I * ys[k] for k in range(n)])
cabs2 = lambda z: (z * z.conjugate()).expand()
lhs = (u.conjugate() * D * u).expand()
rhs = cabs2(u[0]) + sum(cabs2(u[k + 1] - u[k]) for k in range(n - 1)) + cabs2(u[n - 1])
print("summation by parts holds:", bool((lhs - rhs).expand() == 0))
B = (D + identity_matrix(n)).change_ring(RDF)
print("||B^-1|| = %.6f" % B.inverse().norm(2), "; at most 1:", B.inverse().norm(2) <= 1)
forget()
```

```{.text .sage-output}
summation by parts holds: True
||B^-1|| = 0.834681 ; at most 1: True
```
::::
:::

Part (3) uses the completeness of $\mathcal H$ through the uniform boundedness principle, and on an incomplete inner product space it
fails. The sixth exercise gives the counterexample on finitely supported sequences.

::: {#exr-sf-separate-boundedness-fails}
#### Separate boundedness on $c_{00}$

On $c_{00}$ with the inner product of $\ell^2$, let $b(a, c) = \sum_nna_n^*c_n$. Show that $u \mapsto b(u, c)$ and $v \mapsto b(a, v)$ are
bounded for fixed $c$ and $a$, but that $b$ is not bounded.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The sum is finite, and $b$ is sesquilinear. Fix $c$, with $c_n = 0$ for $n > N$. Then $b(u, c) = \sum_{n \leq N}nu_n^*c_n$, and $|b(u, c)|
\leq N\|c\|\,\|u\|$ by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; likewise for fixed $a$. But $b(\delta^{(n)}, \delta^{(n)}) = n$ with
$\|\delta^{(n)}\| = 1$, so no constant bounds $|b(u, v)|/(\|u\|\,\|v\|)$. Part (3) does not apply because $c_{00}$ is not complete: it is
dense in $\ell^2$ and not equal to it (@def-hilbert-space (3)).

## SageMath

The code evaluates $b(\delta^{(n)}, \delta^{(n)})$ and the bound $N\|c\|$ for a fixed $c$ with $N = 3$.

```{.python .sage}
b = lambda a, c: sum((n + 1) * conjugate(a[n]) * c[n] for n in range(min(len(a), len(c))))
d = lambda n, N: [1 if k == n else 0 for k in range(N)]
print("b(d_n, d_n) for n = 1..6:", [b(d(n, 6), d(n, 6)) for n in range(6)])
c = [1, 1, 1]
print("sup over unit u of |b(u, c)| = ||(n c_n)|| =", sqrt(sum(((n + 1) * c[n])^2 for n in range(3))), "<= N ||c|| =", 3 * sqrt(3))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
b(d_n, d_n) for n = 1..6: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
sup over unit u of |b(u, c)| = ||(n c_n)|| = sqrt(14) <= N ||c|| = 3*sqrt(3)
```
::::
:::

An infinite matrix with square-summable entries defines a bounded form on $\ell^2$, the discrete counterpart of the Hilbert-Schmidt bound
of @def-bounded-operator (6). The seventh exercise proves it and compares the bound with the norm for the entries $1/(j + k)^2$.

::: {#exr-sf-hilbert-schmidt-matrix}
#### Square-summable matrices

Let $\beta^2 = \sum_{j, k \geq 1}|b_{jk}|^2 < \infty$. Show that $b(a, c) = \sum_{j, k}a_j^*b_{jk}c_k$ converges absolutely on $\ell^2 \times
\ell^2$ and defines a bounded form with $\|b\| \leq \beta$. Compute $\beta$ for $b_{jk} = 1/(j + k)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for sums, $\sum_k|b_{jk}c_k| \leq (\sum_k|b_{jk}|^2)^{1/2}\|c\|$, and again
$$
\sum_j|a_j|\sum_k|b_{jk}c_k| \leq \|a\|\Bigl(\sum_j\sum_k|b_{jk}|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\|c\| = \beta\|a\|\,\|c\| ,
$$
so the double series converges absolutely, may be summed in any order, and is sesquilinear with $|b(a, c)| \leq \beta\|a\|\,\|c\|$. For
$b_{jk} = (j + k)^{-2}$, the pairs with $j + k = n$ number $n - 1$, so $\beta^2 = \sum_{n \geq 2}(n - 1)/n^4 = \zeta(3) - \zeta(4) \approx
0.1197$ and $\beta \approx 0.346$.

## SageMath

The code computes $\beta$ and the norms of the $N \times N$ truncations, which increase towards $\|b\| \leq \beta$.

```{.python .sage}
beta = sqrt(zeta(3) - zeta(4))
print("beta = %.6f" % beta.n())
for N in [10, 100, 400]:
    M = matrix(RDF, N, N, lambda j, k: 1 / (j + k + 2)^2)
    print("N =", N, ": norm of truncation = %.6f" % M.norm(2))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
beta = 0.346026
N = 10 : norm of truncation = 0.339908
N = 100 : norm of truncation = 0.341965
N = 400 : norm of truncation = 0.341970
```
::::
:::

An everywhere-defined symmetric operator is bounded, and this rules out the number operator of the oscillator as such an operator. The
eighth exercise draws this consequence of part (5).

::: {#exr-sf-number-operator}
#### No everywhere-defined number operator

Show that there is no linear map $N : \ell^2 \to \ell^2$ with $\langle Na, c\rangle = \langle a, Nc\rangle$ for all $a, c$ and
$N\delta^{(n)} = n\delta^{(n)}$ for all $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By part (5) such an $N$ would be bounded, so $n = \|N\delta^{(n)}\| \leq \|N\|$ for every $n$, which is impossible. The number operator
can therefore only be defined on a proper subspace of $\ell^2$, such as the sequences with $\sum_nn^2|a_n|^2 < \infty$
(@exm-fan-hellinger-toeplitz).

## SageMath

Check on the diagonal truncations $\operatorname{diag}(1, \dots, N)$: the code prints their norms, which grow without bound.

```{.python .sage}
for N in [1, 10, 100, 1000]:
    print("N =", N, ": norm of diag(1..N) =", max(abs(k) for k in range(1, N + 1)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
N = 1 : norm of diag(1..N) = 1
N = 10 : norm of diag(1..N) = 10
N = 100 : norm of diag(1..N) = 100
N = 1000 : norm of diag(1..N) = 1000
```
::::
:::

If all matrix elements of a sequence of operators converge, the limits are the matrix elements of a bounded operator. The ninth exercise
proves this with part (2) and @exr-bo-weakly-bounded, which is @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Thm. VI.1].

::: {#exr-sf-weak-limit}
#### Limits of matrix elements

Let $T_n \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ with $\lim_n\langle u, T_nv\rangle$ existing for all $u, v$. Show that there is $T \in \mathcal
B(\mathcal H)$ with $\langle u, T_nv\rangle \to \langle u, Tv\rangle$. Check it for the projections $P_n$ onto the first $n$ coordinates of
$\ell^2$ with $u = v = (1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A convergent sequence of numbers is bounded, so by @exr-bo-weakly-bounded $C = \sup_n\|T_n\| < \infty$. Let $b(u, v) = \lim_n\langle u,
T_nv\rangle$. It is sesquilinear by the limit rules, and $|b(u, v)| \leq C\|u\|\,\|v\|$. By part (2), $b = b_T$ for a unique $T \in \mathcal
B(\mathcal H)$. For $P_na = (a_1, \dots, a_n, 0, \dots)$, $\langle u, P_nu\rangle = \sum_{k \leq n}k^{-2} \to \pi^2/6 = \langle u, u\rangle$,
and in general $\langle u, P_nv\rangle = \sum_{k \leq n}u_k^*v_k \to \langle u, v\rangle$, so $T = 1$.

## SageMath

The code computes $\langle u, P_nu\rangle$ and its distance to $\pi^2/6$.

```{.python .sage}
for n in [1, 10, 100, 1000]:
    s = sum(1 / QQ(k)^2 for k in range(1, n + 1))
    print("n =", n, ": <u, P_n u> = %.8f ; pi^2/6 - <u, P_n u> = %.8f" % (s.n(), (pi^2 / 6 - s).n()))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
n = 1 : <u, P_n u> = 1.00000000 ; pi^2/6 - <u, P_n u> = 0.64493407
n = 10 : <u, P_n u> = 1.54976773 ; pi^2/6 - <u, P_n u> = 0.09516634
n = 100 : <u, P_n u> = 1.63498390 ; pi^2/6 - <u, P_n u> = 0.00995017
n = 1000 : <u, P_n u> = 1.64393457 ; pi^2/6 - <u, P_n u> = 0.00099950
```
::::
:::

An integral equation of the second kind, $f + \lambda Kf = w$, has a coercive form when $|\lambda|\,\|k\|_2 < 1$, and part (4) then
solves it. The last exercise proves this and solves an example with a rank-one kernel.

::: {#exr-sf-integral-equation}
#### An integral equation

Let $K$ have the continuous kernel $k$ on $[a, b]$ and $|\lambda|\,\|k\|_2 < 1$. Show that $1 + \lambda K$ has a coercive form, so that
$F + \lambda KF = W$ has exactly one solution in $L^2[a, b]$ for each $W$. Solve $f(x) + \int_0^1xyf(y)\,dy = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\operatorname{Re}\langle F, (1 + \lambda K)F\rangle \geq \|F\|^2 - |\lambda|\,|\langle F, KF\rangle| \geq (1 - |\lambda|\,\|k\|_2)\|F\|^2$ by
@def-bounded-operator (2) and (6), so the form of $1 + \lambda K$ is coercive with $c = 1 - |\lambda|\,\|k\|_2$, and part (4) applies. For
$k = xy$ on $[0, 1]$, $\|k\|_2 = \tfrac13$ and $\lambda = 1$. A solution has the form $f = 1 - \gamma x$ with $\gamma = \int_0^1yf(y)\,dy =
\tfrac12 - \tfrac\gamma3$, so $\gamma = \tfrac38$ and $f(x) = 1 - \tfrac38x$; it is the only one by part (4).

## SageMath

The code substitutes $f = 1 - 3x/8$ into the equation.

```{.python .sage}
x, y = var("x y")
f = 1 - 3 * x / 8
print("f + K f - 1 =", (f + x * integrate(y * f.subs(x=y), y, 0, 1) - 1).simplify_full(), "; ||k||_2 =", sqrt(integrate(integrate(x^2 * y^2, x, 0, 1), y, 0, 1)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
f + K f - 1 = 0 ; ||k||_2 = 1/3
```
::::
:::
::::

### The adjoint

Moving an operator from one slot of the inner product to the other produces, in general, a different operator; for matrices it is the
conjugate transpose. The definition below introduces it for bounded operators, where @thm-sesquilinear-forms (2) guarantees that it
exists, and lists its rules, its relation to kernels and ranges, and its form for the model operators.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-adjoint-operator}
#### Adjoint operator

The **adjoint** of $A \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ is the operator $A^\dagger$ with $\langle Au, v\rangle = \langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle$ for all
$u, v \in \mathcal H$. In Dirac's notation, $|w\rangle\langle v|$ is the operator $u \mapsto \langle v, u\rangle w$. Then:

1. $A^\dagger$ exists, is unique, and lies in $\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$;
2. $(\alpha A + B)^\dagger = \alpha^*A^\dagger + B^\dagger$, $(AB)^\dagger = B^\dagger A^\dagger$, $(A^\dagger)^\dagger = A$ and $1^\dagger = 1$;
   if $A$ has an inverse $A^{-1} \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$, then $A^\dagger$ is invertible and $(A^\dagger)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^\dagger$;
3. $\|A^\dagger\| = \|A\|$ and $\|A^\dagger A\| = \|A\|^2$; so $A \mapsto A^\dagger$ is continuous;
4. $\ker A^\dagger = (\operatorname{ran}A)^\perp$ and $(\ker A^\dagger)^\perp$ is the closure of $\operatorname{ran}A$, so $\mathcal H =
   \overline{\operatorname{ran}A} \oplus \ker A^\dagger$;
5. on $\mathbb{C}^n$ with $\langle\mathbf u, \mathbf v\rangle = \mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf v$, the adjoint of a matrix is its conjugate
   transpose $\mathbf A^\dagger = (\mathbf A^*)^\top$, and $(|w\rangle\langle v|)^\dagger = |v\rangle\langle w|$;
6. for the operators of @def-bounded-operator (4)-(6): $S^\dagger = L$ and $D^\dagger$ is the diagonal operator with entries $d_n^*$;
   $M_g^\dagger = M_{g^*}$; and $K^\dagger$ is the integral operator with the continuous kernel $k^\dagger(x, y) = k(y, x)^*$.
:::
::::

*Proof.* (1) $b(u, v) = \langle Au, v\rangle$ is sesquilinear by @def-inner-product (1) and bounded by $\|A\|$, so by
@thm-sesquilinear-forms (2) there is exactly one $B \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ with $\langle Au, v\rangle = \langle u, Bv\rangle$.

(2) Each identity follows from the uniqueness in (1): $\langle(\alpha A + B)u, v\rangle = \alpha^*\langle Au, v\rangle + \langle Bu, v\rangle
= \langle u, (\alpha^*A^\dagger + B^\dagger)v\rangle$; $\langle ABu, v\rangle = \langle Bu, A^\dagger v\rangle = \langle u, B^\dagger A^\dagger
v\rangle$; $\langle A^\dagger u, v\rangle = \langle v, A^\dagger u\rangle^* = \langle Av, u\rangle^* = \langle u, Av\rangle$, so
$(A^\dagger)^\dagger = A$; and $1^\dagger = 1$ is clear. Applying the product rule to $AA^{-1} = 1 = A^{-1}A$ gives $(A^{-1})^\dagger
A^\dagger = 1 = A^\dagger(A^{-1})^\dagger$.

(3) By @def-bounded-operator (2), $\|A^\dagger\| = \sup|\langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle| = \sup|\langle Au, v\rangle| = \|A\|$, the suprema over
$\|u\|, \|v\| \leq 1$. Then $\|A^\dagger A\| \leq \|A^\dagger\|\,\|A\| = \|A\|^2$, and $\|Au\|^2 = \langle u, A^\dagger Au\rangle \leq \|A^\dagger
A\|\,\|u\|^2$ gives $\|A\|^2 \leq \|A^\dagger A\|$. Continuity follows from $\|A^\dagger - B^\dagger\| = \|(A - B)^\dagger\| = \|A - B\|$.

(4) $v \in \ker A^\dagger$ if and only if $\langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle = 0$ for all $u$ (@def-inner-product (2)), that is $\langle Au,
v\rangle = 0$ for all $u$, that is $v \perp \operatorname{ran}A$. Since $\operatorname{ran}A$ is a subspace, @thm-projection (3) gives
$(\ker A^\dagger)^\perp = (\operatorname{ran}A)^{\perp\perp} = \overline{\operatorname{ran}A}$. A vector orthogonal to $\operatorname{ran}A$ is
orthogonal to its closure, by continuity of the inner product (@thm-cauchy-schwarz (3)), so $\overline{\operatorname{ran}A}^\perp =
\ker A^\dagger$, and @thm-projection (2) gives the decomposition.

(5) $\langle\mathbf A\mathbf u, \mathbf v\rangle = (\mathbf A\mathbf u)^\dagger\mathbf v = \mathbf u^\dagger(\mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf v)$.
For the rank-one operator, $\langle\langle v, u\rangle w, x\rangle = \langle v, u\rangle^*\langle w, x\rangle = \langle u, \langle w,
x\rangle v\rangle$.

(6) For $a, c \in \ell^2$, $\langle Sa, c\rangle = \sum_{n \geq 2}a_{n-1}^*c_n = \sum_{n \geq 1}a_n^*c_{n+1} = \langle a, Lc\rangle$, the
series converging absolutely (@def-hilbert-space (3)), and $\langle Da, c\rangle = \sum_n d_n^*a_n^*c_n = \langle a, D'c\rangle$ with
$(D'c)_n = d_n^*c_n$. For continuous $f, h$, $\langle M_gf, h\rangle = \int_a^b(gf)^*h = \int_a^bf^*(g^*h) = \langle f, M_{g^*}h\rangle$; both
sides are continuous on $L^2[a, b] \times L^2[a, b]$ (@thm-cauchy-schwarz (3)) and $C[a, b]$ is dense, so the identity holds on $L^2[a,
b]$. For $K$ and continuous $f, h$, Fubini's theorem (@def-multiple-integral (4)) for the continuous integrand gives
$$
\langle Kf, h\rangle = \int_a^b\!\!\int_a^bk(x, y)^*f(y)^*h(x)\,dy\,dx = \int_a^bf(y)^*\Bigl(\int_a^bk(x, y)^*h(x)\,dx\Bigr)dy = \langle f,
K'h\rangle ,
$$
where $K'$ is the integral operator with kernel $k'(y, x) = k(x, y)^*$, continuous; by density again $K^\dagger = K'$. $\square$

These are @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Thm. VI.3], @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.20] and @gasinski2014exercises [Def. 5.108(a), Problem 5.123].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The conjugate transpose is the adjoint because the standard inner product on $\mathbb{C}^n$ conjugates the first vector. The first example
verifies the defining identity on a matrix with a complex entry, where the conjugation matters.

::: {#exm-adj-matrix}
#### The conjugate transpose

For $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & i \\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf A^\dagger = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -i & 2\end{pmatrix}$. With
$\mathbf u = \mathbf e_2$ and $\mathbf v = \mathbf e_1$: $\mathbf A\mathbf u = (i, 2)$, so $\langle\mathbf A\mathbf u, \mathbf v\rangle = i^*
= -i$, and $\mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf v = (1, -i)$, so $\langle\mathbf u, \mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf v\rangle = -i$. With the plain transpose in
place of $\mathbf A^\dagger$ the right side would be $i \neq -i$.
:::

Dirac's notation turns the adjoint of a rank-one operator into the exchange of a bra and a ket. The second example uses part (5) on the
operator that maps one spin state to another.

::: {#exm-adj-rank-one}
#### Exchanging bra and ket

On $\mathbb{C}^2$ with $\mathbf e_\uparrow = \mathbf e_1$ and $\mathbf e_\downarrow = \mathbf e_2$, $|\mathbf e_\uparrow\rangle\langle\mathbf
e_\downarrow|$ maps $\mathbf e_\downarrow$ to $\mathbf e_\uparrow$ and $\mathbf e_\uparrow$ to $\mathbf 0$: it is the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\
0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. By part (5) its adjoint is $|\mathbf e_\downarrow\rangle\langle\mathbf e_\uparrow| = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 &
0\end{pmatrix}$, the conjugate transpose, and $|e\rangle\langle e|$ equals its own adjoint for every $e$.
:::

The adjoint of the right shift is the left shift, and the two compositions differ, which is impossible for square matrices. The third
example combines part (6) with @def-bounded-operator (4).

::: {#exm-adj-shift}
#### The adjoint of the shift

$\langle Sa, b\rangle = \sum_{n \geq 2}a_{n-1}^*b_n = \sum_{n \geq 1}a_n^*b_{n+1} = \langle a, Lb\rangle$, so $S^\dagger = L$, the left shift.
$S^\dagger S = 1$, but $SS^\dagger a = (0, a_2, a_3, \dots)$, so $SS^\dagger = 1 - P_1$: a one-sided inverse that is not two-sided. The
finite truncations of @exr-boc-shift-matrix lose a coordinate at the end and so have $\mathbf S_N^\top\mathbf S_N \neq \mathbf I$.
:::

For multiplication and integral operators the adjoint is found by rewriting an integral: conjugate the multiplier, or conjugate and
transpose the kernel. The fourth example applies the rules, which cover most operators met in practice.

::: {#exm-adj-multiplication}
#### Multiplication and integral operators

On $L^2[0, 1]$, $M_{e^{2\pi ix}}^\dagger = M_{e^{-2\pi ix}}$ and $M_x^\dagger = M_x$, by part (6). The integral operator with kernel $k(x, y) =
e^{x - y} + i(x - y)$ has adjoint kernel $k(y, x)^* = e^{y - x} + i(x - y)$; and the string kernel $\min(x, y) - xy$ of
@exm-bo-integral-string, real and symmetric, gives an operator equal to its own adjoint.
:::

Part (4) turns questions about the range of an operator into questions about the kernel of its adjoint. The fifth example computes both
for the shift.

::: {#exm-adj-kernel-range}
#### Kernel and range of the shift

$\operatorname{ran}S = \{a : a_1 = 0\}$, a closed subspace, and $\ker S^\dagger = \ker L = \{a : a_2 = a_3 = \dots = 0\} = \mathbb{C}\delta^{(1)}$.
Part (4) says $\ker L = (\operatorname{ran}S)^\perp$, which is visible here, and $\ell^2 = \operatorname{ran}S \oplus \mathbb{C}\delta^{(1)}$.
For $L$, $\operatorname{ran}L = \ell^2$ and $\ker L^\dagger = \ker S = \{0\}$.
:::

The spin raising and lowering matrices are adjoints of each other, which is why their products give spin projections. The sixth example
computes them from the Pauli matrices.

::: {#exm-adj-pauli-ladder}
#### Raising and lowering a spin

$\sigma_\pm = \tfrac12(\sigma_1 \pm i\sigma_2)$ give $\sigma_+ = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\sigma_- = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0
\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. Since $\sigma_1, \sigma_2$ equal their conjugate transposes, part (2) gives $\sigma_+^\dagger = \tfrac12(\sigma_1 -
i\sigma_2) = \sigma_-$. The products $\sigma_+\sigma_- = \operatorname{diag}(1, 0)$ and $\sigma_-\sigma_+ = \operatorname{diag}(0, 1)$ pick out
spin up and spin down, and $\|\sigma_+\|^2 = \|\sigma_+^\dagger\sigma_+\| = 1$ by part (3).
:::

A particle pushed from rest by a force $f$ has the position $u(t) = \int_0^t(t - s)f(s)\,ds$, an integral operator with a continuous kernel.
The seventh example finds its adjoint, which runs time backwards.

::: {#exm-adj-newton}
#### A particle driven from rest

On $[0, 1]$ let $k(t, s) = (t - s)_+$, continuous, so $(Kf)(t) = \int_0^t(t - s)f(s)\,ds$ satisfies $u'' = f$, $u(0) = u'(0) = 0$. By part (6),
$K^\dagger$ has kernel $(s - t)_+$: $(K^\dagger h)(t) = \int_t^1(s - t)h(s)\,ds$, which satisfies $v'' = h$ with $v(1) = v'(1) = 0$, the
same law of motion with final instead of initial conditions.
:::

In optics a beam splitter mixes two modes by a $2 \times 2$ matrix whose adjoint is its inverse, so that no light is lost. The eighth example
computes both.

::: {#exm-adj-beam-splitter}
#### A beam splitter

$\mathbf B = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & i \\ i & 1\end{pmatrix}$ has $\mathbf B^\dagger = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -i \\ -i &
1\end{pmatrix}$, and $\mathbf B^\dagger\mathbf B = \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix} = \mathbf I$. So $\|\mathbf B\mathbf u\|^2
= \langle\mathbf u, \mathbf B^\dagger\mathbf B\mathbf u\rangle = \|\mathbf u\|^2$: the total intensity is preserved, and $\mathbf B^{-1} =
\mathbf B^\dagger$ by part (2).
:::

The adjoint depends on the inner product, and the conjugate transpose is the adjoint only for the standard one. The ninth example changes
the inner product of $\mathbb{C}^2$ and finds a different adjoint.

::: {#exm-adj-weighted-inner-product}
#### The adjoint for another inner product

With $\langle\mathbf u, \mathbf v\rangle_{\mathbf W} = \mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf W\mathbf v$, $\mathbf W = \operatorname{diag}(1, 2)$, the identity
$(\mathbf A\mathbf u)^\dagger\mathbf W\mathbf v = \mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf W(\mathbf W^{-1}\mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf W)\mathbf v$ shows that the
adjoint is $\mathbf W^{-1}\mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf W$. For $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ it is $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0
\\ 2 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, not the conjugate transpose.
:::

Norm continuity of the adjoint (part (3)) does not extend to vector-by-vector convergence. The last example, from @reed1980methods [Vol. I,
Thm. VI.3(e)], shows a sequence that converges on every vector while its adjoints do not.

::: {#exm-adj-strong-not-continuous}
#### Adjoints of converging powers

$\|L^na\|^2 = \sum_{k > n}|a_k|^2 \to 0$ for every $a \in \ell^2$, so $L^na \to 0$ for each $a$. The adjoints are $(L^n)^\dagger = S^n$ by part
(2), and $\|S^na\| = \|a\|$, so $S^na \not\to 0$ for $a \neq 0$. Convergence on each vector is not preserved by $A \mapsto A^\dagger$,
although $\|L^n\| = 1$ for all $n$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
With symbolic vectors Sage verifies the defining identity of the adjoint as a polynomial identity in the components. The first exercise
does this for a $3 \times 3$ complex matrix and checks the product rule of part (2).

::: {#exr-adj-sage-check}
#### The adjoint identity in Sage

For $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & i & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 - i \\ 0 & 3i & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and symbolic $\mathbf u, \mathbf v \in \mathbb{C}^3$,
check $\langle\mathbf A\mathbf u, \mathbf v\rangle = \langle\mathbf u, \mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf v\rangle$, show that the identity fails for the
plain transpose, and verify $(\mathbf A\mathbf B)^\dagger = \mathbf B^\dagger\mathbf A^\dagger$ for $\mathbf B = \mathbf A^2 + i\mathbf A$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By part (5), $\langle\mathbf A\mathbf u, \mathbf v\rangle = \mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf v = \langle\mathbf u, \mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf
v\rangle$ for all $\mathbf u, \mathbf v$, and the product rule is part (2). With $\mathbf A^\top$ in place of $\mathbf A^\dagger$ the difference
is $\mathbf u^\dagger(\mathbf A^\dagger - \mathbf A^\top)\mathbf v$, and $\mathbf A^\dagger - \mathbf A^\top = (\mathbf A^* - \mathbf A)^\top$
is $-2i$ times the transpose of the imaginary part of $\mathbf A$, which is non-zero.

## SageMath

The code expands both sides with symbolic components and conjugates.

```{.python .sage}
A = matrix(SR, [[1, I, 0], [2, 0, 1 - I], [0, 3 * I, 1]])
u = vector(SR, var("u1 u2 u3")); v = vector(SR, var("v1 v2 v3"))
ip = lambda a, b: sum(conjugate(x) * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
print("A^dagger ="); print(A.conjugate_transpose())
print("<A u, v> - <u, A^dagger v> =", (ip(A * u, v) - ip(u, A.conjugate_transpose() * v)).simplify_full())
print("<A u, v> - <u, A^T v> =", (ip(A * u, v) - ip(u, A.transpose() * v)).simplify_full())
B = A^2 + I * A
print("(AB)^dagger = B^dagger A^dagger:", bool((A * B).conjugate_transpose() == B.conjugate_transpose() * A.conjugate_transpose()))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
A^dagger =
[    1     2     0]
[   -I     0  -3*I]
[    0 I + 1     1]
<A u, v> - <u, A^dagger v> = 0
<A u, v> - <u, A^T v> = -2*I*u2*v1 + 2*I*u3*v2 - 6*I*u2*v3
(AB)^dagger = B^dagger A^dagger: True
```
::::
:::

The identity $\|A^\dagger A\| = \|A\|^2$ of part (3), applied repeatedly, gives the norms of all powers of $A^\dagger A$ of the form $2^m$. The
second exercise proves this and checks it on a matrix.

::: {#exr-adj-properties}
#### Powers of $A^\dagger A$

Show that $\|AA^\dagger\| = \|A\|^2$, that $B = A^\dagger A$ satisfies $B^\dagger = B$ and $\|B^2\| = \|B\|^2$, and deduce $\|(A^\dagger
A)^{2^m}\| = \|A\|^{2^{m+1}}$ for $m \geq 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By part (2), $(AA^\dagger) = (A^\dagger)^\dagger A^\dagger$, so part (3) for $A^\dagger$ gives $\|AA^\dagger\| = \|A^\dagger\|^2 = \|A\|^2$. Also
$B^\dagger = A^\dagger(A^\dagger)^\dagger = A^\dagger A = B$, and part (3) for $B$ gives $\|B^2\| = \|B^\dagger B\| = \|B\|^2$. Each power
$B^{2^m}$ equals its adjoint by the product rule, so induction gives $\|B^{2^{m+1}}\| = \|(B^{2^m})^2\| = \|B^{2^m}\|^2$, hence
$\|B^{2^m}\| = \|B\|^{2^m} = \|A\|^{2^{m+1}}$.

## SageMath

Check on $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$: the code compares $\|(\mathbf A^\top\mathbf A)^{2^m}\|$ with
$\|\mathbf A\|^{2^{m+1}}$ for $m = 0, 1, 2$.

```{.python .sage}
A = matrix(QQbar, [[2, 1], [0, 1]])
nrm = lambda M: sqrt(max((M.conjugate_transpose() * M).eigenvalues()))
B = A.conjugate_transpose() * A
print("||A A^dagger|| = ||A||^2:", nrm(A * A.conjugate_transpose()) == nrm(A)^2)
for m in range(3):
    print("m =", m, ": ||B^(2^m)|| =", nrm(B^(2^m)).n(digits=10), "; ||A||^(2^(m+1)) =", (nrm(A)^(2^(m + 1))).n(digits=10), "; equal:", nrm(B^(2^m)) == nrm(A)^(2^(m + 1)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
||A A^dagger|| = ||A||^2: True
m = 0 : ||B^(2^m)|| = 5.236067978 ; ||A||^(2^(m+1)) = 5.236067978 ; equal: True
m = 1 : ||B^(2^m)|| = 27.41640787 ; ||A||^(2^(m+1)) = 27.41640787 ; equal: True
m = 2 : ||B^(2^m)|| = 751.6594202 ; ||A||^(2^(m+1)) = 751.6594202 ; equal: True
```
::::
:::

The integral operators are the infinite-dimensional matrices, and the rule of part (6) for their adjoints is the conjugate transpose of
the kernel. The third exercise decides for four kernels whether the operator equals its adjoint.

::: {#exr-adj-integral-operator}
#### The adjoint kernel

For $K$ on $L^2[0, 1]$ with continuous kernel $k$, show that $K = K^\dagger$ exactly when $k(x, y) = k(y, x)^*$ for all $x, y$. Which of $k =
xy$, $k = x - y$, $k = i(x - y)$, $k = e^{i(x - y)}$ give $K = K^\dagger$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By part (6), $K - K^\dagger$ is the integral operator with the continuous kernel $m(x, y) = k(x, y) - k(y, x)^*$. If $m = 0$, then $K =
K^\dagger$. Conversely let $K = K^\dagger$ and fix $x_0$. For the continuous $h = m(x_0, \cdot)^*$, the function $(K - K^\dagger)h$ is continuous
(@def-bounded-operator (6)) and is $0$ in $L^2[0, 1]$, so it vanishes identically, as a continuous function of norm $0$; at $x_0$ it is
$\int_0^1|m(x_0, y)|^2dy = 0$, so $m(x_0, \cdot) = 0$. Of the four kernels: $xy$ is real and symmetric, so $K = K^\dagger$; $x - y$ gives
$k(y, x)^* = y - x \neq k$; $i(x - y)$ gives $(i(y - x))^* = i(x - y) = k$; and $e^{i(x - y)}$ gives $(e^{i(y - x)})^* = e^{i(x - y)} = k$.

## SageMath

The code computes $k(x, y) - k(y, x)^*$ for the four kernels, with real $x, y$.

```{.python .sage}
x, y = var("x y", domain="real")
for k in [x * y, x - y, I * (x - y), exp(I * (x - y))]:
    print("k =", k, ": k(x, y) - k(y, x)^* =", (k - conjugate(k.subs({x: y, y: x}, ))).simplify_full())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
k = x*y : k(x, y) - k(y, x)^* = 0
k = x - y : k(x, y) - k(y, x)^* = 2*x - 2*y
k = I*x - I*y : k(x, y) - k(y, x)^* = 0
k = e^(I*x - I*y) : k(x, y) - k(y, x)^* = 0
```
::::
:::

Part (4) gives the closure of the range of a matrix as the orthogonal complement of the kernel of its adjoint. The fourth exercise checks
this on a singular $3 \times 3$ complex matrix.

::: {#exr-adj-kernel-range}
#### Range and kernel of a matrix

For $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & i & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2i & i\end{pmatrix}$, compute $\ker\mathbf A^\dagger$ and $\operatorname{ran}\mathbf
A$, and verify that they are orthogonal complements in $\mathbb{C}^3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The third row is the first plus $i$ times the second, so $\mathbf A$ has rank $2$ and $\operatorname{ran}\mathbf A$ is spanned by the first two
columns $(1, 0, 1)$ and $(i, 1, 2i)$. A vector $\mathbf v$ is in $\ker\mathbf A^\dagger$ when it is orthogonal to both columns: $v_1 + v_3 = 0$
and $-iv_1 + v_2 - 2iv_3 = 0$, so $\mathbf v = t(1, -i, -1)$. In finite dimension the range is closed, and part (4) says $\mathbb{C}^3 =
\operatorname{ran}\mathbf A \oplus \ker\mathbf A^\dagger$, consistent with $2 + 1 = 3$.

## SageMath

The code computes the column space and $\ker\mathbf A^\dagger$ and their mutual inner products.

```{.python .sage}
K.<i> = QuadraticField(-1)
A = matrix(K, [[1, i, 0], [0, 1, 1], [1, 2 * i, i]])
R = A.column_space().basis(); N = A.conjugate_transpose().right_kernel().basis()
print("rank:", A.rank(), "; ker A^dagger:", N)
print("inner products <col, v>:", [sum(c[j].conjugate() * n[j] for j in range(3)) for c in R for n in N])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
rank: 2 ; ker A^dagger: [
(1, -i, -1)
]
inner products <col, v>: [0, 0]
```
::::
:::

A diagonal operator and its adjoint differ only by conjugating the entries, and a weighted shift has a weighted left shift as adjoint.
The fifth exercise asks for both.

::: {#exr-adj-diagonal}
#### Diagonal and weighted shifts

Let $(w_n)$ be bounded. Find the adjoint of the weighted shift $W(a_1, a_2, \dots) = (0, w_1a_1, w_2a_2, \dots)$ on $\ell^2$, and compute
$W^\dagger W$ and $WW^\dagger$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$W = SD$ with $D$ the diagonal operator of the $w_n$, so $W$ is bounded (@def-bounded-operator (1), (4)) and, by parts (2) and (6),
$W^\dagger = D^\dagger S^\dagger = D^\dagger L$: $W^\dagger(c_1, c_2, \dots) = (w_1^*c_2, w_2^*c_3, \dots)$. Then $W^\dagger Wa = D^\dagger LSDa =
D^\dagger Da$ has entries $|w_n|^2a_n$, and $WW^\dagger c = SDD^\dagger Lc = (0, |w_1|^2c_2, |w_2|^2c_3, \dots)$.

## SageMath

Check on $N \times N$ truncations with $w_n = 1/n$: the code compares the conjugate transpose with $\mathbf D^\dagger\mathbf L$ and prints
the diagonals of the two products.

```{.python .sage}
N = 5
S = matrix(QQ, N, N, lambda j, k: 1 if j == k + 1 else 0)
D = diagonal_matrix(QQ, [1 / QQ(n) for n in range(1, N + 1)])
W = S * D
print("W^dagger = D^dagger L:", W.conjugate_transpose() == D.conjugate_transpose() * S.transpose())
print("W^dagger W diagonal:", (W.conjugate_transpose() * W).diagonal())
print("W W^dagger diagonal:", (W * W.conjugate_transpose()).diagonal())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
W^dagger = D^dagger L: True
W^dagger W diagonal: [1, 1/4, 1/9, 1/16, 0]
W W^dagger diagonal: [0, 1, 1/4, 1/9, 1/16]
```
::::
:::

The range of a bounded operator can be dense without being closed, which never happens in finite dimension. The sixth exercise, after
@reed1980methods [Vol. I, Problem VI.7], shows it for a diagonal operator, with part (4) giving the density.

::: {#exr-adj-range-not-closed}
#### A dense range that is not closed

Let $D$ be the diagonal operator with entries $1/n$ on $\ell^2$. Show that $\operatorname{ran}D$ is dense but that $(1/n)_n \notin
\operatorname{ran}D$, so $\operatorname{ran}D$ is not closed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$D^\dagger = D$ by part (6), and $Dc = 0$ forces $c_n/n = 0$ for all $n$, so $\ker D^\dagger = \{0\}$ and $\operatorname{ran}D$ is dense by part
(4). If $Da = (1/n)$, then $a_n/n = 1/n$, so $a = (1, 1, \dots) \notin \ell^2$; hence $(1/n) \in \ell^2$ is not in $\operatorname{ran}D$, and a
dense subspace that is not everything is not closed.

## SageMath

The code computes $\|a^{(N)}\|$ for the truncations $a^{(N)} = (1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots)$, whose images $Da^{(N)}$ converge to $(1/n)$.

```{.python .sage}
for N in [10, 100, 1000]:
    dist = sqrt(sum(1 / QQ(n)^2 for n in range(N + 1, 20 * N)))
    print("N =", N, ": ||a^(N)|| = sqrt(N) = %.3f ; ||D a^(N) - (1/n)|| about %.5f" % (sqrt(N).n(), dist.n()))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
N = 10 : ||a^(N)|| = sqrt(N) = 3.162 ; ||D a^(N) - (1/n)|| about 0.30026
N = 100 : ||a^(N)|| = sqrt(N) = 10.000 ; ||D a^(N) - (1/n)|| about 0.09721
N = 1000 : ||a^(N)|| = sqrt(N) = 31.623 ; ||D a^(N) - (1/n)|| about 0.03081
```
::::
:::

The operator of a particle driven from rest, @exm-adj-newton, has an explicit adjoint, and $K^\dagger K$ is an integral operator whose
kernel @exr-bo-integral-composition computes. The seventh exercise finds both and the Hilbert-Schmidt bound.

::: {#exr-adj-newton}
#### The driven particle in Sage

For $k(t, s) = (t - s)_+$ on $[0, 1]$, compute $\|k\|_2$, the kernel of $K^\dagger K$ at $t \leq s$, and check $\langle Kf, h\rangle = \langle f,
K^\dagger h\rangle$ for $f = 1$, $h = t$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\|k\|_2^2 = \int_0^1\int_0^t(t - s)^2ds\,dt = \int_0^1t^3/3\,dt = \tfrac1{12}$. By @exr-bo-integral-composition and part (6), $K^\dagger K$ has kernel
$\int_0^1k(r, t)k(r, s)\,dr = \int_{\max(t, s)}^1(r - t)(r - s)\,dr$, which for $t \leq s$ is $\tfrac13(1 - s)^3 + \tfrac12(s - t)(1 - s)^2$. For
$f = 1$, $Kf = t^2/2$ and $\langle Kf, h\rangle = \int_0^1t^3/2 = \tfrac18$; $K^\dagger h(s) = \int_s^1(r - s)r\,dr$ and $\langle f, K^\dagger
h\rangle = \int_0^1\int_s^1(r - s)r\,dr\,ds = \tfrac18$.

## SageMath

The code computes the three quantities symbolically.

```{.python .sage}
t, s, r = var("t s r")
assume(0 < t, t < s, s < 1)
print("||k||_2^2 =", integrate(integrate((t - s)^2, s, 0, t), t, 0, 1))
kk = integrate((r - t) * (r - s), r, s, 1).factor()
print("kernel of K^dagger K for t <= s:", kk, "; matches:", bool((kk - ((1 - s)^3 / 3 + (s - t) * (1 - s)^2 / 2)).expand() == 0))
forget()
lhs = integrate(integrate(t - s, s, 0, t) * t, t, 0, 1)
rhs = integrate(integrate((r - s) * r, r, s, 1), s, 0, 1)
print("<K 1, t> =", lhs, "; <1, K^dagger t> =", rhs)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
||k||_2^2 = 1/12
kernel of K^dagger K for t <= s: 1/6*(s - 3*t + 2)*(s - 1)^2 ; matches: True
<K 1, t> = 1/8 ; <1, K^dagger t> = 1/8
```
::::
:::

The identity $\|A^\dagger A\| = \|A\|^2$ can be checked directly on the model operators, where both sides are explicit. The eighth exercise
does this for a multiplication operator and for a weighted shift.

::: {#exr-adj-norm-identity}
#### $\|A^\dagger A\| = \|A\|^2$ on examples

Verify part (3) for $M_g$ on $L^2[0, 1]$ with $g(x) = x + ix^2$, and for the weighted shift $W$ of @exr-adj-diagonal with $w_n = 1 -
2^{-n}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By part (6) and @def-bounded-operator (5), $M_g^\dagger M_g = M_{g^*}M_g = M_{|g|^2}$, of norm $\||g|^2\|_\infty = \|g\|_\infty^2$. Here $|g|^2 =
x^2 + x^4$ has maximum $2$ at $x = 1$, so $\|M_g\| = \sqrt2$ and $\|M_g^\dagger M_g\| = 2$. For $W$, $W^\dagger W$ is diagonal with entries
$|w_n|^2$ (@exr-adj-diagonal), of norm $\sup_n(1 - 2^{-n})^2 = 1$, and $\|W\| = \sup_n|w_n| = 1$ since $\|Wa\|^2 = \sum|w_n|^2|a_n|^2$.

## SageMath

Check on these two operators: the code computes $\max|g|^2$ and the norms of truncations of $W$ and $W^\dagger W$.

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x")
print("max of |g|^2 on [0, 1]:", max((x^2 + x^4).subs(x=QQ(j) / 100) for j in range(101)))
for N in [5, 20]:
    W = matrix(RDF, N, N, lambda j, k: 1 - 2^(-(k + 1)) if j == k + 1 else 0)
    print("N =", N, ": ||W_N||^2 = %.8f ; ||W_N^T W_N|| = %.8f" % (W.norm(2)^2, (W.transpose() * W).norm(2)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
max of |g|^2 on [0, 1]: 2
N = 5 : ||W_N||^2 = 0.87890625 ; ||W_N^T W_N|| = 0.87890625
N = 20 : ||W_N||^2 = 0.99999619 ; ||W_N^T W_N|| = 0.99999619
```
::::
:::

The adjoint of a Hilbert space operator is related, through the Riesz map, to the dual map $\varphi \mapsto \varphi \circ A$ on
$\mathcal H^*$. The ninth exercise proves the relation of @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Sec. VI.2].

::: {#exr-adj-dual-map}
#### The adjoint and the dual map

For $A \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ let $A'\varphi = \varphi \circ A$ on $\mathcal H^*$, and $C v = \langle v, \cdot\rangle$ the antilinear bijection of
@thm-riesz-representation (2). Show that $A' \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H^*)$ with $\|A'\| \leq \|A\|$, and that $A^\dagger = C^{-1}A'C$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\varphi \circ A$ is linear and $|\varphi(Au)| \leq \|\varphi\|\,\|A\|\,\|u\|$, so $A'\varphi \in \mathcal H^*$ with $\|A'\varphi\| \leq
\|A\|\,\|\varphi\|$, and $A'$ is linear. For $v \in \mathcal H$, $(A'Cv)(u) = \langle v, Au\rangle = \langle A^\dagger v, u\rangle = (CA^\dagger
v)(u)$, so $A'C = CA^\dagger$ and $A^\dagger = C^{-1}A'C$. Since $C$ and $C^{-1}$ are isometric, $\|A'\| = \|A^\dagger\| = \|A\|$ by part (3).

## SageMath

Check on $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & i \\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$: a functional is a row $\mathbf r$ with $\varphi(\mathbf u) = \mathbf
r\mathbf u$, $C\mathbf v$ is the row $\mathbf v^\dagger$, and $A'$ maps $\mathbf r$ to $\mathbf r\mathbf A$; the code compares $C^{-1}A'C\mathbf
v$ with $\mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf v$.

```{.python .sage}
K.<i> = QuadraticField(-1)
A = matrix(K, [[1, i], [2, 3]])
conj = lambda w: vector(K, [z.conjugate() for z in w])
v = vector(K, [1 + 2 * i, -3])
row = conj(v)                       # C v
row2 = row * A                      # A'(C v)
print("C^-1 A' C v =", conj(row2), "; A^dagger v =", A.conjugate_transpose() * v, "; equal:", conj(row2) == A.conjugate_transpose() * v)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
C^-1 A' C v = (2*i - 5, -i - 7) ; A^dagger v = (2*i - 5, -i - 7) ; equal: True
```
::::
:::

The operator of a bounded form is the adjoint of the operator of the form with its slots exchanged and conjugated. The last exercise proves
this, which combines part (1) with @thm-sesquilinear-forms (2).

::: {#exr-adj-sesquilinear-form}
#### The adjoint of a form

Let $b$ be a bounded sesquilinear form with operator $A$, and $b^\star(u, v) = b(v, u)^*$. Show that $b^\star$ is a bounded sesquilinear form
with operator $A^\dagger$, and that $b$ is hermitian if and only if $A = A^\dagger$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$b^\star$ is antilinear in $u$ and linear in $v$, since conjugation exchanges the two, and $|b^\star(u, v)| \leq \|b\|\,\|u\|\,\|v\|$. Further
$b^\star(u, v) = \langle v, Au\rangle^* = \langle Au, v\rangle = \langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle$, so its operator is $A^\dagger$. $b$ is hermitian
exactly when $b = b^\star$, which by the uniqueness in @thm-sesquilinear-forms (2) means $A = A^\dagger$.

## SageMath

Check on $b(\mathbf u, \mathbf v) = \mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf B\mathbf v$ with $\mathbf B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ i & 0\end{pmatrix}$: the
code reads the matrix of $b^\star$ from its values on the standard basis.

```{.python .sage}
K.<i> = QuadraticField(-1)
B = matrix(K, [[1, 2], [i, 0]])
E = identity_matrix(K, 2).columns()
b = lambda u, v: vector(K, [z.conjugate() for z in u]) * B * v
Bstar = matrix(K, 2, 2, lambda j, k: b(E[k], E[j]).conjugate())
print("matrix of b*:", Bstar.rows(), "; equals B^dagger:", Bstar == B.conjugate_transpose())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
matrix of b*: [(1, -i), (2, 0)] ; equals B^dagger: True
```
::::
:::
::::

### Self-adjoint operators

Operators equal to their own adjoint are the infinite-dimensional Hermitian matrices, and they are the operators whose expectation values
$\langle u, Au\rangle$ are real. The definition below fixes the terms, characterises self-adjointness by real expectation values, computes the
norm from them, and records the Hellinger-Toeplitz theorem in this language.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-self-adjoint-operator}
#### Self-adjoint operator

An operator $A \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ is **self-adjoint** (or **Hermitian**) if $A^\dagger = A$, that is, $\langle Au, v\rangle = \langle u,
Av\rangle$ for all $u, v$. A self-adjoint $A$ is **positive**, $A \geq 0$, if $\langle u, Au\rangle \geq 0$ for all $u$, and $A \leq B$ means $B - A
\geq 0$. On a complex Hilbert space:

1. $A$ is self-adjoint if and only if $\langle u, Au\rangle$ is real for every $u$;
2. every $A \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ is uniquely $A = B + iC$ with $B, C$ self-adjoint, namely $B = \tfrac12(A + A^\dagger)$ and $C =
   \tfrac1{2i}(A - A^\dagger)$;
3. if $A$ is self-adjoint, $\|A\| = \sup_{\|u\| = 1}|\langle u, Au\rangle|$, and $\|A^n\| = \|A\|^n$ for every $n \geq 1$;
4. for every $A \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$, $A^\dagger A \geq 0$ and $AA^\dagger \geq 0$; sums of positive operators and their multiples by $t \geq 0$
   are positive;
5. (**Hellinger-Toeplitz**) a linear map $A : \mathcal H \to \mathcal H$ with $\langle Au, v\rangle = \langle u, Av\rangle$ for all $u, v$ is
   bounded, hence self-adjoint;
6. for $g \in C[a, b]$, $M_g$ is self-adjoint if and only if $g$ is real, and positive if and only if $g \geq 0$; an integral operator with
   continuous kernel $k$ is self-adjoint if and only if $k(x, y) = k(y, x)^*$ for all $x, y$.
:::
::::

*Proof.* (1) The form $b_A(u, v) = \langle u, Av\rangle$ is hermitian exactly when $\langle v, Au\rangle = \langle u, Av\rangle^* =
\langle Av, u\rangle$ for all $u, v$, that is, by the uniqueness in @def-adjoint-operator (1), when $A = A^\dagger$. By @thm-sesquilinear-forms (1)
this happens exactly when $q(u) = \langle u, Au\rangle$ is real for all $u$.

(2) $B$ and $C$ are self-adjoint by @def-adjoint-operator (2): $B^\dagger = \tfrac12(A^\dagger + A)$ and $C^\dagger = -\tfrac1{2i}(A^\dagger - A) =
C$; and $B + iC = A$. If $A = B' + iC'$ with $B', C'$ self-adjoint, then $A^\dagger = B' - iC'$, so $B' = \tfrac12(A + A^\dagger) = B$ and $C' =
C$.

(3) Let $m = \sup_{\|u\| = 1}|\langle u, Au\rangle|$, so $m \leq \|A\|$ and $|\langle w, Aw\rangle| \leq m\|w\|^2$ for all $w$. For unit $u, v$,
self-adjointness gives $\langle u + v, A(u + v)\rangle - \langle u - v, A(u - v)\rangle = 2\langle u, Av\rangle + 2\langle v, Au\rangle =
4\operatorname{Re}\langle v, Au\rangle$, so by the parallelogram law (@thm-cauchy-schwarz (4))
$$
|\operatorname{Re}\langle v, Au\rangle| \leq \tfrac m4(\|u + v\|^2 + \|u - v\|^2) = \tfrac m4(2\|u\|^2 + 2\|v\|^2) = m .
$$
Replacing $v$ by $e^{i\theta}v$ with $e^{-i\theta}\langle v, Au\rangle \geq 0$ gives $|\langle v, Au\rangle| \leq m$, and
@def-bounded-operator (2) gives $\|A\| \leq m$. Next, $\|A^2\| = \|A^\dagger A\| = \|A\|^2$ by @def-adjoint-operator (3); each $A^{2^j}$ is
self-adjoint, so by induction $\|A^{2^j}\| = \|A\|^{2^j}$. For $n \geq 1$ choose $2^j \geq n$; then $\|A\|^{2^j} = \|A^{2^j}\| \leq
\|A^n\|\,\|A\|^{2^j - n}$, so $\|A^n\| \geq \|A\|^n$ if $A \neq 0$, while $\|A^n\| \leq \|A\|^n$ by @def-bounded-operator (1).

(4) $(A^\dagger A)^\dagger = A^\dagger A$ and $\langle u, A^\dagger Au\rangle = \|Au\|^2 \geq 0$; the same for $AA^\dagger = (A^\dagger)^\dagger
A^\dagger$. Sums and non-negative multiples preserve both conditions.

(5) @thm-sesquilinear-forms (5) with $B = A$ makes $A$ bounded, and then the identity says $A^\dagger = A$.

(6) $M_g^\dagger = M_{g^*}$ (@def-adjoint-operator (6)), and $M_g - M_{g^*} = M_{g - g^*}$ has norm $\|g - g^*\|_\infty$
(@def-bounded-operator (5)), which vanishes exactly when $g$ is real. If $g \geq 0$, $\langle f, M_gf\rangle = \int g|f|^2 \geq 0$ for
continuous $f$, hence for all $F$ by continuity. If $g(x_0) < 0$, a continuous tent $f \neq 0$ supported where $g < 0$ gives $\int g|f|^2 < 0$.
For the integral operator, $K - K^\dagger$ is the integral operator with the continuous kernel $m(x, y) = k(x, y) - k(y, x)^*$
(@def-adjoint-operator (6)); if $K = K^\dagger$, then for fixed $x_0$ and $h = m(x_0, \cdot)^*$ the continuous function $(K - K^\dagger)h$ has norm
$0$, hence vanishes, and at $x_0$ it is $\int|m(x_0, y)|^2dy$; so $m = 0$. $\square$

These are @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Sec. VI.2 and Problem VI.9], @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.22, Cor. 3.7] and @gasinski2014exercises [Def.
5.108(b), Problems 5.114 and 5.168].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Pauli matrices are the basic Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrices, and together with the identity they span all of them with real
coefficients. The first example records this, which is the reason they parametrise the observables of a two-level system.

::: {#exm-sa-pauli}
#### Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrices

$\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3$ are Hermitian: $\sigma_2^\dagger = (\sigma_2^*)^\top = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & i \\ -i & 0\end{pmatrix}^\top =
\sigma_2$. A matrix $a_0\mathbf I + \sum_aa_a\sigma_a = \begin{pmatrix} a_0 + a_3 & a_1 - ia_2 \\ a_1 + ia_2 & a_0 - a_3\end{pmatrix}$ is
Hermitian exactly when all $a_\mu$ are real, and every Hermitian matrix has this form (@exr-ip-sage-matrices gave $a = (2, 2, 1, -1)$ for an
example). Since $\sigma_a^2 = \mathbf I$, each $\sigma_a^2$ is positive.
:::

A Hermitian matrix with negative entries can still be positive, as @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Problem VI.13] observes. The second example
gives one and a non-negative matrix that is not positive.

::: {#exm-sa-positive-matrices}
#### Positivity is not about the entries

$\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ has $\mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf A\mathbf u = |u_1|^2 + |u_2|^2 + |u_1 - u_2|^2
\geq 0$, so $\mathbf A \geq 0$ although two entries are negative. $\mathbf B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ has only positive
entries, but $\mathbf u = (1, -1)$ gives $\mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf B\mathbf u = -2$, so $\mathbf B$ is not positive.
:::

A multiplication operator is self-adjoint exactly when its multiplier is real, and positive when the multiplier is non-negative. The third
example applies part (6) to the position operator and to potentials, which are all of this type.

::: {#exm-sa-multiplication}
#### Real multiplication operators

By part (6), the position operator $M_x$ on $L^2[0, 1]$ is positive; multiplication by $\cos x$ on $L^2[0, 2\pi]$ is self-adjoint but not
positive; multiplication by $e^{ix}$ is not self-adjoint, and its decomposition of part (2) is $M_{\cos x} + iM_{\sin x}$, since
$\tfrac12(M_{e^{ix}} + M_{e^{-ix}}) = M_{\cos x}$ by @def-bounded-operator (5).
:::

A Gram matrix $\mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf A$ is positive by part (4), and its quadratic form is a squared length. The fourth example takes a
rank-one Gram matrix, the projector onto a spin state.

::: {#exm-sa-gram}
#### Gram matrices

For $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf A^\top\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 14 \\ 14 & 20\end{pmatrix}$, and
$\mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf A^\top\mathbf A\mathbf u = \|\mathbf A\mathbf u\|^2$. For a unit vector $\mathbf e$, $|\mathbf e\rangle\langle\mathbf e|
= \mathbf e\mathbf e^\dagger$ is a Gram matrix with $\langle\mathbf u, \mathbf e\mathbf e^\dagger\mathbf u\rangle = |\langle\mathbf e, \mathbf
u\rangle|^2$, the probability of finding the spin state $\mathbf u$ in the state $\mathbf e$.
:::

The Green kernel of a string is real and symmetric, so its operator is self-adjoint by part (6), and it is positive because its quadratic
form is an energy. The fifth example proves this with an integration by parts.

::: {#exm-sa-string-positive}
#### The string kernel is positive

For $k(x, y) = \min(x, y) - xy$ and continuous $f$, $u = Kf$ satisfies $-u'' = f$, $u(0) = u(1) = 0$ (@exm-bo-integral-string). So
$\langle f, Kf\rangle = \int_0^1f^*u = -\int_0^1u''^*u = \int_0^1|u'|^2 - [u'^*u]_0^1 = \int_0^1|u'|^2 \geq 0$: the elastic energy of the
displaced string. By continuity $\langle F, KF\rangle \geq 0$ for all $F$, so $K \geq 0$.
:::

The operator $-i\,d/dx$ on smooth periodic functions satisfies the symmetry of part (5), but it is not bounded. The sixth example performs
the integration by parts and draws the consequence of the Hellinger-Toeplitz theorem.

::: {#exm-sa-derivative-periodic}
#### $-i\,d/dx$ on periodic functions

On smooth $2\pi$-periodic $f, g$, $\langle -if', g\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi}(-if')^*g\,dx = i\int_0^{2\pi}f'^*g\,dx = i[f^*g]_0^{2\pi} -
i\int_0^{2\pi}f^*g'\,dx = \langle f, -ig'\rangle$, the boundary term vanishing by periodicity. The operator is symmetric, and $-i(e^{inx})' =
ne^{inx}$ with real $n$. It is not bounded (@exr-bo-differentiation-unbounded), so by part (5) it has no extension to a linear map on all of
$L^2[0, 2\pi]$ with the same symmetry.
:::

A spin observable along a direction is a Hermitian matrix of norm one, and part (3) bounds its expectation values. The seventh example computes
them, which gives the Bloch vector of a state.

::: {#exm-sa-spin-observable}
#### Spin along a direction

$\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$ is Hermitian with $\|\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma\| = 1$ (@exm-sf-spin-energy). For a unit
$\mathbf u \in \mathbb{C}^2$ the numbers $s_a = \langle\mathbf u, \sigma_a\mathbf u\rangle$ are real by part (1), and $\langle\mathbf u,
(\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)\mathbf u\rangle = \hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\mathbf s \in [-1, 1]$ by part (3). For $\mathbf u = (\cos\tfrac\theta2,
e^{i\varphi}\sin\tfrac\theta2)$, $\mathbf s = (\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \sin\theta\sin\varphi, \cos\theta)$, a point of the unit sphere $S^2$.
:::

Bounded functions of the oscillator energy are positive operators on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, defined through the Hermite basis. The eighth example
checks positivity for the operator of @exm-bo-oscillator.

::: {#exm-sa-oscillator}
#### A positive function of the energy

For $AF = \sum_n(2n + 1)^{-1}\langle h_n, F\rangle h_n$, $\langle G, AF\rangle = \sum_n(2n + 1)^{-1}\langle h_n, G\rangle^*\langle h_n, F\rangle$ by
@def-orthonormal-basis (2)(e). This is symmetric under $F \leftrightarrow G$ with conjugation, so $A$ is self-adjoint, and $\langle F, AF\rangle
= \sum_n|\langle h_n, F\rangle|^2/(2n + 1) \geq 0$, so $A \geq 0$, with $\|A\| = \sup\langle F, AF\rangle = 1$ at $F = h_0$, as part (3) predicts.
:::

Part (3) fails without self-adjointness: the expectation values of a nilpotent matrix can be smaller than its norm. The ninth example is the
counterexample of @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Problem VI.9(b)].

::: {#exm-sa-norm-nonselfadjoint}
#### Expectation values do not give the norm

For $\mathbf N = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, $\langle\mathbf u, \mathbf N\mathbf u\rangle = u_1^*u_2$, of modulus at most
$\tfrac12$ on unit vectors, attained at $(1, 1)/\sqrt2$. But $\|\mathbf N\| = 1$, attained at $\mathbf e_2$. Also $\|\mathbf N^2\| = 0 \neq
\|\mathbf N\|^2$, so the second claim of part (3) fails too.
:::

The product of two self-adjoint operators is self-adjoint only when they commute, because the adjoint reverses the order. The last example
shows this with two Pauli matrices.

::: {#exm-sa-product-not-sa}
#### Products of Hermitian matrices

$(\sigma_1\sigma_3)^\dagger = \sigma_3\sigma_1$ by @def-adjoint-operator (2), and $\sigma_1\sigma_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 &
0\end{pmatrix} = -\sigma_3\sigma_1$. So $\sigma_1\sigma_3$ is not Hermitian: it is $-i\sigma_2$, anti-Hermitian. Its parts of part (2) are $B = 0$
and $C = -\sigma_2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Sage's `is_hermitian` decides the property for an explicit matrix, and symbolic vectors show the reality of expectation values as an identity.
The first exercise runs these checks on a tridiagonal Hermitian matrix and decomposes a non-Hermitian one.

::: {#exr-sa-sage-random}
#### Hermitian checks in Sage

For $\mathbf M = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & i & 0 \\ -i & 2 & i \\ 0 & -i & 2\end{pmatrix}$, check that $\mathbf M$ is Hermitian and that
$\langle\mathbf u, \mathbf M\mathbf u\rangle$ is real for a symbolic $\mathbf u \in \mathbb{C}^3$; then compute the parts of part (2) of $\mathbf
N = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4i\end{pmatrix}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$M_{kj} = M_{jk}^*$ for every entry, so $\mathbf M$ is Hermitian, and $\langle\mathbf u, \mathbf M\mathbf u\rangle = 2\sum|u_k|^2 + iu_1^*u_2 -
iu_2^*u_1 + iu_2^*u_3 - iu_3^*u_2 = 2\sum|u_k|^2 - 2\operatorname{Im}(u_1^*u_2 + u_2^*u_3)$, real, as part (1) requires. For $\mathbf N$, $\mathbf
B = \tfrac12(\mathbf N + \mathbf N^\dagger) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 5/2 \\ 5/2 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf C = \tfrac1{2i}(\mathbf N - \mathbf
N^\dagger) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & i/2 \\ -i/2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.

## SageMath

The code tests the Hermitian property, expands $\langle\mathbf u, \mathbf M\mathbf u\rangle$ with real and imaginary parts of the components,
and computes $\mathbf B$, $\mathbf C$.

```{.python .sage}
M = matrix(SR, [[2, I, 0], [-I, 2, I], [0, -I, 2]])
print("M is Hermitian:", M.is_hermitian())
xs = var("x1 x2 x3", domain="real"); ys = var("y1 y2 y3", domain="real")
u = vector([xs[k] + I * ys[k] for k in range(3)])
q = (u.conjugate() * M * u).expand()
print("imaginary part of <u, M u>:", q.imag().simplify_full())
N = matrix(SR, [[1, 2], [3, 4 * I]])
B = (N + N.conjugate_transpose()) / 2; C = (N - N.conjugate_transpose()) / (2 * I)
print("B =", B.rows(), "; C =", C.rows(), "; Hermitian:", B.is_hermitian(), C.is_hermitian(), "; B + iC = N:", bool(B + I * C == N))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
M is Hermitian: True
imaginary part of <u, M u>: 0
B = [(1, 5/2), (5/2, 0)] ; C = [(0, 1/2*I), (-1/2*I, 4)] ; Hermitian: True True ; B + iC = N: True
```
::::
:::

The parts of part (2) of an operator need not commute, and an operator is determined by its expectation values on a complex space. The second
exercise computes the parts for a Jordan block and proves the determination.

::: {#exr-sa-decomposition}
#### Hermitian and anti-Hermitian parts

Decompose $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ as $\mathbf B + i\mathbf C$ with $\mathbf B, \mathbf C$ Hermitian,
compute $[\mathbf B, \mathbf C] = \mathbf B\mathbf C - \mathbf C\mathbf B$, and show that two operators $A, A'$ on a complex Hilbert space with
$\langle u, Au\rangle = \langle u, A'u\rangle$ for all $u$ are equal.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathbf B = \tfrac12(\mathbf A + \mathbf A^\top) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf C = \tfrac1{2i}(\mathbf A -
\mathbf A^\top) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0\end{pmatrix} = \sigma_2$. Then $\mathbf B\mathbf C = \begin{pmatrix} i & -i \\ i &
-i\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf C\mathbf B = \begin{pmatrix} -i & -i \\ i & i\end{pmatrix}$ and $[\mathbf B, \mathbf C] = 2i\sigma_3 \neq \mathbf 0$.
If $\langle u, (A - A')u\rangle = 0$ for all $u$, the form $b_{A - A'}$ has zero quadratic form, so it is zero by @thm-sesquilinear-forms (1),
and $A = A'$ by @thm-sesquilinear-forms (2).

## SageMath

The code computes $\mathbf B$, $\mathbf C$ and their commutator.

```{.python .sage}
A = matrix(QQbar, [[1, 2], [0, 1]])
B = (A + A.conjugate_transpose()) / 2; C = (A - A.conjugate_transpose()) / (2 * I)
print("B =", B.rows(), "; C =", C.rows())
print("[B, C] =", (B * C - C * B).rows(), "; equals 2i sigma_3:", B * C - C * B == 2 * I * matrix(QQbar, [[1, 0], [0, -1]]))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
B = [(1, 1), (1, 1)] ; C = [(0, -I), (I, 0)]
[B, C] = [(2*I, 0), (0, -2*I)] ; equals 2i sigma_3: True
```
::::
:::

Part (1) needs complex scalars, and on $\mathbb{R}^2$ a rotation has vanishing expectation values without being symmetric. The third exercise
gives this counterexample and reads the same matrix on $\mathbb{C}^2$.

::: {#exr-sa-real-expectation}
#### Real expectation values over $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$

Show that the rotation $\mathbf J = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $\mathbf x^\top\mathbf J\mathbf x = 0$ for all
$\mathbf x \in \mathbb{R}^2$ although $\mathbf J^\top \neq \mathbf J$, and that on $\mathbb{C}^2$ the numbers $\langle\mathbf u, \mathbf J\mathbf
u\rangle$ are purely imaginary and not all zero, so that $i\mathbf J$ is Hermitian and $\mathbf J$ is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathbf x^\top\mathbf J\mathbf x = -x_1x_2 + x_2x_1 = 0$ and $\mathbf J^\top = -\mathbf J \neq \mathbf J$. On $\mathbb{C}^2$, $\langle\mathbf
u, \mathbf J\mathbf u\rangle = -u_1^*u_2 + u_2^*u_1 = 2i\operatorname{Im}(u_2^*u_1)$, purely imaginary, and $\mathbf u = (1, i)$ gives $-2i$. By
part (1) $\mathbf J$ is not Hermitian, while $\langle\mathbf u, i\mathbf J\mathbf u\rangle = -2\operatorname{Im}(u_2^*u_1)$ is real, and indeed
$i\mathbf J = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0\end{pmatrix} = \sigma_2$ is Hermitian.

## SageMath

The code evaluates both forms with symbolic real coordinates and on $\mathbf u = (1, i)$.

```{.python .sage}
x1, x2, y1, y2 = var("x1 x2 y1 y2", domain="real")
J = matrix(SR, [[0, -1], [1, 0]])
x = vector([x1, x2]); u = vector([x1 + I * y1, x2 + I * y2])
print("x^T J x =", (x * J * x).expand())
print("real part of <u, J u> =", (u.conjugate() * J * u).expand().real().simplify_full(), "; <(1, i), J (1, i)> =", vector(SR, [1, -I]) * J * vector(SR, [1, I]))
print("i J = sigma_2:", I * J == matrix(SR, [[0, -I], [I, 0]]))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
x^T J x = 0
real part of <u, J u> = 0 ; <(1, i), J (1, i)> = -2*I
i J = sigma_2: True
```
::::
:::

A $2 \times 2$ Hermitian matrix is positive exactly when its diagonal entries and its determinant are non-negative, which answers
@reed1980methods [Vol. I, Problem VI.13(b)] for $n = 2$. The fourth exercise proves it by completing the square.

::: {#exr-sa-positive-matrix-test}
#### Positive $2 \times 2$ matrices

Show that $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b^* & d\end{pmatrix}$ with real $a, d$ is positive if and only if $a \geq 0$, $d \geq 0$ and
$ad \geq |b|^2$. Test $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 + i \\ 1 - i & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2i \\ -2i & 3\end{pmatrix}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$q(\mathbf u) = a|u_1|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}(bu_1^*u_2) + d|u_2|^2$. If $\mathbf A \geq 0$, then $a = q(\mathbf e_1) \geq 0$, $d = q(\mathbf
e_2) \geq 0$, and $|b|^2 \leq ad$ by @exr-sf-cauchy-schwarz-form applied to $|b_{\mathbf A}(\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2)|^2$. Conversely, if
$a > 0$, $aq(\mathbf u) = |au_1 + bu_2|^2 + (ad - |b|^2)|u_2|^2 \geq 0$; if $a = 0$, then $b = 0$ and $q(\mathbf u) = d|u_2|^2 \geq 0$. For the
first matrix $ad = 2 = |1 + i|^2$, so it is positive; for the second $ad = 3 < 4 = |2i|^2$, so it is not.

## SageMath

The code applies the test and, independently, computes the minimum of $q$ on the vectors $(1, s + it)$ with $s, t$ in a grid of step $\tfrac13$.

```{.python .sage}
for A in [matrix(QQbar, [[2, 1 + I], [1 - I, 1]]), matrix(QQbar, [[1, 2 * I], [-2 * I, 3]])]:
    a, b, d = A[0, 0], A[0, 1], A[1, 1]
    test = a >= 0 and d >= 0 and a * d >= abs(b)^2
    qmin = min((vector(QQbar, [1, s + t * I]).conjugate() * A * vector(QQbar, [1, s + t * I])).real() for s in [QQ(j) / 3 for j in range(-9, 10)] for t in [QQ(j) / 3 for j in range(-9, 10)])
    print(A.rows(), ": criterion", test, "; minimum of q on the grid:", qmin)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
[(2, I + 1), (-I + 1, 1)] : criterion True ; minimum of q on the grid: 0
[(1, 2*I), (-2*I, 3)] : criterion False ; minimum of q on the grid: -1/3
```
::::
:::

For a Hermitian matrix part (3) computes the norm as the largest modulus of an expectation value, which is the largest modulus of an
eigenvalue. The fifth exercise does this for a $2 \times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues of both signs.

::: {#exr-sa-quadratic-norm}
#### The norm from expectation values

For $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{pmatrix}$, compute $\max$ and $\min$ of $\langle\mathbf u, \mathbf A\mathbf u\rangle$ over unit
vectors and deduce $\|\mathbf A\|$ from part (3).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathbf A$ is real symmetric with characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2 + \lambda - 6 = (\lambda - 2)(\lambda + 3)$ and orthonormal eigenvectors
$\mathbf v_+ = (2, 1)/\sqrt5$, $\mathbf v_- = (1, -2)/\sqrt5$. Writing $\mathbf u = \alpha\mathbf v_+ + \beta\mathbf v_-$ with $|\alpha|^2 +
|\beta|^2 = 1$, $\langle\mathbf u, \mathbf A\mathbf u\rangle = 2|\alpha|^2 - 3|\beta|^2 \in [-3, 2]$, with both ends attained. By part (3),
$\|\mathbf A\| = \max(|{-3}|, |2|) = 3$.

## SageMath

The code samples $q$ on real unit vectors $(\cos t, \sin t)$ and compares with the norm.

```{.python .sage}
A = matrix(RDF, [[1, 2], [2, -2]])
vals = [vector(RDF, [cos(2 * pi * j / 3600), sin(2 * pi * j / 3600)]) * A * vector(RDF, [cos(2 * pi * j / 3600), sin(2 * pi * j / 3600)]) for j in range(3600)]
print("max q = %.6f, min q = %.6f, ||A|| = %.6f" % (max(vals), min(vals), A.norm(2)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
max q = 1.999998, min q = -2.999998, ||A|| = 3.000000
```
::::
:::

The identity $\|A^n\| = \|A\|^n$ of part (3) is special to self-adjoint operators, as the nilpotent matrix of @exm-sa-norm-nonselfadjoint shows.
The sixth exercise checks it on a Hermitian matrix and finds a matrix where $\|\mathbf A^2\| < \|\mathbf A\|^2$ without being nilpotent.

::: {#exr-sa-powers}
#### Norms of powers

Verify $\|\mathbf H^3\| = \|\mathbf H\|^3$ for $\mathbf H = \sigma_1 + 2\sigma_3$, and show that $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 &
1\end{pmatrix}$ has $\|\mathbf A^2\| < \|\mathbf A\|^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathbf H$ is Hermitian with $\mathbf H^2 = \sigma_1^2 + 2(\sigma_1\sigma_3 + \sigma_3\sigma_1) + 4\sigma_3^2 = 5\mathbf I$, so $\|\mathbf H\| =
\sqrt5$ and $\mathbf H^3 = 5\mathbf H$ has norm $5\sqrt5$, as part (3) says. $\|\mathbf A\| = (1 + \sqrt5)/2$ (@exr-bo-norm-2x2), so
$\|\mathbf A\|^2 = (3 + \sqrt5)/2 \approx 2.618$; $\mathbf A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ has $\mathbf A^{2\top}\mathbf A^2 =
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{pmatrix}$, largest eigenvalue $3 + 2\sqrt2$, so $\|\mathbf A^2\| = 1 + \sqrt2 \approx 2.414 < 2.618$.

## SageMath

The code computes the norms exactly in $\overline{\mathbb Q}$.

```{.python .sage}
nrm = lambda M: sqrt(max((M.conjugate_transpose() * M).eigenvalues()))
s1 = matrix(QQbar, [[0, 1], [1, 0]]); s3 = matrix(QQbar, [[1, 0], [0, -1]])
H = s1 + 2 * s3
print("||H^3|| = ||H||^3:", nrm(H^3) == nrm(H)^3, "; ||H|| =", nrm(H))
A = matrix(QQbar, [[1, 1], [0, 1]])
print("||A^2|| =", nrm(A^2).n(digits=8), "; ||A||^2 =", (nrm(A)^2).n(digits=8), "; ||A^2|| = 1 + sqrt 2:", nrm(A^2) == QQbar(1 + sqrt(2)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
||H^3|| = ||H||^3: True ; ||H|| = 2.236067977499790?
||A^2|| = 2.4142136 ; ||A||^2 = 2.6180340 ; ||A^2|| = 1 + sqrt 2: True
```
::::
:::

A positive operator is controlled by its quadratic form: its values and its kernel are determined by the expectation values. The seventh exercise,
after @gasinski2014exercises [Problem 5.114], proves this with @exr-sf-cauchy-schwarz-form.

::: {#exr-sa-positive-estimates}
#### Estimates for positive operators

Let $A \geq 0$. Show that $|\langle u, Av\rangle|^2 \leq \langle u, Au\rangle\langle v, Av\rangle$, that $\|Av\|^2 \leq \|A\|\langle v, Av\rangle$,
and that $\ker A = \{v : \langle v, Av\rangle = 0\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$b_A$ is hermitian with $q \geq 0$ (@exr-adj-sesquilinear-form), so the first inequality is @exr-sf-cauchy-schwarz-form. With $u = Av$,
$\|Av\|^4 = |\langle Av, Av\rangle|^2 \leq \langle Av, A^2v\rangle\langle v, Av\rangle \leq \|A\|\,\|Av\|^2\langle v, Av\rangle$, since
$\langle Av, A(Av)\rangle \leq \|A\|\,\|Av\|^2$; dividing by $\|Av\|^2$ (if non-zero) gives the second. If $\langle v, Av\rangle = 0$, the second
inequality gives $Av = 0$; the converse is clear.

## SageMath

Check on the positive matrix $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$: the code tests both inequalities on random
rational vectors.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(2)
A = matrix(QQ, [[2, -1], [-1, 2]]); nA = 3
ok1 = ok2 = True
for _ in range(300):
    u = vector(QQ, [QQ.random_element(10, 10) for _ in range(2)]); v = vector(QQ, [QQ.random_element(10, 10) for _ in range(2)])
    ok1 = ok1 and (u * A * v)^2 <= (u * A * u) * (v * A * v)
    ok2 = ok2 and (A * v) * (A * v) <= nA * (v * A * v)
print("||A|| =", max(A.eigenvalues()), "; first inequality:", ok1, "; second:", ok2)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
||A|| = 3 ; first inequality: True ; second: True
```
::::
:::

Even powers of a self-adjoint operator are positive, and odd powers of a positive one are positive too. The eighth exercise, @gasinski2014exercises
[Problem 5.116], proves both by moving powers across the inner product.

::: {#exr-sa-even-powers}
#### Powers and positivity

Let $A$ be self-adjoint. Show that $A^{2n} \geq 0$ for $n \geq 1$, and that $A \geq 0$ implies $A^{2n+1} \geq 0$. Show that $\sigma_3^3$ is not
positive.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Powers of $A$ are self-adjoint by @def-adjoint-operator (2). $\langle u, A^{2n}u\rangle = \langle A^nu, A^nu\rangle = \|A^nu\|^2 \geq 0$, and
$\langle u, A^{2n+1}u\rangle = \langle A^nu, A(A^nu)\rangle \geq 0$ if $A \geq 0$. Without $A \geq 0$ odd powers can fail: $\sigma_3^3 = \sigma_3$ and
$\langle\mathbf e_2, \sigma_3\mathbf e_2\rangle = -1$.

## SageMath

Check on the Hermitian matrix $\mathbf H = \sigma_1 + 2\sigma_3$ and the positive $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$: the code
prints the smallest eigenvalues of $\mathbf H^2, \mathbf H^4$ and $\mathbf A^3$.

```{.python .sage}
H = matrix(QQ, [[2, 1], [1, -2]]); A = matrix(QQ, [[2, -1], [-1, 2]])
print("min eigenvalue of H^2, H^4:", min((H^2).eigenvalues()), min((H^4).eigenvalues()), "; of H^3:", min(RR(e) for e in (H^3).eigenvalues()))
print("min eigenvalue of A^3:", min((A^3).eigenvalues()), "; sigma_3^3 diagonal:", (matrix(QQ, [[1, 0], [0, -1]])^3).diagonal())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
min eigenvalue of H^2, H^4: 5 25 ; of H^3: -11.1803398874989
min eigenvalue of A^3: 1 ; sigma_3^3 diagonal: [1, -1]
```
::::
:::

The product of two self-adjoint operators is self-adjoint exactly when they commute, a fact behind the compatibility of observables. The ninth
exercise proves it, after @arcozzi2025 [Cor. 3.7(i)].

::: {#exr-sa-commuting-product}
#### When a product is self-adjoint

For self-adjoint $A, B$, show that $AB$ is self-adjoint if and only if $AB = BA$. Check this for $\sigma_3$ and $\operatorname{diag}(1, 2)$, and for
$\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$(AB)^\dagger = B^\dagger A^\dagger = BA$ by @def-adjoint-operator (2), so $(AB)^\dagger = AB$ exactly when $BA = AB$. Diagonal matrices commute,
so $\sigma_3\operatorname{diag}(1, 2) = \operatorname{diag}(1, -2)$ is Hermitian; $\sigma_1\sigma_3 = -\sigma_3\sigma_1 \neq \sigma_3\sigma_1$ is
not (@exm-sa-product-not-sa).

## SageMath

The code tests commutation and the Hermitian property of the products.

```{.python .sage}
s1 = matrix(QQbar, [[0, 1], [1, 0]]); s3 = matrix(QQbar, [[1, 0], [0, -1]]); D = diagonal_matrix(QQbar, [1, 2])
for A, B, name in [(s3, D, "sigma_3, diag(1, 2)"), (s1, s3, "sigma_1, sigma_3")]:
    print(name, ": commute", A * B == B * A, "; product Hermitian", (A * B).is_hermitian())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
sigma_3, diag(1, 2) : commute True ; product Hermitian True
sigma_1, sigma_3 : commute False ; product Hermitian False
```
::::
:::

The Hellinger-Toeplitz theorem forbids an everywhere-defined position operator on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, since multiplication by $x$ is unbounded. The
last exercise proves this with part (5) and @exm-bo-unbounded-multiplication.

::: {#exr-sa-no-position-operator}
#### No everywhere-defined position operator

Show that there is no linear map $X : L^2(\mathbb{R}) \to L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with $\langle XF, G\rangle = \langle F, XG\rangle$ for all $F, G$ and
$Xf = xf$ for every $f \in C_c(\mathbb{R})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By part (5), such an $X$ would be bounded, so $\|xf\| \leq \|X\|\,\|f\|$ for all $f \in C_c(\mathbb{R})$. The tents $f_n$ of
@exm-bo-unbounded-multiplication have $\|xf_n\| \geq (n - 1)\|f_n\|$, a contradiction for $n > \|X\| + 1$.

## SageMath

The code computes $\|xf_n\|/\|f_n\|$ for the tents of height $1$ on $[n - 1, n + 1]$.

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x")
for n in [1, 5, 25, 125]:
    f1 = x - (n - 1); f2 = n + 1 - x
    nf = integrate(f1^2, x, n - 1, n) + integrate(f2^2, x, n, n + 1)
    nxf = integrate((x * f1)^2, x, n - 1, n) + integrate((x * f2)^2, x, n, n + 1)
    print("n =", n, ": ||x f_n|| / ||f_n|| = %.4f" % sqrt(nxf / nf).n())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
n = 1 : ||x f_n|| / ||f_n|| = 1.0488
n = 5 : ||x f_n|| / ||f_n|| = 5.0100
n = 25 : ||x f_n|| / ||f_n|| = 25.0020
n = 125 : ||x f_n|| / ||f_n|| = 125.0004
```
::::
:::
::::

### Unitary operators and isometries

Operators that preserve all inner products, hence all lengths and angles, are the symmetries of a Hilbert space, and they generalise
rotations. The definition below separates isometries from unitary operators, which in infinite dimensions differ, and records that the
Fourier transform of @thm-plancherel-l2 is unitary.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-unitary-operator}
#### Unitary operator and isometry

An operator $U \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ is an **isometry** if $\|Uu\| = \|u\|$ for all $u$, and **unitary** if $U^\dagger U = UU^\dagger = 1$.
Then:

1. $U$ is an isometry if and only if $\langle Uu, Uv\rangle = \langle u, v\rangle$ for all $u, v$, if and only if $U^\dagger U = 1$; an isometry
   has closed range and, if $\mathcal H \neq \{0\}$, norm $1$;
2. $U$ is unitary if and only if it is a surjective isometry, if and only if it is bijective with $U^{-1} = U^\dagger$; if $\dim\mathcal H <
   \infty$, every isometry is unitary;
3. products of unitary operators and the inverse of a unitary operator are unitary; a unitary operator maps orthonormal bases to orthonormal
   bases, and if $(e_k)$, $(f_k)$ are orthonormal bases indexed by the same set, finite or $\{1, 2, \dots\}$, there is exactly one unitary $U$
   with $Ue_k = f_k$ for all $k$;
4. (**Plancherel**) the operator $U$ of @thm-plancherel-l2 is unitary on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, and $U^\dagger = U^{-1}$;
5. the right shift $S$ on $\ell^2$ is an isometry that is not unitary; for $g \in C[a, b]$, $M_g$ is unitary if and only if $|g| = 1$.
:::
::::

*Proof.* (1) If $U$ is an isometry, the polarisation identity of @thm-cauchy-schwarz (4) expresses $\langle Uu, Uv\rangle$ through the norms
$\|U(u + i^kv)\| = \|u + i^kv\|$, so $\langle Uu, Uv\rangle = \langle u, v\rangle$. This says $\langle u, (U^\dagger U - 1)v\rangle = 0$ for all $u,
v$, so $U^\dagger U = 1$; and $U^\dagger U = 1$ gives $\|Uu\|^2 = \langle u, U^\dagger Uu\rangle = \|u\|^2$. If $Uu_n \to w$, then $\|u_n - u_m\| =
\|Uu_n - Uu_m\|$, so $(u_n)$ is Cauchy, $u_n \to u$, and $w = Uu$ by continuity: the range is closed. $\|U\| = 1$ is clear.

(2) If $U$ is unitary, it is an isometry by (1), and $UU^\dagger = 1$ makes it surjective. A surjective isometry is injective, hence bijective, and
$U^{-1} = (U^\dagger U)U^{-1} = U^\dagger$. If $U$ is bijective with $U^{-1} = U^\dagger$, then $U^\dagger U = UU^\dagger = 1$. In finite dimension an
isometry is injective, hence surjective by rank-nullity.

(3) $(UV)^\dagger UV = V^\dagger U^\dagger UV = 1$ and $UV(UV)^\dagger = UVV^\dagger U^\dagger = 1$, by @def-adjoint-operator (2); and $U^{-1} = U^\dagger$
has $(U^\dagger)^\dagger U^\dagger = UU^\dagger = 1$ and $U^\dagger(U^\dagger)^\dagger = 1$. If $(e_k)$ is an orthonormal basis, $\langle Ue_j,
Ue_k\rangle = \delta_{jk}$ by (1), and if $v \perp Ue_k$ for all $k$, then $\langle e_k, U^\dagger v\rangle = \langle Ue_k, v\rangle = 0$, so $U^\dagger v = 0$
and $v = UU^\dagger v = 0$: $(Ue_k)$ is complete. For two orthonormal bases, define $Uu = \sum_k\langle e_k, u\rangle f_k$. The series converges and
$\|Uu\|^2 = \sum_k|\langle e_k, u\rangle|^2 = \|u\|^2$ by @def-orthonormal-basis (1) and Parseval's identity (2)(d); $U$ is linear, $Ue_k = f_k$, and
it is onto, since $v = \sum_k\langle f_k, v\rangle f_k = U(\sum_k\langle f_k, v\rangle e_k)$ by @def-orthonormal-basis (2)(c). By (2) it is unitary.
A bounded operator with $Ue_k = f_k$ is determined on the span of the $e_k$, which is dense, hence everywhere.

(4) By @thm-plancherel-l2 (1) and (3), $U$ is a linear bijection of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ that preserves norms; by (2) it is unitary and $U^{-1} =
U^\dagger$.

(5) $S$ is an isometry by @def-bounded-operator (4) and not onto, since $\delta^{(1)} \perp \operatorname{ran}S$. For $M_g$, $M_g^\dagger M_g =
M_gM_g^\dagger = M_{|g|^2}$ (@def-adjoint-operator (6), @def-bounded-operator (5)), and $\|M_{|g|^2} - 1\| = \||g|^2 - 1\|_\infty$ vanishes exactly
when $|g| = 1$. $\square$

These are @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Sec. II.3 and Problem VI.7], @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 1.3.1] and @gasinski2014exercises [Def. 5.108(d), Problem 5.126].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Rotations of the plane and diagonal phase matrices are the unitary matrices one can draw. The first example records them, together with the
exponential of $i\theta\sigma_2$, which produces a rotation.

::: {#exm-un-rotation}
#### Rotations and phases

$\mathbf R_\theta = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $\mathbf R_\theta^\top\mathbf
R_\theta = \mathbf I$: it is unitary and maps the unit circle onto itself (@fig-operator-norm-ellipse). The diagonal matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\theta}, e^{-i\theta})$ is unitary with determinant $1$. Since $\sigma_2^2 = \mathbf I$, the exponential series splits
into even and odd powers, $e^{-i\theta\sigma_2} = \cos\theta\,\mathbf I - i\sin\theta\,\sigma_2 = \mathbf R_\theta$.
:::

On function spaces the basic unitary operators are multiplication by a phase, translation, and the Fourier transform itself. The second example
proves the first two and cites part (4) for the third.

::: {#exm-un-phase}
#### Phases, translations and the Fourier transform
