(@exm-ev-multiplication-none), so there is no orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Diagonal operators, such as the operator $A$ of
@exm-ev-oscillator in the Hermite basis, do have one. The rest of this section replaces eigenvectors by the spectrum and the sum
$\sum_\lambda p(\lambda)\mathbf P_\lambda$ by a limit of polynomials $p(A)$, which needs no eigenvectors.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Sage's `eigenmatrix_right` returns $\mathbf D$ and a matrix of eigenvectors; normalising the columns gives the unitary of part
(2). The first exercise constructs it for the $3 \times 3$ example and verifies the forms of the decomposition.

::: {#exr-sth-sage-decomposition}
#### The decomposition in Sage

For $\mathbf A$ of @exm-sth-3x3, obtain $\mathbf D$ and the normalised eigenvector matrix $\mathbf U$, and check $\mathbf U^\top\mathbf U
= \mathbf I$, $\mathbf A = \mathbf U\mathbf D\mathbf U^\top$, $\mathbf A = \sum_k\lambda_k\mathbf e_k\mathbf e_k^\top$, $\sum_k\mathbf
e_k\mathbf e_k^\top = \mathbf I$ and $\mathbf P_k\mathbf P_l = \delta_{kl}\mathbf P_k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The eigenvectors are $(1, \pm\sqrt2, 1)$ and $(1, 0, -1)$ (@exr-ev-sage-3x3), of norms $2$ and $\sqrt2$. Dividing by them gives the
orthonormal columns of @exm-sth-3x3, so $\mathbf U$ is orthogonal. The other identities are @thm-spectral-theorem-hermitian (2) for
this matrix: $\mathbf A\mathbf U = \mathbf U\mathbf D$ column by column, $\mathbf U\mathbf D\mathbf U^\top = \sum_k\lambda_k\mathbf
e_k\mathbf e_k^\top$, $\mathbf U\mathbf U^\top = \sum_k\mathbf e_k\mathbf e_k^\top = \mathbf I$, and $\mathbf e_k^\top\mathbf e_l =
\delta_{kl}$ gives $\mathbf P_k\mathbf P_l = \delta_{kl}\mathbf P_k$.

## SageMath

The code normalises the eigenvectors and checks the identities exactly.

```{.python .sage}
A = matrix(SR, [[2, 1, 0], [1, 2, 1], [0, 1, 2]])
D, V = A.eigenmatrix_right()
U = matrix(SR, [c / c.norm() for c in V.columns()]).transpose().simplify_full()
print("D = diag", D.diagonal()); print("U ="); print(U)
print("U^T U = 1:", bool((U.transpose() * U).simplify_full() == identity_matrix(3)))
print("A = U D U^T:", bool((U * D * U.transpose()).simplify_full() == A))
Ps = [(U.column(k).column() * U.column(k).column().transpose()).simplify_full() for k in range(3)]
print("A = sum lambda_k P_k:", bool((sum(D[k, k] * Ps[k] for k in range(3))).simplify_full() == A), "; sum P_k = 1:", bool(sum(Ps).simplify_full() == identity_matrix(3)))
print("P_k P_l = delta_kl P_k:", all(bool((Ps[k] * Ps[l]).simplify_full() == (Ps[k] if k == l else 0)) for k in range(3) for l in range(3)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
D = diag [-sqrt(2) + 2, sqrt(2) + 2, 2]
U =
[         1/2          1/2  1/2*sqrt(2)]
[-1/2*sqrt(2)  1/2*sqrt(2)            0]
[         1/2          1/2 -1/2*sqrt(2)]
U^T U = 1: True
A = U D U^T: True
A = sum lambda_k P_k: True ; sum P_k = 1: True
P_k P_l = delta_kl P_k: True
```
::::
:::

The general $2 \times 2$ Hermitian matrix is $a_0\mathbf I + \mathbf a\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$, and its spectral decomposition has a
closed form. The second exercise derives it from the square of $\mathbf a\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$ and checks it on one matrix.

::: {#exr-sth-pauli-general}
#### Two-by-two Hermitian matrices

For real $a_0$ and $\mathbf a \neq \mathbf 0$, show that $\mathbf A = a_0\mathbf I + \mathbf a\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$ has eigenvalues
$a_0 \pm |\mathbf a|$ with projections $\mathbf P_\pm = \tfrac12(\mathbf I \pm \hat{\mathbf a}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)$. Compute them
for $a_0 = 1$, $\mathbf a = (1, 2, 2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$(\hat{\mathbf a}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)^2 = \mathbf I$ (@exm-sth-pauli-decomposition), so $\mathbf P_\pm$ are Hermitian with
$\mathbf P_\pm^2 = \tfrac14(\mathbf I \pm 2\hat{\mathbf a}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma + \mathbf I) = \mathbf P_\pm$, $\mathbf P_+\mathbf
P_- = \tfrac14(\mathbf I - \mathbf I) = \mathbf 0$ and $\mathbf P_+ + \mathbf P_- = \mathbf I$. Neither is $\mathbf 0$, since
$\hat{\mathbf a}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma \neq \pm\mathbf I$ has trace $0$. Then $(a_0 + |\mathbf a|)\mathbf P_+ + (a_0 - |\mathbf
a|)\mathbf P_- = a_0\mathbf I + |\mathbf a|\hat{\mathbf a}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma = \mathbf A$, and $\mathbf A\mathbf P_\pm = (a_0 \pm
|\mathbf a|)\mathbf P_\pm$ shows that the non-zero vectors in the ranges are eigenvectors; so this is the decomposition of
@thm-spectral-theorem-hermitian (2). For $a_0 = 1$, $\mathbf a = (1, 2, 2)$, $|\mathbf a| = 3$: the eigenvalues are $4$ and $-2$.

## SageMath

The code builds $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf P_\pm$ in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ and checks the decomposition.

```{.python .sage}
K.<i> = QuadraticField(-1)
s = [matrix(K, [[0, 1], [1, 0]]), matrix(K, [[0, -i], [i, 0]]), matrix(K, [[1, 0], [0, -1]])]
a0, a = 1, [1, 2, 2]; na = 3
A = a0 * identity_matrix(K, 2) + sum(a[j] * s[j] for j in range(3))
Pp = (identity_matrix(K, 2) + sum(a[j] * s[j] for j in range(3)) / na) / 2; Pm = identity_matrix(K, 2) - Pp
print("A ="); print(A)
print("eigenvalues:", A.charpoly().roots())
print("P+^2 = P+, P+ P- = 0, P+ Hermitian:", Pp ** 2 == Pp, Pp * Pm == 0, Pp == Pp.conjugate_transpose())
print("A = 4 P+ - 2 P-:", A == 4 * Pp - 2 * Pm)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
A =
[       3 -2*i + 1]
[ 2*i + 1       -1]
eigenvalues: [(4, 1), (-2, 1)]
P+^2 = P+, P+ P- = 0, P+ Hermitian: True True True
A = 4 P+ - 2 P-: True
```
::::
:::

Two Hermitian matrices can be diagonalised in the same basis exactly when they commute, which is the mathematical content of
"compatible observables". The third exercise asks for the converse of part (4) and for two examples.

::: {#exr-sth-commuting-simultaneous}
#### Simultaneous diagonalisation

Show that matrices with a common orthonormal eigenbasis commute, so that part (4) is an equivalence. Find a common eigenbasis of
$\sigma_3$ and $\operatorname{diag}(1, 5)$, and show that $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_3$ have none.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $\mathbf A = \mathbf U\mathbf D\mathbf U^\dagger$ and $\mathbf B = \mathbf U\mathbf D'\mathbf U^\dagger$ with the same unitary
$\mathbf U$ and diagonal $\mathbf D$, $\mathbf D'$, then $\mathbf A\mathbf B = \mathbf U\mathbf D\mathbf D'\mathbf U^\dagger = \mathbf
U\mathbf D'\mathbf D\mathbf U^\dagger = \mathbf B\mathbf A$, since diagonal matrices commute. $\sigma_3$ and $\operatorname{diag}(1,
5)$ are both diagonal in the standard basis. $[\sigma_1, \sigma_3] = -2i\sigma_2 \neq \mathbf 0$, so by the first part no common
eigenbasis exists; indeed the eigenvectors $(1, \pm1)/\sqrt2$ of $\sigma_1$ are not eigenvectors of $\sigma_3$, and both
eigenspaces of $\sigma_1$ are lines, so it has no other eigenvectors.

## SageMath

The code computes the commutators and tests whether the eigenvectors of $\sigma_1$ are eigenvectors of $\sigma_3$.

```{.python .sage}
K.<i> = QuadraticField(-1)
s1 = matrix(K, [[0, 1], [1, 0]]); s2 = matrix(K, [[0, -i], [i, 0]]); s3 = matrix(K, [[1, 0], [0, -1]])
D = diagonal_matrix(K, [1, 5])
print("[s3, diag(1, 5)] = 0:", s3 * D == D * s3)
print("[s1, s3] = -2i s2:", s1 * s3 - s3 * s1 == -2 * i * s2)
for v in [vector(K, [1, 1]), vector(K, [1, -1])]:
    w = s3 * v
    print("v =", v, ": s3 v =", w, "; parallel to v:", matrix([v, w]).rank() == 1)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
[s3, diag(1, 5)] = 0: True
[s1, s3] = -2i s2: True
v = (1, 1) : s3 v = (1, -1) ; parallel to v: False
v = (1, -1) : s3 v = (1, 1) ; parallel to v: False
```
::::
:::

A normal matrix that is not Hermitian has complex eigenvalues on orthogonal eigenvectors. The fourth exercise finds them for a
rotation-dilation and checks that the Hermitian parts commute.

::: {#exr-sth-normal-matrices}
#### A normal matrix

Show that $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ is normal but not Hermitian, compute its Hermitian parts $\mathbf B$,
$\mathbf C$ of part (5), and find its orthonormal eigenbasis and eigenvalues.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathbf A^\dagger = \mathbf A^\top = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix} \neq \mathbf A$, and $\mathbf A\mathbf A^\dagger =
2\mathbf I = \mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf A$. Here $\mathbf B = \tfrac12(\mathbf A + \mathbf A^\dagger) = \mathbf I$ and $\mathbf C =
\tfrac1{2i}(\mathbf A - \mathbf A^\dagger) = \tfrac1{2i}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{pmatrix} = -\sigma_2$, which commute. The
eigenvectors of $\sigma_2$ are $(1, \pm i)/\sqrt2$ with eigenvalues $\pm1$, so $\mathbf C$ has eigenvalues $\mp1$ on them and $\mathbf
A = \mathbf B + i\mathbf C$ has eigenvalues $1 - i$ on $(1, i)/\sqrt2$ and $1 + i$ on $(1, -i)/\sqrt2$; these are orthonormal, as part
(5) asserts.

## SageMath

The code checks normality and the eigenvector equations, and the orthogonality of the eigenvectors.

```{.python .sage}
K.<i> = QuadraticField(-1)
A = matrix(K, [[1, -1], [1, 1]]); Ad = A.conjugate_transpose()
print("normal:", A * Ad == Ad * A, "; Hermitian:", A == Ad)
print("B =", ((A + Ad) / 2).rows(), "; C =", ((A - Ad) / (2 * i)).rows())
v1 = vector(K, [1, i]); v2 = vector(K, [1, -i])
print("A v1 = (1 - i) v1:", A * v1 == (1 - i) * v1, "; A v2 = (1 + i) v2:", A * v2 == (1 + i) * v2)
print("<v1, v2> =", v1.conjugate() * v2)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
normal: True ; Hermitian: False
B = [(1, 0), (0, 1)] ; C = [(0, i), (-i, 0)]
A v1 = (1 - i) v1: True ; A v2 = (1 + i) v2: True
<v1, v2> = 0
```
::::
:::

The trace and the determinant do not change under a unitary change of basis, so they are the sum and product of the eigenvalues.
The fifth exercise proves this together with the identity for the sum of the squared moduli of the entries.

::: {#exr-sth-trace-det}
#### Trace, determinant and the entries

For a Hermitian matrix $\mathbf A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$ (with multiplicity), show $\operatorname{tr}\mathbf A
= \sum_k\lambda_k$, $\det\mathbf A = \prod_k\lambda_k$ and $\sum_{j, k}|A_{jk}|^2 = \sum_k\lambda_k^2$. Check on the $4 \times 4$
matrix with $1$ on the diagonal, $i$ above it and $-i$ below it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By @thm-spectral-theorem-hermitian (2), $\mathbf A = \mathbf U\mathbf D\mathbf U^\dagger$. By @prp-trace-cyclic, $\operatorname{tr}\mathbf
A = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf D\mathbf U^\dagger\mathbf U) = \operatorname{tr}\mathbf D = \sum_k\lambda_k$. By @thm-determinant-product,
$\det\mathbf A = \det\mathbf U\det\mathbf D\det\mathbf U^\dagger = \det\mathbf D\det(\mathbf U^\dagger\mathbf U) = \prod_k\lambda_k$.
Finally $\sum_{j, k}|A_{jk}|^2 = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf A) = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf A^2) = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf
U\mathbf D^2\mathbf U^\dagger) = \sum_k\lambda_k^2$. For the $4 \times 4$ matrix the trace is $4$, the sum of squared moduli is $4 + 6
= 10$, and the determinant is computed in the code.

## SageMath

The code computes the eigenvalues exactly and compares their sum, product and sum of squares with the trace, the determinant and
the entries.

```{.python .sage}
A = matrix(QQbar, 4, 4, lambda j, k: 1 if j == k else (I if k == j + 1 else (-I if k == j - 1 else 0)))
ev = A.charpoly().roots(QQbar, multiplicities=False)
print("eigenvalues:", [e.radical_expression() for e in ev])
print("sum =", sum(ev), "; tr =", A.trace())
print("product =", prod(ev), "; det =", A.det())
print("sum of squares =", sum(e ** 2 for e in ev), "; sum |A_jk|^2 =", sum(abs(a) ** 2 for a in A.list()))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
eigenvalues: [-1/2*sqrt(5) + 1/2, -1/2*sqrt(5) + 3/2, 1/2*sqrt(5) + 1/2, 1/2*sqrt(5) + 3/2]
sum = 4.000000000000000? ; tr = 4
product = -1.000000000000000? ; det = -1
sum of squares = 10.00000000000000? ; sum |A_jk|^2 = 10
```
::::
:::

A Hermitian matrix is positive exactly when its eigenvalues are non-negative, and then the theorem gives it a positive square root.
The sixth exercise proves both and computes the root of the matrix of the figure.

::: {#exr-sth-positive-sqrt}
#### Positive matrices and square roots

Show that a Hermitian matrix $\mathbf A$ satisfies $\mathbf A \geq 0$ if and only if all its eigenvalues are $\geq 0$, and that then
$\sqrt{\mathbf A} = \sum_\lambda\sqrt\lambda\,\mathbf P_\lambda$ is positive with $(\sqrt{\mathbf A})^2 = \mathbf A$. Compute
$\sqrt{\mathbf A}$ for $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $\mathbf A \geq 0$, its eigenvalues are $\geq 0$ by @def-operator-eigenvalue (3). Conversely, with the orthonormal eigenbasis of
@thm-spectral-theorem-hermitian (1) and $\mathbf u = \sum_kc_k\mathbf e_k$, $\mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf A\mathbf u = \sum_k\lambda_k
|c_k|^2 \geq 0$. The matrix $\sqrt{\mathbf A}$ is Hermitian with eigenvalues $\sqrt\lambda \geq 0$, hence positive, and $\mathbf
P_\lambda\mathbf P_\mu = \delta_{\lambda\mu}\mathbf P_\lambda$ gives $(\sqrt{\mathbf A})^2 = \sum_\lambda\lambda\mathbf P_\lambda =
\mathbf A$. For the example, $\mathbf A = 3\mathbf P_3 + \mathbf P_1$ (@exm-sth-lagrange), so $\sqrt{\mathbf A} = \sqrt3\mathbf P_3 +
\mathbf P_1 = \tfrac{\sqrt3 + 1}{2}\mathbf I + \tfrac{\sqrt3 - 1}{2}\sigma_1$.

## SageMath

The code squares the proposed root and checks its eigenvalues.

```{.python .sage}
A = matrix(SR, [[2, 1], [1, 2]]); s1 = matrix(SR, [[0, 1], [1, 0]])
sq = (sqrt(3) + 1) / 2 * identity_matrix(2) + (sqrt(3) - 1) / 2 * s1
print("sqrt A ="); print(sq)
print("(sqrt A)^2 = A:", bool((sq * sq).simplify_full() == A))
print("eigenvalues of sqrt A:", sq.eigenvalues())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
sqrt A =
[1/2*sqrt(3) + 1/2 1/2*sqrt(3) - 1/2]
[1/2*sqrt(3) - 1/2 1/2*sqrt(3) + 1/2]
(sqrt A)^2 = A: True
eigenvalues of sqrt A: [sqrt(3), 1]
```
::::
:::

The largest and smallest eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix are the extreme values of its quadratic form on unit vectors, the
variational principle behind every ground-state estimate. The seventh exercise proves this for matrices.

::: {#exr-sth-rayleigh}
#### The Rayleigh quotient

For a Hermitian matrix with eigenvalues $\lambda_{\min} \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{\max}$, show that $\lambda_{\min} \leq \mathbf
u^\dagger\mathbf A\mathbf u \leq \lambda_{\max}$ for every unit vector $\mathbf u$, with equality at the corresponding eigenvectors.
Check it on the matrix of @exm-sth-3x3 with many random unit vectors.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

With $\mathbf u = \sum_kc_k\mathbf e_k$ in the eigenbasis of @thm-spectral-theorem-hermitian (1) and $\sum_k|c_k|^2 = 1$, $\mathbf
u^\dagger\mathbf A\mathbf u = \sum_k\lambda_k|c_k|^2$ is a weighted average of the eigenvalues with weights $|c_k|^2 \geq 0$ summing to
$1$, hence between $\lambda_{\min}$ and $\lambda_{\max}$. For $\mathbf u = \mathbf e_k$ it equals $\lambda_k$.

## SageMath

Check on $\mathbf A$ of @exm-sth-3x3: the code samples $2000$ random unit vectors and compares the extreme values of the quadratic
form with $2 \pm \sqrt2$.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(1)
A = matrix(RDF, [[2, 1, 0], [1, 2, 1], [0, 1, 2]])
vals = []
for _ in range(2000):
    u = vector(RDF, [normalvariate(0, 1) for _ in range(3)]); u = u / u.norm()
    vals.append(u * A * u)
print("min sampled = %.4f >= 2 - sqrt 2 = %.4f" % (min(vals), 2 - sqrt(2.)))
print("max sampled = %.4f <= 2 + sqrt 2 = %.4f" % (max(vals), 2 + sqrt(2.)))
print("all within the bounds:", all(2 - sqrt(2.) - 1e-12 <= v <= 2 + sqrt(2.) + 1e-12 for v in vals))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
min sampled = 0.5881 >= 2 - sqrt 2 = 0.5858
max sampled = 3.4137 <= 2 + sqrt 2 = 3.4142
all within the bounds: True
```
::::
:::

A circulant matrix is a polynomial in the cyclic shift, so all circulants of one size share the Fourier eigenbasis of
@exm-sth-ring. The eighth exercise proves this and reads off the eigenvalues.

::: {#exr-sth-circulant}
#### Circulant matrices

Let $\mathbf A = \sum_{j = 0}^{N-1}c_j\mathbf C^j$ with $\mathbf C$ the cyclic shift of @exm-sth-ring. Show that $\mathbf A$ is
normal and that $\mathbf A\mathbf f_k = \hat c_k\mathbf f_k$ with $\hat c_k = \sum_jc_j\omega^{-jk}$. Compute the eigenvalues for $N =
4$, $c = (2, 1, 0, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathbf C$ is unitary, since it permutes an orthonormal basis, so $\mathbf C^\dagger = \mathbf C^{-1} = \mathbf C^{N-1}$ and $\mathbf
A^\dagger = \sum_jc_j^*\mathbf C^{-j}$ is again a polynomial in $\mathbf C$; polynomials in one matrix commute, so $\mathbf A$ is
normal. From $\mathbf C\mathbf f_k = \omega^{-k}\mathbf f_k$ (@exm-sth-ring) and @def-operator-eigenvalue (2), $\mathbf A\mathbf f_k =
\sum_jc_j\omega^{-jk}\mathbf f_k$. For $c = (2, 1, 0, 1)$, $\mathbf A = 2\mathbf I + \mathbf C + \mathbf C^{-1}$ and $\hat c_k = 2 +
2\cos(\pi k/2)$: the eigenvalues are $4, 2, 0, 2$.

## SageMath

The code builds the circulant and applies it to the Fourier vectors.

```{.python .sage}
N = 4; c = [2, 1, 0, 1]
C = matrix(QQbar, N, N, lambda j, k: 1 if j == (k + 1) % N else 0)
A = sum(c[j] * C ** j for j in range(N))
w = QQbar(exp(2 * pi * I / N))
print("A ="); print(A)
for k in range(N):
    f = vector(QQbar, [w ** (j * k) for j in range(N)])
    ck = sum(c[j] * w ** (-j * k) for j in range(N))
    print("k =", k, ": A f_k = c_k f_k:", A * f == ck * f, "; c_k =", ck)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
A =
[2 1 0 1]
[1 2 1 0]
[0 1 2 1]
[1 0 1 2]
k = 0 : A f_k = c_k f_k: True ; c_k = 4
k = 1 : A f_k = c_k f_k: True ; c_k = 2
k = 2 : A f_k = c_k f_k: True ; c_k = 0
k = 3 : A f_k = c_k f_k: True ; c_k = 2
```
::::
:::

Two polynomials that agree on the eigenvalues define the same matrix, and this is the reason the Cayley-Hamilton theorem holds for
Hermitian matrices and a function of a matrix is a polynomial in it. The ninth exercise asks for these consequences of part (3).

::: {#exr-sd-polynomial-identity}
#### Polynomials agreeing on the spectrum

For a Hermitian matrix $\mathbf A$ show that $p(\mathbf A) = q(\mathbf A)$ whenever $p(\lambda) = q(\lambda)$ for all eigenvalues, that
the characteristic polynomial satisfies $\chi_{\mathbf A}(\mathbf A) = \mathbf 0$, and that $\sum_\lambda f(\lambda)\mathbf P_\lambda =
p(\mathbf A)$ for any function $f$ on the eigenvalues and its interpolation polynomial $p$. Find $p$ for $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 2
& 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ and $f = \exp$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By @thm-spectral-theorem-hermitian (3), $p(\mathbf A) = \sum_\lambda p(\lambda)\mathbf P_\lambda = \sum_\lambda q(\lambda)\mathbf
P_\lambda = q(\mathbf A)$. $\chi_{\mathbf A}(\lambda) = 0$ for every eigenvalue, so $\chi_{\mathbf A}(\mathbf A) = \sum_\lambda
0\cdot\mathbf P_\lambda = \mathbf 0$. The Lagrange polynomial $p = \sum_\lambda f(\lambda)\prod_{\mu \neq \lambda}(x - \mu)/(\lambda
- \mu)$ has $p(\lambda) = f(\lambda)$, so $p(\mathbf A) = \sum f(\lambda)\mathbf P_\lambda$. For the example, $p(x) = e^3\tfrac{x -
1}{2} - e\tfrac{x - 3}{2} = \tfrac{e^3 - e}{2}x + \tfrac{3e - e^3}{2}$.

## SageMath

The code compares $p(\mathbf A)$ with Sage's matrix exponential and checks Cayley-Hamilton.

```{.python .sage}
A = matrix(SR, [[2, 1], [1, 2]])
p = lambda M: (e ** 3 - e) / 2 * M + (3 * e - e ** 3) / 2 * identity_matrix(2)
print("p(A) = exp(A):", bool((p(A) - A.exp()).simplify_full() == 0))
chi = A.change_ring(QQ).charpoly()
print("characteristic polynomial:", chi, "; chi(A) = 0:", chi(A.change_ring(QQ)) == 0)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
p(A) = exp(A): True
characteristic polynomial: x^2 - 4*x + 3 ; chi(A) = 0: True
```
::::
:::

The time evolution of a two-level system is the exponential of its Hamiltonian, and part (3) together with the exponential series
computes it in closed form. The last exercise derives the Rabi oscillation between the two levels.

::: {#exr-sth-rabi}
#### Rabi oscillations

For $\mathbf H = \Delta\sigma_1$ with real $\Delta$, show that $e^{-it\mathbf H} = \sum_\lambda e^{-it\lambda}\mathbf P_\lambda = \cos(\Delta
t)\mathbf I - i\sin(\Delta t)\sigma_1$, with the matrix exponential of @def-matrix-exp, and that the probability $|\mathbf
e_2^\dagger e^{-it\mathbf H}\mathbf e_1|^2$ of finding the system in the second level at time $t$ is $\sin^2(\Delta t)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By @thm-spectral-theorem-hermitian (2), $-it\mathbf H = \mathbf U(-it\mathbf D)\mathbf U^\dagger$ with $\mathbf D = \operatorname{diag}(\Delta,
-\Delta)$, so $e^{-it\mathbf H} = \mathbf Ue^{-it\mathbf D}\mathbf U^\dagger$ by @def-matrix-exp (3), and $e^{-it\mathbf D} =
\operatorname{diag}(e^{-it\Delta}, e^{it\Delta})$ since the series acts entry by entry on a diagonal matrix. Hence $e^{-it\mathbf H} =
e^{-it\Delta}\mathbf P_+ + e^{it\Delta}\mathbf P_-$ with $\mathbf P_\pm = \tfrac12(\mathbf I \pm \sigma_1)$, which is $\cos(\Delta t)(\mathbf
P_+ + \mathbf P_-) - i\sin(\Delta t)(\mathbf P_+ - \mathbf P_-) = \cos(\Delta t)\mathbf I - i\sin(\Delta t)\sigma_1$. Its $(2, 1)$ entry is
$-i\sin(\Delta t)$, of squared modulus $\sin^2(\Delta t)$: the system moves fully to the second level at $t = \pi/(2|\Delta|)$.

## SageMath

The code compares Sage's matrix exponential with the closed form for symbolic $t$ and $\Delta$.

```{.python .sage}
t, Dl = var("t Delta", domain="real")
s1 = matrix(SR, [[0, 1], [1, 0]])
E = (-I * t * Dl * s1).exp().apply_map(lambda z: z.rectform().simplify_full())
closed = cos(Dl * t) * identity_matrix(2) - I * sin(Dl * t) * s1
print("exp(-itH) ="); print(E)
print("equals cos(Dt) - i sin(Dt) sigma_1:", bool((E - closed).simplify_full() == 0))
print("|e_2^dagger exp(-itH) e_1|^2 =", (abs(E[1, 0]) ** 2).simplify_full())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
exp(-itH) =
[   cos(Delta*t) -I*sin(Delta*t)]
[-I*sin(Delta*t)    cos(Delta*t)]
equals cos(Dt) - i sin(Dt) sigma_1: True
|e_2^dagger exp(-itH) e_1|^2 = sin(Delta*t)^2
```
::::
:::
::::

### The spectrum

An eigenvalue makes $A - \lambda$ non-injective; in infinite dimensions $A - \lambda$ can also fail to be invertible by having a
range that is too small, dense or not. The definition below collects all such $\lambda$ into the spectrum, sorts them into three
kinds, and computes the spectrum for the model operators of @sec-bounded-operators.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-spectrum}
#### Spectrum

Let $\mathcal H \neq \{0\}$ and $A \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$. A number $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$ is in the **resolvent set** of $A$ if
$A - \lambda$ is a bijection of $\mathcal H$ onto itself; its inverse is then bounded (@thm-open-mapping (2)) and is the **resolvent**
$R_\lambda(A) = (A - \lambda)^{-1} \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$. The **spectrum** $\sigma(A)$ is the complement of the resolvent set.
It splits into the **point spectrum** $\sigma_p(A)$, where $A - \lambda$ is not injective (the eigenvalues); the **continuous
spectrum** $\sigma_c(A)$, where $A - \lambda$ is injective with dense range but not onto; and the **residual spectrum**
$\sigma_r(A)$, where $A - \lambda$ is injective and its range is not dense. A number $\lambda$ is an **approximate eigenvalue** if
there are unit vectors $u_n$ with $\|(A - \lambda)u_n\| \to 0$. Then:

1. (**Neumann series**) if $B \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ has $\|B\| < 1$, then $1 - B$ is a bijection, $(1 - B)^{-1} = \sum_{n \geq
   0}B^n$ with convergence in norm, and $\|(1 - B)^{-1}\| \leq 1/(1 - \|B\|)$; hence every $\lambda$ with $|\lambda| > \|A\|$ is in the
   resolvent set, $R_\lambda(A) = -\sum_{n \geq 0}A^n/\lambda^{n+1}$ and $\|R_\lambda(A)\| \leq 1/(|\lambda| - \|A\|)$;
2. $\lambda$ is in the resolvent set if and only if $A - \lambda$ is **bounded below**, $\|(A - \lambda)u\| \geq c\|u\|$ for some
   $c > 0$ and all $u$, and has dense range; $\sigma(A)$ is the disjoint union of $\sigma_p(A)$, $\sigma_c(A)$ and $\sigma_r(A)$, every
   approximate eigenvalue lies in $\sigma(A)$, and every point of $\sigma_p(A) \cup \sigma_c(A)$ is an approximate eigenvalue;
3. $\sigma(A^\dagger) = \{\lambda^* : \lambda \in \sigma(A)\}$ and $R_{\lambda^*}(A^\dagger) = R_\lambda(A)^\dagger$; if $\lambda \in
   \sigma_r(A)$, then $\lambda^* \in \sigma_p(A^\dagger)$, and if $\lambda \in \sigma_p(A)$, then $\lambda^* \in \sigma_p(A^\dagger) \cup
   \sigma_r(A^\dagger)$;
4. if $A$ is normal, $\sigma_r(A)$ is empty and every point of $\sigma(A)$ is an approximate eigenvalue;
5. if $V : \mathcal H \to \mathcal K$ is a bijective isometry onto a Hilbert space $\mathcal K$, then $VAV^{-1}$ has the same
   spectrum, point spectrum, continuous spectrum and residual spectrum as $A$; for an $n \times n$ matrix, $\sigma(\mathbf A) =
   \sigma_p(\mathbf A)$ is the set of eigenvalues, a non-empty set of at most $n$ points;
6. for $g \in C[a, b]$, $\sigma(M_g) = g([a, b])$ on $L^2[a, b]$, $\sigma_r(M_g)$ is empty, and for $\lambda \notin g([a, b])$,
   $R_\lambda(M_g) = M_{1/(g - \lambda)}$ with $\|R_\lambda(M_g)\| = 1/\operatorname{dist}(\lambda, g([a, b]))$;
7. for the shifts on $\ell^2$, $\sigma(S) = \sigma(L) = \{|\lambda| \leq 1\}$, with $\sigma_p(S) = \emptyset$, $\sigma_r(S) = \{|\lambda|
   < 1\}$, $\sigma_c(S) = \{|\lambda| = 1\}$, and $\sigma_p(L) = \{|\lambda| < 1\}$, $\sigma_c(L) = \{|\lambda| = 1\}$, $\sigma_r(L) =
   \emptyset$.
:::
::::

*Proof.* (1) $\|B^n\| \leq \|B\|^n$ (@def-bounded-operator (1)), and $\sum_n\|B\|^n = 1/(1 - \|B\|)$, so the series converges in the
Banach space $\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ to some $C$ with $\|C\| \leq 1/(1 - \|B\|)$ (@thm-absolute-series). Since $(1 - B)\sum_{n \leq
N}B^n = \sum_{n \leq N}B^n(1 - B) = 1 - B^{N+1}$ and $\|B^{N+1}\| \to 0$, continuity of multiplication (@def-bounded-operator (1))
gives $(1 - B)C = C(1 - B) = 1$, so $1 - B$ is a bijection with inverse $C$. For $|\lambda| > \|A\|$, $A - \lambda = -\lambda(1 -
A/\lambda)$ with $\|A/\lambda\| < 1$, which gives the series for $R_\lambda(A)$ and the bound $|\lambda|^{-1}/(1 - \|A\|/|\lambda|)$.

(2) If $\lambda$ is in the resolvent set, $\|u\| = \|R_\lambda(A - \lambda)u\| \leq \|R_\lambda\|\,\|(A - \lambda)u\|$, so $A -
\lambda$ is bounded below with $c = 1/\|R_\lambda\|$, and its range is $\mathcal H$. Conversely let $T = A - \lambda$ be bounded below
with dense range. Then $T$ is injective, and its range is closed: if $Tu_n \to w$, then $\|u_n - u_m\| \leq \|Tu_n - Tu_m\|/c$, so
$u_n \to u$ and $w = Tu$. A closed dense range is $\mathcal H$, so $T$ is a bijection. The three parts are disjoint and exhaust
$\sigma(A)$ by their definitions. An approximate eigenvalue $\lambda$ makes $A - \lambda$ not bounded below, so $\lambda \in
\sigma(A)$. An eigenvalue is approximate with the constant sequence of a unit eigenvector. If $\lambda \in \sigma_c(A)$, $A - \lambda$
has dense range but is not a bijection, so it is not bounded below: for each $n$ some unit $u_n$ has $\|(A - \lambda)u_n\| < 1/n$.

(3) $(A - \lambda)^\dagger = A^\dagger - \lambda^*$. If $A - \lambda$ has a bounded inverse, so has its adjoint, with inverse
$R_\lambda(A)^\dagger$ (@def-adjoint-operator (2)); applied to $A^\dagger$ and $(A^\dagger)^\dagger = A$ this gives the converse. If
$\lambda \in \sigma_r(A)$, $\ker(A^\dagger - \lambda^*) = \operatorname{ran}(A - \lambda)^\perp \neq \{0\}$ by @def-adjoint-operator (4)
and @thm-projection (3). If $\lambda \in \sigma_p(A)$, the same part applied to $A^\dagger - \lambda^*$ gives
$\operatorname{ran}(A^\dagger - \lambda^*)^\perp = \ker(A - \lambda) \neq \{0\}$, so the range of $A^\dagger - \lambda^*$ is not dense
and $\lambda^* \in \sigma(A^\dagger) \setminus \sigma_c(A^\dagger)$.

(4) $A - \lambda$ is normal, so $\ker(A - \lambda) = \ker(A^\dagger - \lambda^*) = \operatorname{ran}(A - \lambda)^\perp$
(@def-normal-operator (1), @def-adjoint-operator (4)). If $A - \lambda$ is injective, its range is therefore dense: $\sigma_r(A) =
\emptyset$, and by (2) every point of $\sigma(A) = \sigma_p(A) \cup \sigma_c(A)$ is an approximate eigenvalue.

(5) $VAV^{-1} - \lambda = V(A - \lambda)V^{-1}$, and $V$, $V^{-1}$ are linear bijections preserving norms. So $VAV^{-1} - \lambda$ is
injective, onto, or has dense range exactly when $A - \lambda$ does, since $V$ maps $\ker(A - \lambda)$ onto $\ker(VAV^{-1} - \lambda)$
and the range of $A - \lambda$, and its closure, onto those of $VAV^{-1} - \lambda$. For a matrix, rank-nullity makes $\mathbf A -
\lambda$ injective if and only if it is onto, so $\sigma(\mathbf A) = \sigma_p(\mathbf A)$, described by @def-operator-eigenvalue (4).

(6) If $\lambda \notin g([a, b])$, $h = 1/(g - \lambda)$ is continuous and $M_hM_{g - \lambda} = M_{g - \lambda}M_h = M_1 = 1$
(@def-bounded-operator (5)), so $R_\lambda(M_g) = M_h$ with $\|M_h\| = \|h\|_\infty = 1/\min_x|g(x) - \lambda|$, and the minimum over
the compact interval is the distance to the compact set $g([a, b])$. If $\lambda = g(x_0)$, let $\varepsilon > 0$ and choose an
interval $I \ni x_0$ of positive length in $[a, b]$ with $|g - \lambda| \leq \varepsilon$ on $I$; a tent $f \neq 0$ vanishing outside
$I$ has $\|(M_g - \lambda)f\| \leq \varepsilon\|f\|$. So $\lambda$ is an approximate eigenvalue and lies in $\sigma(M_g)$ by (2). $M_g$
is normal (@def-normal-operator (2)), so $\sigma_r(M_g) = \emptyset$ by (4).

(7) $\|S\| = \|L\| = 1$, so both spectra lie in the closed unit disc by (1). By @def-operator-eigenvalue (5), $\sigma_p(S) = \emptyset$
and $\sigma_p(L) = \{|\lambda| < 1\}$. Since $L = S^\dagger$ (@def-adjoint-operator (6)), $\operatorname{ran}(S - \lambda)^\perp = \ker(L
- \lambda^*)$ is non-zero for $|\lambda| < 1$, so $\sigma_r(S) \supseteq \{|\lambda| < 1\}$, and it is $\{0\}$ for $|\lambda| = 1$,
so then $S - \lambda$ is injective with dense range. Likewise $\operatorname{ran}(L - \lambda)^\perp = \ker(S - \lambda^*) = \{0\}$ for
every $\lambda$, so $\sigma_r(L) = \emptyset$. For $|\lambda| = 1$ both $S - \lambda$ and $L - \lambda$ fail to be bounded below: with
$u_N = N^{-1/2}(1, \lambda^*, \dots, (\lambda^*)^{N-1}, 0, \dots)$, $(S - \lambda)u_N = N^{-1/2}(-\lambda, 0, \dots, 0, (\lambda^*)^{N-1},
0, \dots)$ has norm $\sqrt{2/N}$, and with $v_N = N^{-1/2}(1, \lambda, \dots, \lambda^{N-1}, 0, \dots)$, $(L - \lambda)v_N = -N^{-1/2}\lambda^N\delta^{(N)}$
has norm $N^{-1/2}$. So the unit circle lies in $\sigma_c(S)$ and in $\sigma_c(L)$, which completes the description. $\square$

The decomposition into three parts and parts (3), (4) are @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 3.9.2, Prop. 3.10 and Cor. 3.9]; part (1) and the
spectra of the shifts are @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Thm. VI.5, its corollary and the example of Sec. VI.3], there on $\ell^1$ and
$\ell^\infty$, and @gasinski2014exercises [Problem 5.165]; part (6) is @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 6.1.3] for continuous multipliers.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For a matrix the spectrum is exactly the set of eigenvalues, and the resolvent is a matrix of rational functions of $\lambda$ with
poles there. The first example computes it for the matrix of @fig-operator-norm-ellipse.

::: {#exm-sp-matrix}
#### The resolvent of a matrix

For $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, $(\mathbf A - \lambda)^{-1} = \frac{1}{(2 - \lambda)(1 - \lambda)}
\begin{pmatrix} 1 - \lambda & -1 \\ 0 & 2 - \lambda\end{pmatrix}$ exists for $\lambda \neq 1, 2$: $\sigma(\mathbf A) = \{1, 2\}$, the
eigenvalues, as part (5) says. The entries have simple poles at the eigenvalues, and $\|R_\lambda(\mathbf A)\| \to \infty$ as $\lambda$
approaches the spectrum, like the reciprocal of the distance.
:::

A diagonal operator has its diagonal entries as eigenvalues, and their limit points join the spectrum without being eigenvalues.
The second example computes the spectrum and its parts.

::: {#exm-sp-diagonal}
#### Diagonal operators

For the diagonal operator $D$ with bounded entries $d_n$, $\sigma(D)$ is the closure of $\{d_n\}$. If $\lambda$ is not in the
closure, $\delta = \inf_n|d_n - \lambda| > 0$ and the diagonal operator with entries $1/(d_n - \lambda)$, of norm at most $1/\delta$
(@def-bounded-operator (4)), inverts $D - \lambda$; if $d_{n_k} \to \lambda$, then $\|(D - \lambda)\delta^{(n_k)}\| \to 0$, so $\lambda$
is an approximate eigenvalue and lies in $\sigma(D)$ by part (2). For $d_n = 1/n$,
$\sigma(D) = \{1/n : n \geq 1\} \cup \{0\}$. The numbers $1/n$ are eigenvalues; $0$ is not, but $D$ has dense range, containing every
finitely supported sequence, and it is not onto, since $Da = (1/n)_n$ would need $a = (1, 1, \dots) \notin \ell^2$. So $0 \in
\sigma_c(D)$, and $\|D\delta^{(n)}\| = 1/n \to 0$ exhibits it as an approximate eigenvalue.
:::

The position operator on $L^2[0, 1]$ has spectrum the whole interval $[0, 1]$ and no eigenvalues. The third example reads this off
part (6), giving the first purely continuous spectrum.

::: {#exm-sp-multiplication}
#### The continuous spectrum of the position operator

By part (6), $\sigma(M_x) = [0, 1]$ on $L^2[0, 1]$, and by @def-operator-eigenvalue (6) there are no eigenvalues; $M_x$ is normal,
so $\sigma(M_x) = \sigma_c(M_x)$. The approximate eigenvectors of @exm-ev-multiplication-none show directly that no bounded inverse of
$M_x - \lambda$ exists for $\lambda \in [0, 1]$. For $\lambda \notin [0, 1]$ the resolvent is multiplication by $1/(x - \lambda)$, of
norm $1/\operatorname{dist}(\lambda, [0, 1])$.
:::

The shift has the closed unit disc as spectrum without a single eigenvalue, while the left shift has the open disc as eigenvalues.
The figure shows the three parts of both spectra, and the fourth example explains why they are mirror images.

![The spectra of the right shift $S$ (left) and the left shift $L$ (right) on $\ell^2$: both are the closed unit disc. For $S$ the
open disc is residual spectrum and the circle is continuous spectrum; for $L$ the open disc consists of eigenvalues and the circle
is continuous spectrum.](figures/fa2-shift-spectra.svg){#fig-fa2-shift-spectra width=90%}

::: {#exm-sp-shift}
#### Spectra of the shifts

Part (7) gives the spectra in @fig-fa2-shift-spectra. They are related by part (3): $L = S^\dagger$, the residual spectrum of $S$ is
the conjugate of the point spectrum of $L$, and the two spectra are each other's conjugates. For $|\lambda| < 1$ the range of $S -
\lambda$ is orthogonal to the eigenvector $(1, \lambda^*, (\lambda^*)^2, \dots)$ of $L$; for $\lambda = 0$ this is $\delta^{(1)}
\perp \operatorname{ran}S$.
:::

The bilateral shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ is unitary, and the Fourier series turn it into a multiplication operator. The fifth
example uses part (5) to compute its spectrum, the unit circle.

::: {#exm-sp-bilateral-shift}
#### The bilateral shift

Let $(Wa)_n = a_{n-1}$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$. The coefficient map $C : L^2[-\pi, \pi] \to \ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ of
@exr-un-fourier-plancherel is a bijective isometry with $CM_{e^{ix}}C^{-1} = W$. By parts (5) and (6), $\sigma(W) = \{e^{ix} : x \in
[-\pi, \pi]\}$, the unit circle, and $e^{ix} - \lambda$ has at most two zeros, so by @def-operator-eigenvalue (6) there are no
eigenvalues: the whole circle is continuous spectrum.
:::

An electron hopping between neighbouring sites of an infinite chain has a band of allowed energies instead of discrete levels. The
sixth example obtains the band as the spectrum of a multiplication operator.

::: {#exm-sp-tight-binding-band}
#### The band of an infinite chain

On $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ the tight-binding Hamiltonian is $H = -(W + W^\dagger)$, $(Ha)_n = -a_{n-1} - a_{n+1}$. With $C$ as in
@exm-sp-bilateral-shift, $C^{-1}HC = -(M_{e^{ix}} + M_{e^{-ix}}) = M_{-2\cos x}$, so by parts (5) and (6) $\sigma(H) = [-2, 2]$. Since
$-2\cos x - \lambda$ has at most two zeros on $[-\pi, \pi]$, $H$ has no eigenvalue: the band is continuous spectrum, and the plane waves
$e^{inx}$ that would be its eigenvectors are not square-summable.
:::

The oscillator operator of @exm-ev-oscillator is diagonal in the Hermite basis, so part (5) reduces its spectrum to that of a diagonal
operator. The seventh example finds that its accumulation point $0$ is continuous spectrum.

::: {#exm-sp-oscillator}
#### The inverse oscillator energies

The coefficient map $F \mapsto (\langle h_n, F\rangle)_{n \geq 0}$ is a bijective isometry of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ onto $\ell^2$
(@thm-hermite-basis, @def-orthonormal-basis (3)), and it carries the operator $A$ of @exm-ev-oscillator to the diagonal operator with
entries $1/(2n + 1)$. By part (5) and @exm-sp-diagonal, $\sigma(A) = \{1/(2n + 1) : n \geq 0\} \cup \{0\}$, with $0 \in \sigma_c(A)$:
arbitrarily highly excited states are approximate eigenvectors for $0$.
:::

The bound states of hydrogen have energies $-1/(2n^2)$ in atomic units, accumulating at the ionisation threshold $0$. The eighth
example models them by a diagonal operator with the right multiplicities.

::: {#exm-sp-hydrogen}
#### A diagonal model of the hydrogen levels

Let $D$ be the diagonal operator on $\ell^2$ whose entries list $-1/(2n^2)$ exactly $n^2$ times, for $n = 1, 2, \dots$ (spin
ignored). By @exm-sp-diagonal, $\sigma(D) = \{-1/(2n^2)\} \cup \{0\}$: each level is an eigenvalue of
multiplicity $n^2$, and the threshold $0$ is in the spectrum without being an eigenvalue. In the true atom the continuum above $0$ is
added by the scattering states, which this bounded model leaves out.
:::

The Fourier transform on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ satisfies $U^4 = 1$, which pins its spectrum to four points. The ninth example writes the
resolvent explicitly as a polynomial in $U$.

::: {#exm-sp-fourier}
#### The spectrum of the Fourier transform

For $\lambda^4 \neq 1$, $(U - \lambda)(U^3 + \lambda U^2 + \lambda^2U + \lambda^3) = U^4 - \lambda^4 = 1 - \lambda^4$, and the two
factors commute, so $R_\lambda(U) = (U^3 + \lambda U^2 + \lambda^2U + \lambda^3)/(1 - \lambda^4)$. With @exm-ev-fourier, $\sigma(U) =
\sigma_p(U) = \{1, -i, -1, i\}$, each eigenvalue of infinite multiplicity.
:::

In finite dimensions a one-sided inverse is automatically two-sided; in infinite dimensions it is not, and this is why the
spectrum is defined through bijectivity. The last example is the shift pair.

::: {#exm-sp-left-inverse}
#### One-sided inverses are not enough

$LS = 1$ (@def-bounded-operator (4)), yet $0 \in \sigma(S)$ and $0 \in \sigma(L)$: $S$ is injective but not onto ($\delta^{(1)}
\notin \operatorname{ran}S$) and $L$ is onto but not injective ($L\delta^{(1)} = 0$). For square matrices $\mathbf L\mathbf S =
\mathbf I$ forces both to be invertible. Also $S$ is bounded below, $\|Sa\| = \|a\|$, so $0 \in \sigma(S)$ is not an approximate
eigenvalue: for an operator that is not normal, the approximate eigenvalues need not fill the spectrum.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Sage inverts $\mathbf A - \lambda$ symbolically, which displays the poles of the resolvent and allows the growth of its norm near
the spectrum to be measured. The first exercise does this for two matrices.

::: {#exr-sp-resolvent-2x2}
#### Resolvents in Sage

Compute $(\mathbf A - \lambda)^{-1}$ for $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and for $\sigma_1$, and show that
$\|R_{2 + \varepsilon}(\mathbf A)\|\,\varepsilon \to \sqrt2$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The resolvent of $\mathbf A$ is in @exm-sp-matrix, and that of $\sigma_1$ is $(\sigma_1 - \lambda)^{-1} = (1 - \lambda^2)^{-1}
\begin{pmatrix} -\lambda & -1 \\ -1 & -\lambda\end{pmatrix}$, with poles at $\pm1$. At $\lambda = 2 + \varepsilon$,
$\varepsilon R_\lambda(\mathbf A) = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & -1/(1 + \varepsilon) \\ 0 & -\varepsilon/(1 + \varepsilon)\end{pmatrix} \to
\begin{pmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, whose norm is $\|(1, 1)\| = \sqrt2$ (a matrix with one non-zero row $\mathbf r$
has norm $\|\mathbf r\|$). Since the norm is continuous, $\varepsilon\|R_{2 + \varepsilon}(\mathbf A)\| \to \sqrt2$: a simple pole
with residue of norm $\sqrt2$.

## SageMath

The code inverts symbolically and evaluates $\varepsilon\|R_{2 + \varepsilon}(\mathbf A)\|$ for three values of $\varepsilon$.

```{.python .sage}
lam = var("lambda_")
A = matrix(SR, [[2, 1], [0, 1]]); s1 = matrix(SR, [[0, 1], [1, 0]])
R = lambda M, z: (M - z * identity_matrix(2)).inverse()
print("R_A(lambda) ="); print(R(A, lam).simplify_full())
print("R_sigma1(lambda) ="); print(R(s1, lam).simplify_full())
for eps in [QQ(1) / 10, QQ(1) / 100, QQ(1) / 1000]:
    nr = R(A, 2 + eps).change_ring(QQ).change_ring(RDF).norm(2)
    print("epsilon =", eps, ": epsilon ||R|| = %.6f" % (eps * nr), "; sqrt 2 = %.6f" % sqrt(2.))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
R_A(lambda) =
[              -1/(lambda_ - 2) -1/(lambda_^2 - 3*lambda_ + 2)]
[                             0               -1/(lambda_ - 1)]
R_sigma1(lambda) =
[-lambda_/(lambda_^2 - 1)       -1/(lambda_^2 - 1)]
[      -1/(lambda_^2 - 1) -lambda_/(lambda_^2 - 1)]
epsilon = 1/10 : epsilon ||R|| = 1.352847 ; sqrt 2 = 1.414214
epsilon = 1/100 : epsilon ||R|| = 1.407247 ; sqrt 2 = 1.414214
epsilon = 1/1000 : epsilon ||R|| = 1.413508 ; sqrt 2 = 1.414214
```
::::
:::

A diagonal operator is inverted entry by entry, which gives its spectrum completely. The second exercise computes the norm of the resolvent
of a diagonal operator and sorts its spectrum into the three parts.

::: {#exr-sp-diagonal-closure}
#### The spectrum of a diagonal operator

For the diagonal operator $D$ with bounded entries $d_n$, show that $\|R_\lambda(D)\| = 1/\operatorname{dist}(\lambda, \{d_n\})$ for
$\lambda \notin \sigma(D)$, that $\sigma_p(D) = \{d_n\}$, and that the remaining points of the closure of $\{d_n\}$ form $\sigma_c(D)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By @exm-sp-diagonal, $\sigma(D)$ is the closure of $\{d_n\}$, and for $\lambda$ outside it $R_\lambda(D)$ is the diagonal operator with
entries $1/(d_n - \lambda)$, whose norm is $\sup_n1/|d_n - \lambda| = 1/\inf_n|d_n - \lambda|$ by @def-bounded-operator (4). The eigenvalues are the $d_n$ (@exm-ev-diagonal). $D$ is normal
(@def-normal-operator (2)), so $\sigma_r(D) = \emptyset$ (@def-spectrum (4)), and the points of the closure that are not eigenvalues
are in $\sigma_c(D)$.

## SageMath

Check on $d_n = 1/n$ truncated to $N = 200$ entries: the code computes $\min_n|d_n - \lambda|$ and the norm of the truncated
resolvent for $\lambda = -\tfrac12$, $\tfrac23$ and $0.015$.

```{.python .sage}
N = 200
d = [1 / RDF(n) for n in range(1, N + 1)]
for lam in [RDF(-0.5), RDF(2) / 3, RDF(0.015)]:
    dist = min(abs(x - lam) for x in d)
    Rn = max(1 / abs(x - lam) for x in d)
    print("lambda = %.4f : dist to {1/n} = %.6f ; ||R_lambda|| = %.6f ; product = %.6f" % (lam, dist, Rn, dist * Rn))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
lambda = -0.5000 : dist to {1/n} = 0.505000 ; ||R_lambda|| = 1.980198 ; product = 1.000000
lambda = 0.6667 : dist to {1/n} = 0.166667 ; ||R_lambda|| = 6.000000 ; product = 1.000000
lambda = 0.0150 : dist to {1/n} = 0.000075 ; ||R_lambda|| = 13400.000000 ; product = 1.000000
```
::::
:::

For a multiplication operator the resolvent is again a multiplication operator, and its norm is a supremum of a function. The third
exercise checks part (6) on a multiplier whose range is covered twice.

::: {#exr-sp-multiplication-resolvent}
#### The resolvent of $M_{x^2}$

On $L^2[-1, 1]$ let $g(x) = x^2$. Show that $\sigma(M_g) = [0, 1]$ with no eigenvalues, and compute $\|R_\lambda(M_g)\|$ for $\lambda =
2$, $i$ and $-1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$g([-1, 1]) = [0, 1]$, so $\sigma(M_g) = [0, 1]$ by @def-spectrum (6). For each $\lambda$, $x^2 - \lambda$ has at most two zeros, so
there are no eigenvalues (@def-operator-eigenvalue (6)). By @def-spectrum (6), $\|R_\lambda(M_g)\| = 1/\operatorname{dist}(\lambda, [0,
1])$: for $\lambda = 2$ the distance is $1$; for $\lambda = i$ it is $|i - 0| = 1$; for $\lambda = -1$ it is $1$. So all three norms
equal $1$, although the three points lie on different sides of the spectrum.

## SageMath

The code computes $\max_{x \in [-1, 1]}|1/(x^2 - \lambda)|$ on a fine grid for the three values.

```{.python .sage}
xs = [RDF(-1 + k / 5000) for k in range(10001)]
for lam in [CDF(2), CDF(0, 1), CDF(-1)]:
    print("lambda =", lam, ": max |1/(x^2 - lambda)| = %.6f" % max(abs(1 / (x ** 2 - lam)) for x in xs))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
lambda = 2.0 : max |1/(x^2 - lambda)| = 1.000000
lambda = 1.0*I : max |1/(x^2 - lambda)| = 1.000000
lambda = -1.0 : max |1/(x^2 - lambda)| = 1.000000
```
::::
:::

The residual spectrum of an operator is detected by eigenvectors of its adjoint. The fourth exercise sharpens part (3) to an exact
description and checks it on the shift.

::: {#exr-sp-adjoint-relation}
#### Residual spectrum and the adjoint

Show that $\sigma_r(A) = \{\lambda \notin \sigma_p(A) : \lambda^* \in \sigma_p(A^\dagger)\}$ for every $A \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$, and
deduce $\sigma_r(S) = \{|\lambda| < 1\}$. Check that $\langle(1, \lambda^*, (\lambda^*)^2, \dots), (S - \lambda)a\rangle = 0$ for
finitely supported $a$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By @def-adjoint-operator (4), $\operatorname{ran}(A - \lambda)^\perp = \ker(A^\dagger - \lambda^*)$, and a subspace is dense exactly
when its orthogonal complement is $\{0\}$ (@thm-projection (3)). So for $\lambda \notin \sigma_p(A)$, the range of $A - \lambda$ fails
to be dense exactly when $\lambda^*$ is an eigenvalue of $A^\dagger$. For $S$, $\sigma_p(S) = \emptyset$ and $\sigma_p(L) = \{|\lambda|
< 1\}$, a set closed under conjugation (@def-operator-eigenvalue (5)). For the check, with $v = (1, \lambda^*, \dots)$ and $\langle v,
w\rangle = \sum_nv_n^*w_n$: $\langle v, Sa\rangle = \sum_{n \geq 1}\lambda^na_n$ and $\langle v, \lambda a\rangle = \lambda\sum_{n \geq
1}\lambda^{n-1}a_n$ are equal.

## SageMath

The code evaluates $\langle v, (S - \lambda)a\rangle$ for a symbolic finitely supported $a$ of length $5$.

```{.python .sage}
lam = var("lambda_"); a = list(var("a1 a2 a3 a4 a5"))
Sa = [0] + a; lama = [lam * c for c in a] + [0]
v = [lam ** n for n in range(6)]          # conjugate of (1, lambda^*, ...) entries: lambda^n
ip = sum(v[n] * (Sa[n] - lama[n]) for n in range(6))
print("<v, (S - lambda) a> =", ip.expand())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
<v, (S - lambda) a> = 0
```
::::
:::

A weighted shift with weights tending to zero is injective, but its range misses the first coordinate. The fifth exercise finds the
point and residual spectra of such a shift at $0$.

::: {#exr-sp-weighted-shift-zero}
#### A weighted shift at zero

Let $W\delta^{(n)} = \delta^{(n+1)}/n$, that is $(Wa)_{n+1} = a_n/n$ and $(Wa)_1 = 0$. Show that $W \in \mathcal B(\ell^2)$ with $\|W\| =
1$, that $W$ has no eigenvalues, that $0 \in \sigma_r(W)$, and that $0$ is an eigenvalue of $W^\dagger$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$W = SD$ with $D$ diagonal with entries $1/n$, so $W$ is bounded with $\|W\| \leq 1$, and $\|W\delta^{(1)}\| = 1$. If $Wa = \lambda a$, the
first coordinate gives $\lambda a_1 = 0$; if $\lambda \neq 0$, then $a_1 = 0$ and $\lambda a_{n+1} = a_n/n$ gives $a = 0$ inductively,
and if $\lambda = 0$, then $a_n/n = 0$ for all $n$. So $\sigma_p(W) = \emptyset$. The range of $W$ is orthogonal to $\delta^{(1)}$, so it
is not dense and $0 \in \sigma_r(W)$. Accordingly $W^\dagger = DL$ has $W^\dagger\delta^{(1)} = DL\delta^{(1)} = 0$, as
@exr-sp-adjoint-relation predicts.

## SageMath

Check on the $8 \times 8$ truncation: the code builds the matrix of $W$, prints its norm, its kernel and the kernel of its adjoint.

```{.python .sage}
N = 8
W = matrix(QQ, N, N, lambda j, k: QQ(1) / (k + 1) if j == k + 1 else 0)
print("||W_8|| =", W.change_ring(RDF).norm(2))
print("kernel of W_8 (only the last column is lost to truncation):", W.right_kernel().basis())
print("kernel of W_8^T contains delta^(1):", vector(QQ, [1] + [0] * (N - 1)) in W.transpose().right_kernel())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
||W_8|| = 1.0
kernel of W_8 (only the last column is lost to truncation): [
(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1)
]
kernel of W_8^T contains delta^(1): True
```
::::
:::

Approximate eigenvalues always lie in the spectrum, in every Banach space, but for an operator that is not normal they need not fill
it. The sixth exercise proves the first statement directly and shows the second with the shift.

::: {#exr-sp-approx-criterion}
#### Approximate eigenvalues

Show directly that if unit vectors $u_n$ satisfy $\|(A - \lambda)u_n\| \to 0$, then $A - \lambda$ has no bounded inverse. Show that $S$
has no approximate eigenvalue $\lambda$ with $|\lambda| < 1$, although these $\lambda$ lie in $\sigma(S)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $B$ were a bounded inverse, $1 = \|u_n\| = \|B(A - \lambda)u_n\| \leq \|B\|\,\|(A - \lambda)u_n\| \to 0$, a contradiction
[@gasinski2014exercises, Problem 5.170]. For the shift, $\|(S - \lambda)a\| \geq \|Sa\| - |\lambda|\,\|a\| = (1 - |\lambda|)\|a\|$, so $S
- \lambda$ is bounded below for $|\lambda| < 1$ and no unit vectors make $\|(S - \lambda)u_n\|$ small; yet $\{|\lambda| < 1\} =
\sigma_r(S)$ (@def-spectrum (7)). The spectrum of $S$ minus its approximate eigenvalues is exactly this residual part.

## SageMath

Check on $\lambda = \tfrac12$: the code computes the smallest singular value of the $N \times N$ truncation of $S - \lambda$ padded
with one extra row, which stays at least $1 - |\lambda| = \tfrac12$.

```{.python .sage}
lam = RDF(0.5)
for N in [5, 20, 80]:
    T = matrix(RDF, N + 1, N, lambda j, k: (1 if j == k + 1 else 0) - (lam if j == k else 0))
    print("N =", N, ": min singular value of (S - 1/2) on C^N = %.6f" % min(T.singular_values()))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
N = 5 : min singular value of (S - 1/2) on C^N = 0.619657
N = 20 : min singular value of (S - 1/2) on C^N = 0.511047
N = 80 : min singular value of (S - 1/2) on C^N = 0.500751
```
::::
:::

The approximate eigenvectors of the shift on its circle are truncated geometric sequences, and their defect can be computed
exactly. The seventh exercise does this and compares with the bound $\sqrt{2/N}$ used in the proof of part (7).

::: {#exr-sp-shift-circle}
#### The circle for the shift

For $|\lambda| = 1$ and $u_N = N^{-1/2}(1, \lambda^*, \dots, (\lambda^*)^{N-1}, 0, \dots)$, show that $\|(S - \lambda)u_N\| = \sqrt{2/N}$,
and conclude that no $\lambda$ on the circle is in the resolvent set of $S$ even though $S - \lambda$ is injective with dense range.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\sqrt NSu_N = (0, 1, \lambda^*, \dots, (\lambda^*)^{N-1}, 0, \dots)$ and $\sqrt N\lambda u_N = (\lambda, \lambda\lambda^*, \dots,
\lambda(\lambda^*)^{N-1}, 0, \dots) = (\lambda, 1, \lambda^*, \dots, (\lambda^*)^{N-2}, 0, \dots)$, using $\lambda\lambda^* = 1$. The
difference is $(-\lambda, 0, \dots, 0, (\lambda^*)^{N-1}, 0, \dots)$, with entries of modulus $1$ in places $1$ and $N + 1$, so $\|(S -
\lambda)u_N\| = \sqrt{2/N} \to 0$. Thus $S - \lambda$ is not bounded below and $\lambda \in \sigma(S)$ (@def-spectrum (2)), while
injectivity and density of the range hold by @def-spectrum (7): $\lambda \in \sigma_c(S)$.

## SageMath

The code computes $\|(S - \lambda)u_N\|$ for $\lambda = e^{i\pi/3}$ exactly in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3})$ and compares with $2/N$.

```{.python .sage}
K.<w> = CyclotomicField(6)                 # w = e^{i pi/3}
lam = w; lamc = w.conjugate()
for N in [4, 9, 25]:
    u = [lamc ** k for k in range(N)] + [0]            # sqrt(N) u_N, padded
    Su = [0] + u[:-1]
    diff = [Su[k] - lam * u[k] for k in range(N + 1)]
    sq = sum(c * c.conjugate() for c in diff) / N
    print("N =", N, ": ||(S - lambda) u_N||^2 =", sq, "; 2/N =", QQ(2) / N)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
N = 4 : ||(S - lambda) u_N||^2 = 1/2 ; 2/N = 1/2
N = 9 : ||(S - lambda) u_N||^2 = 2/9 ; 2/N = 2/9
N = 25 : ||(S - lambda) u_N||^2 = 2/25 ; 2/N = 2/25
```
::::
:::

Part (5) needs a bijective isometry, but the spectrum itself is invariant under every bounded similarity; the resolvent norms are not.
The eighth exercise proves the first statement and shows the second on a $2 \times 2$ example.

::: {#exr-sp-similarity}
#### Similar operators

Let $V \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ have a bounded inverse. Show that $\sigma(VAV^{-1}) = \sigma(A)$. For $\mathbf B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 &
1 \\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf D = \operatorname{diag}(1, 2) = \mathbf V\mathbf B\mathbf V^{-1}$, compare $\|R_\lambda(\mathbf B)\|$
and $\|R_\lambda(\mathbf D)\|$ at $\lambda = \tfrac32$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$VAV^{-1} - \lambda = V(A - \lambda)V^{-1}$, and if $A - \lambda$ has the bounded inverse $R$, then $VRV^{-1}$ is a bounded inverse of
$VAV^{-1} - \lambda$; the converse follows by exchanging the roles with $V^{-1}$. For the example, $\mathbf V = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0
& 1\end{pmatrix}$ maps the eigenvectors $(1, 0)$, $(1, 1)$ of $\mathbf B$ to $(1, 0)$, $(0, 1)$, and $\mathbf V\mathbf B\mathbf V^{-1} =
\mathbf D$. Both spectra are $\{1, 2\}$. At $\lambda = \tfrac32$, $R_\lambda(\mathbf D) = \operatorname{diag}(-2, 2)$ has norm $2$, while
$R_\lambda(\mathbf B) = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ has norm $\sqrt{12 + \sqrt{128}} = 2 + 2\sqrt2$, larger.

## SageMath

The code computes both resolvents and their norms exactly.

```{.python .sage}
B = matrix(QQ, [[1, 1], [0, 2]]); V = matrix(QQ, [[1, -1], [0, 1]])
D = V * B * V.inverse(); lam = QQ(3) / 2
print("V B V^-1 =", D.rows())
RB = (B - lam).inverse(); RD = (D - lam).inverse()
nB = sqrt(max((RB.transpose() * RB).change_ring(QQbar).eigenvalues()))
nD = sqrt(max((RD.transpose() * RD).change_ring(QQbar).eigenvalues()))
print("R(B) =", RB.rows(), "; ||R(B)|| =", nB, "= 2 + 2 sqrt 2:", nB == QQbar(2 + 2 * sqrt(2)))
print("R(D) =", RD.rows(), "; ||R(D)|| =", nD)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
V B V^-1 = [(1, 0), (0, 2)]
R(B) = [(-2, 4), (0, 2)] ; ||R(B)|| = 4.828427124746190? = 2 + 2 sqrt 2: True
R(D) = [(-2, 0), (0, 2)] ; ||R(D)|| = 2
```
::::
:::

The products $AB$ and $BA$ can have different spectra, but only at $0$. The ninth exercise proves this with an explicit inverse and
applies it to the two products of the shifts.

::: {#exr-sp-products}
#### The spectra of $AB$ and $BA$

Show that if $1 - AB$ has a bounded inverse $C$, then $1 - BA$ has the bounded inverse $1 + BCA$; deduce that $\sigma(AB) \cup \{0\} =
\sigma(BA) \cup \{0\}$. Compute $\sigma(LS)$ and $\sigma(SL)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$(1 - BA)(1 + BCA) = 1 - BA + BCA - BABCA = 1 - BA + B(1 - AB)CA = 1 - BA + BA = 1$, and likewise $(1 + BCA)(1 - BA) = 1 - BA + BCA -
BCABA = 1 - BA + BC(1 - AB)A = 1$. For $\lambda \neq 0$, $AB - \lambda = -\lambda(1 - (A/\lambda)B)$, so by the first part $AB - \lambda$
is invertible if and only if $BA - \lambda$ is. Here $LS = 1$ has spectrum $\{1\}$, and $SL = 1 - P_1$ (@def-bounded-operator (4)) is an
orthogonal projection $\neq 0, 1$, with eigenvalues $0$ and $1$ (@exm-ev-projection); for $\lambda \neq 0, 1$, $(P - \lambda)^{-1} = P/(1
- \lambda) - (1 - P)/\lambda$ for $P = SL$, as one multiplies out using $P^2 = P$. So $\sigma(SL) = \{0, 1\}$, and the two spectra differ
exactly at $0$.

## SageMath

Check on random $3 \times 2$ and $2 \times 3$ integer matrices: the code compares the characteristic polynomials of $\mathbf A\mathbf B$
and $\mathbf B\mathbf A$.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(3)
A = random_matrix(ZZ, 3, 2, x=-3, y=4); B = random_matrix(ZZ, 2, 3, x=-3, y=4)
x = polygen(QQ, "x")
pAB = (A * B).charpoly(); pBA = (B * A).charpoly()
print("char poly of AB:", pAB.factor()); print("char poly of BA:", pBA.factor())
print("p_AB = x p_BA:", pAB == x * pBA)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
char poly of AB: x * (x^2 - 3*x - 42)
char poly of BA: x^2 - 3*x - 42
p_AB = x p_BA: True
```

Cutting the infinite chain to $N$ sites gives a matrix whose eigenvalues crowd into the band $[-2, 2]$ as $N$ grows. The last exercise
combines the finite chain of @exr-ev-tridiagonal-n with @exm-sp-tight-binding-band and shows that the padded eigenvectors are
approximate eigenvectors of the infinite chain.

::: {#exr-sp-tight-binding-finite}
#### Finite chains fill the band

Let $\mathbf H_N$ be the $N \times N$ matrix with $-1$ on the two neighbouring diagonals and $0$ elsewhere. Show that its eigenvalues are
$-2\cos\tfrac{k\pi}{N + 1}$, $k = 1, \dots, N$, that every $\lambda \in [-2, 2]$ is within $2\pi/(N + 1)$ of one of them, and that the
eigenvectors, padded with zeros to elements of $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$, satisfy $\|(H - \lambda_k)v\| \leq 2\|v\|/\sqrt{N + 1}$ for the
operator $H$ of @exm-sp-tight-binding-band.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathbf H_N = \mathbf T_N - 2\mathbf I$ with $\mathbf T_N$ of @exr-ev-tridiagonal-n, so its eigenvalues are $2 - 2\cos\theta_k - 2 =
-2\cos\theta_k$, $\theta_k = k\pi/(N + 1)$, with eigenvectors $v_j = \sin j\theta_k$. Write $\lambda = -2\cos\theta$ with $\theta \in
[0, \pi]$. The points $0, \theta_1, \dots, \theta_N, \pi$ cut $[0, \pi]$ into intervals of length $\pi/(N + 1)$, and the
nearest $\theta_k$ to $\theta$ satisfies $|\theta - \theta_k| \leq \pi/(N + 1)$ (near the ends the nearest grid point may be $0$ or
$\pi$, but then $\theta_1$ or $\theta_N$ is within one spacing). Since $|\cos\theta - \cos\theta_k| \leq |\theta - \theta_k|$, $|\lambda -
\lambda_k| \leq 2\pi/(N + 1)$. Padded with zeros at sites $j \leq 0$ and $j \geq N + 1$, $v$ satisfies $(Hv)_j =
\lambda_kv_j$ for $1 \leq j \leq N$ (the eigenvector equation, using $v_0 = v_{N+1} = 0$), and the only other non-zero entries are $(Hv)_0
= -v_1$ and $(Hv)_{N+1} = -v_N$. So $\|(H - \lambda_k)v\|^2 = v_1^2 + v_N^2 = 2\sin^2\theta_k \leq 2$, while $\|v\|^2 = \sum_{j=1}^N\sin^2
j\theta_k = (N + 1)/2$. Hence $\|(H - \lambda_k)v\| \leq \sqrt2 = 2\|v\|/\sqrt{N + 1}$.

## SageMath

The code computes the largest gap between consecutive eigenvalues of $\mathbf H_N$ and the relative defect of the padded
eigenvector for $k = 1$.

```{.python .sage}
for N in [10, 40, 160]:
    ev = sorted(-2 * cos(k * pi / (N + 1)).n() for k in range(1, N + 1))
    gaps = [ev[0] + 2] + [ev[j + 1] - ev[j] for j in range(N - 1)] + [2 - ev[-1]]
    th = pi.n() / (N + 1)
    v = [sin(j * th) for j in range(1, N + 1)]
    defect = sqrt(v[0] ** 2 + v[-1] ** 2) / sqrt(sum(c ** 2 for c in v))
    print("N = %3d : largest gap = %.5f <= 2 pi/(N+1) = %.5f ; relative defect = %.5f <= 2/sqrt(N+1) = %.5f" % (N, max(gaps), 2 * pi.n() / (N + 1), defect, 2 / sqrt(N + 1.)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
N =  10 : largest gap = 0.56926 <= 2 pi/(N+1) = 0.57120 ; relative defect = 0.16989 <= 2/sqrt(N+1) = 0.60302
N =  40 : largest gap = 0.15321 <= 2 pi/(N+1) = 0.15325 ; relative defect = 0.02391 <= 2/sqrt(N+1) = 0.31235
N = 160 : largest gap = 0.03903 <= 2 pi/(N+1) = 0.03903 ; relative defect = 0.00308 <= 2/sqrt(N+1) = 0.15762
```
