closures, which gives the statements on closedness and closures; symmetry is $\langle VAu, Vv\rangle = \langle Au, v\rangle$, and
self-adjointness follows from the formula for the adjoint. Finally $VAV^{-1} - z = V(A - z)V^{-1}$, with inverse $VR_z(A)V^{-1}$ of the
same norm, and $Au = \lambda u$ if and only if $VAV^{-1}(Vu) = \lambda Vu$. $\square$

The definitions and parts (1)-(3) follow @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Secs. VIII.1-VIII.2, pp. 249-256] and @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 7.3, Lemmas
7.2-7.4 and Remark 7.2]; part (5) is @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Thm. VIII.2] and @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 7.2]. @hall2013quantum [Defs.
9.1, 9.2 and 9.5, pp. 170-172] gives the same notions for physicists, and @gasinski2014exercises [Defs. 5.115 and 5.117] states them
in the language of problem books.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest unbounded operator multiplies the $n$-th coordinate of a sequence by $n$. The first example puts it on the finite
sequences and computes its adjoint, which acts by the same rule on a much larger domain.

::: {#exm-unb-diagonal-domain}
#### A diagonal operator on $\ell^2$

On $\ell^2$ let $D(A) = c_{00}$, the finitely supported sequences, and $(Aa)_n = na_n$. The domain is dense, $A$ is symmetric since
$\langle Aa, b\rangle = \sum_nna_n^*b_n = \langle a, Ab\rangle$, and it is unbounded since $\|A\delta^{(n)}\| = n$. For $v \in \ell^2$,
$\langle v, Aa\rangle = \sum_nnv_n^*a_n$; if $w = (nv_n)$ is in $\ell^2$, this is $\langle w, a\rangle$, bounded by $\|w\|\,\|a\|$. If $w
\notin \ell^2$, the vectors $a^{(N)} = (nv_n)_{n \leq N}$ give $\langle v, Aa^{(N)}\rangle = \sum_{n \leq N}n^2|v_n|^2 = \|a^{(N)}\|^2$,
and $\|a^{(N)}\| \to \infty$, so the functional is unbounded. Hence $D(A^\dagger) = \{v : \sum_nn^2|v_n|^2 < \infty\}$ and $(A^\dagger
v)_n = nv_n$: $A \subset A^\dagger$ with a strictly larger domain, which contains $(1/n)$, for instance.
:::

Differentiation on the line is the first operator from analysis. The second example puts the momentum operator on the Schwartz space
and checks the two defining properties of a symmetric unbounded operator.

::: {#exm-ub-derivative-domain}
#### $-i\,d/dx$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$

The Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb{R})$ of @def-fourier-transform is dense in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, since it contains the Hermite
functions, whose span is dense (@thm-hermite-basis). The momentum $pf = -if'$ maps $\mathcal S$ into itself (@def-test-function (2)).
It is symmetric: for $f, g \in \mathcal S$, integrating by parts on $[-R, R]$,
$$
\int_{-R}^R(-if')^*g\,dx = \bigl[if^*g\bigr]_{-R}^R + \int_{-R}^Rf^*(-ig')\,dx ,
$$
and the boundary term tends to $0$ as $R \to \infty$, so $\langle pf, g\rangle = \langle f, pg\rangle$ by @def-l2-space (3). It is
unbounded: for $f_a = e^{-ax^2}$, $\|pf_a\|^2/\|f_a\|^2 = a$ (@exr-bo-differentiation-unbounded). By part (4), no extension of $p$ that
stays symmetric can be defined on all of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.
:::

Multiplication by $x$ on the line is unbounded because the line is infinite. The third example shows this, and shows that a
square-integrable function which decays too slowly lies outside the domain of the adjoint.

::: {#exm-ub-multiplication-domain}
#### The position operator on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$

Let $(xf)(x) = xf(x)$ on $D = \mathcal S(\mathbb{R})$; it maps $\mathcal S$ to itself and is symmetric, since $\int(xf)^*g = \int
f^*(xg)$. The shifted Gaussians $f_c(x) = e^{-(x - c)^2/2}$ have $\|xf_c\|^2 = (c^2 + \tfrac12)\|f_c\|^2$, so $x$ is unbounded.
The function $v = 1/(1 + |x|)$ defines an element of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ (@def-l2-space (3)), but $v \notin D(x^\dagger)$. Take $s
\geq 1$ and the wide Gaussian $u_s(x) = e^{-(x - 2s)^2/2s^2} \in \mathcal S$, with $\|u_s\| = \pi^{1/4}s^{1/2}$. On $[s, 3s]$, $u_s \geq
e^{-1/2}$ and $x/(1 + |x|) \geq \tfrac12$, so that part of $\langle v, xu_s\rangle = \int\frac{x}{1 + |x|}u_s\,dx$ is at least $e^{-1/2}s
> 0.6s$; the part over $x < 0$ is at least $-\int_{-\infty}^0u_s = -s\int_{-\infty}^{-2}e^{-t^2/2}dt > -0.06s$, and the rest is positive.
So $\langle v, xu_s\rangle/\|u_s\| > 0.4\,s^{1/2} \to \infty$: the functional $u \mapsto \langle v, xu\rangle$ is unbounded, and
"$xv$ is not square-integrable" becomes the statement $v \notin D(x^\dagger)$.
:::

On the circle the second derivative becomes a diagonal operator in the trigonometric basis. The fourth example transports the
first example to it with part (6), which is the pattern for every Laplacian on a closed space.

::: {#exm-ub-laplacian-domain}
#### $-d^2/dx^2$ on the circle

On $L^2[-\pi, \pi]$ let $A = -d^2/dx^2$ on the trigonometric polynomials $\sum_{|n| \leq N}c_ne^{inx}$, a dense subspace
(@thm-trigonometric-basis). With $V : F \mapsto (\langle e_n, F\rangle)_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$, the inner-product preserving bijection onto
$\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ of @thm-trigonometric-basis (2), $VAV^{-1}$ multiplies the finitely supported sequences by $n^2$, since $-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}
e^{inx} = n^2e^{inx}$. The computation of @exm-unb-diagonal-domain, with $n^2$ for $n$ and $\mathbb{Z}$ for $\{1, 2, \dots\}$, and part (6)
give $D(A^\dagger) = \{F : \sum_nn^4|\langle e_n, F\rangle|^2 < \infty\}$ and $A^\dagger F = \sum_nn^2\langle e_n, F\rangle e_n$. The
domain of the adjoint is a decay condition on the Fourier coefficients.
:::

Closing an operator adds to its domain the limits of sequences along which the operator also converges. The fifth example shows that
for the derivative on an interval these limits are continuous functions given by integrals, and the figure shows one of them, a
function with a corner.

![Smooth functions $u_n$ vanishing at $0$ and $1$ (thin) converging to the tent $u(x) = \min(x, 1 - x)$ (thick), with derivatives
converging in mean square. The tent is in the domain of the closure of $-i\,d/dx$ although it is not differentiable at
$\tfrac12$.](figures/unb-graph-closure.svg){#fig-unb-graph-closure width=70%}

::: {#exm-unb-closure-derivative}
#### The closure of the derivative on an interval

Let $T_0 = -i\,d/dx$ on $D(T_0) = \{u \in C^1[0, 1] : u(0) = u(1) = 0\}$, dense in $L^2[0, 1]$ because it contains the functions $\chi P$
of the density argument in the proof of @thm-fred-sturm-liouville-completeness (3). It is symmetric, by integration by parts with
vanishing boundary terms, hence closable (part (3)). For $\chi \in L^2[0, 1]$ and $x \in [0, 1]$ put $(J\chi)(x) = \langle\mathbf
1_{[0, x]}, \chi\rangle$, the integral of $\chi$ over $[0, x]$, where $\mathbf 1_{[0, x]}$ is the indicator function; by the
Cauchy-Schwarz inequality $|(J\chi)(x) - (J\chi)(y)| \leq |x - y|^{1/2}\|\chi\|$, so $J\chi$ is continuous, and $\sup|J\chi| \leq \|\chi\|$.
If $u_n \in D(T_0)$, $u_n \to u$ and $T_0u_n \to \chi$, then $u_n = J(u_n') = iJ(T_0u_n)$ converges uniformly to $iJ\chi$, so the
element $u$ is the continuous function $iJ\chi$, with $u(0) = 0$ and $u(1) = i\langle 1, \chi\rangle = \lim u_n(1) = 0$. The tent of
@fig-unb-graph-closure is such a limit, with $\chi = -i$ on $(0, \tfrac12)$ and $i$ on $(\tfrac12, 1)$.
:::

A closed operator need not be self-adjoint even when its adjoint is symmetric, but when the closure equals the adjoint everything
fits. The sixth example shows this for the diagonal operator, the simplest essentially self-adjoint operator.

::: {#exm-unb-diagonal-essential}
#### The closure of the diagonal operator

For $A$ of @exm-unb-diagonal-domain, $\overline A \subset A^\dagger$ by part (3). Conversely let $v \in D(A^\dagger)$ and let $v^{(N)}$ be
its truncation to the first $N$ entries. Then $v^{(N)} \to v$ and $Av^{(N)} \to (nv_n) = A^\dagger v$ in $\ell^2$, because
$\sum_{n > N}(1 + n^2)|v_n|^2 \to 0$; so $v \in D(\overline A)$ and $\overline A = A^\dagger$. By part (3), $(\overline A)^\dagger =
A^\dagger = \overline A$: the closure is self-adjoint, and $A$ is essentially self-adjoint. The closure acts by $n$ on the domain
$\{\sum n^2|a_n|^2 < \infty\}$.
:::

The quantum harmonic oscillator is diagonal in the Hermite basis, and its number operator is the physical form of the diagonal
operator. The seventh example transports @exm-unb-diagonal-essential to $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.

::: {#exm-unb-number-operator}
#### The number operator of the oscillator

Let $N$ act on the span of the Hermite functions $h_n$ by $Nh_n = nh_n$. The map $V : F \mapsto (\langle h_n, F\rangle)_{n \geq 0}$ preserves
inner products and maps $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ onto $\ell^2$ (@thm-hermite-basis, @def-orthonormal-basis (3)), and carries $N$ to the operator
$a \mapsto (na_n)$ on $c_{00}$, indexed from $0$. By part (6) and @exm-unb-diagonal-essential, $N$ is essentially self-adjoint, and
$\overline N$ acts by $\overline NF = \sum_nn\langle h_n, F\rangle h_n$ on $\{F : \sum_nn^2|\langle h_n, F\rangle|^2 < \infty\}$. The
energy of the oscillator in units $\hbar\omega = 1$ is $\overline N + \tfrac12$.
:::

Angular momentum about an axis acts on functions of the azimuthal angle. The eighth example is the operator $L_z = -i\,d/d\varphi$ on
the circle, with the trigonometric basis as eigenvectors.

::: {#exm-unb-angular-momentum}
#### Angular momentum about an axis

On $L^2[-\pi, \pi]$, the space of states of a particle on a ring with angle $\varphi$, let $L_z = -i\,d/d\varphi$ on the trigonometric
polynomials. Then $L_ze^{im\varphi} = me^{im\varphi}$ for every $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, so $L_z$ is unbounded, and under the map $V$ of
@exm-ub-laplacian-domain it becomes the operator $a \mapsto (ma_m)$ on finitely supported sequences in $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$. The argument
of @exm-unb-diagonal-essential, with $|m|$ for $n$, shows that $L_z$ is essentially self-adjoint, with closure acting by $m$ on $\{F :
\sum_mm^2|\langle e_m, F\rangle|^2 < \infty\}$ and eigenvalues the integers: angular momentum about the axis is quantised in units of
$\hbar$.
:::

The adjoint of a densely defined operator can fail to be densely defined, and then the operator has no closure. The ninth example is
an evaluation functional turned into an operator.

::: {#exm-unb-not-closable}
#### An operator that is not closable

On $L^2[0, 1]$ let $D(A) = C[0, 1]$ and $Af = f(0)\,\mathbf 1$, with $\mathbf 1$ the constant function. Let $t_n$ be the tent with
$t_n(0) = 1$, decreasing linearly to $0$ at $1/n$ and $0$ beyond; then $\|t_n\| = (3n)^{-1/2} \to 0$ while $At_n = \mathbf 1$. By
@def-closed-operator (4), $A$ is not closable. For $v \in L^2[0, 1]$, $\langle v, At_n\rangle = \langle v, \mathbf 1\rangle$ with
$\|t_n\| \to 0$, so $v \in D(A^\dagger)$ forces $\langle v, \mathbf 1\rangle = 0$; conversely such $v$ give $\langle v, Af\rangle = 0$. So
$D(A^\dagger) = \{\mathbf 1\}^\perp$, which is closed and not dense, and $A^\dagger = 0$ on it.
:::

The spectrum of an unbounded operator need not be bounded, and without boundary conditions it can be everything. The last example
shows this for the derivative on $C^1[0, 1]$.

::: {#exm-unb-spectrum-plane}
#### Every number an eigenvalue

Let $A = -i\,d/dx$ on $D(A) = C^1[0, 1]$, dense in $L^2[0, 1]$ by @thm-stone-weierstrass (1). For every $z \in \mathbb{C}$, $e_z(x) = e^{izx}$
lies in $D(A)$ with $Ae_z = ze_z$, so every $z$ is an eigenvalue and $\sigma(A) = \mathbb{C}$. The operator is not symmetric: for $u = 1$
and $v = x$, $\langle Au, v\rangle = 0$ while $\langle u, Av\rangle = \int_0^1(-i)\,dx = -i$. Boundary conditions remove the eigenvalues:
on the subspace $u(0) = u(1) = 0$ of @exm-unb-closure-derivative, $e_z$ is excluded.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Dirichlet second derivative is the first operator of the section in which symmetry and unboundedness can be checked by hand. The
first exercise asks for both on explicit functions.

::: {#exr-unb-dirichlet-unbounded}
#### Symmetric and unbounded

Let $A = -d^2/dx^2$ on $D(A) = \{u \in C^2[0, \pi] : u(0) = u(\pi) = 0\}$ in $L^2[0, \pi]$. Show that $A$ is symmetric and that
$\langle u, Au\rangle = \|u'\|^2 \geq 0$, compute $\|A s_n\|/\|s_n\|$ for $s_n = \sin nx$, and conclude that $A$ is unbounded.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$D(A)$ is dense, since it contains the functions $\chi P$ of the proof of @thm-fred-sturm-liouville-completeness (3). For $u, v \in D(A)$,
two integrations by parts give $\int_0^\pi(-u'')^*v = [-u'^*v]_0^\pi + \int_0^\pi u'^*v' = [-u'^*v + u^*v']_0^\pi + \int_0^\pi u^*(-v'')$, and
the boundary terms vanish because $u$ and $v$ vanish at both ends; so $\langle Au, v\rangle = \langle u, Av\rangle$. The middle expression
with $v = u$ gives $\langle u, Au\rangle = \int|u'|^2 = \|u'\|^2$. For $s_n$, $As_n = n^2s_n$, so $\|As_n\|/\|s_n\| = n^2 \to \infty$, and no
constant $C$ bounds $\|Au\| \leq C\|u\|$.

## SageMath

The code checks symmetry on a pair of functions and the ratios for $n = 1, \dots, 5$.

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x")
u = x * (pi - x); v = sin(x) ** 2 * x
A = lambda f: -diff(f, x, 2)
lhs = integrate(A(u) * v, x, 0, pi); rhs = integrate(u * A(v), x, 0, pi)
print("<Au, v> =", lhs.simplify_full(), "; <u, Av> =", rhs.simplify_full())
print("<u, Au> =", integrate(u * A(u), x, 0, pi), "; ||u'||^2 =", integrate(diff(u, x) ** 2, x, 0, pi))
print("||A s_n|| / ||s_n|| for n = 1..5:", [sqrt(integrate(A(sin(n * x)) ** 2, x, 0, pi) / integrate(sin(n * x) ** 2, x, 0, pi)) for n in range(1, 6)])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
<Au, v> = 1/2*pi^2 ; <u, Av> = 1/2*pi^2
<u, Au> = 1/3*pi^3 ; ||u'||^2 = 1/3*pi^3
||A s_n|| / ||s_n|| for n = 1..5: [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
```
::::
:::

A symmetric operator always sits inside its adjoint, and an everywhere-defined symmetric operator is automatically bounded, which is
why unbounded symmetric operators have restricted domains. The second exercise asks for both, and for an example where the adjoint is
strictly larger.

::: {#exr-ub-closed-graph}
#### Symmetric operators and their adjoints

Show that for a symmetric operator $D(A) \subseteq D(A^\dagger)$ with $A^\dagger = A$ on $D(A)$, and that a symmetric operator defined on
all of $\mathcal H$ is bounded and self-adjoint. For $A = -i\,d/dx$ on the trigonometric polynomials in $L^2[-\pi, \pi]$, show that the
triangle wave $v(x) = |x|$ lies in $D(A^\dagger)$ but not in $D(A)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For $v \in D(A)$, $u \mapsto \langle v, Au\rangle = \langle Av, u\rangle$ is bounded by $\|Av\|\,\|u\|$, so $v \in D(A^\dagger)$, and
$A^\dagger v = Av$ by the uniqueness in part (1). If $D(A) = \mathcal H$, $A$ is bounded by @thm-sesquilinear-forms (5), and then it is
self-adjoint by @def-self-adjoint-operator (5); its adjoint in the sense of this section is the bounded adjoint by part (4). For the
example, $Ae_n = ne_n$, so as in @exm-ub-laplacian-domain, $D(A^\dagger) = \{F : \sum n^2|\langle e_n, F\rangle|^2 < \infty\}$. The
coefficients of $|x|$ are $\langle e_n, |x|\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\pi}^\pi|x|e^{-inx}dx = \frac{2((-1)^n - 1)}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,n^2}$
for $n \neq 0$, so $\sum n^2|\langle e_n, v\rangle|^2 = \frac8\pi\sum_{n \text{ odd}}n^{-2} = 2\pi < \infty$ and $v \in D(A^\dagger)$. It is
not a trigonometric polynomial, since infinitely many coefficients (all odd $n$) are non-zero, so $v \notin D(A)$.

## SageMath

Check on the triangle wave: the code computes its coefficients and the partial sums of $\sum n^2|\langle e_n, v\rangle|^2$.

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x"); n = var("n", domain="integer")
c = lambda k: integrate(abs(x) * exp(-I * k * x), x, -pi, pi) / sqrt(2 * pi)
print("<e_n, |x|> for n = 1..4:", [c(k).simplify_full() for k in range(1, 5)])
S = lambda N: sum(k ** 2 * abs(c(k)) ** 2 for k in range(1, N + 1)) * 2
print("partial sums of sum n^2 |<e_n, v>|^2 for N = 5, 10, 20:", [round(S(N).n(), 6) for N in [5, 10, 20]], "; limit 2 (8/pi)(pi^2/8) = 2 pi =", round((2 * pi).n(), 6))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
<e_n, |x|> for n = 1..4: [-2*sqrt(2)/sqrt(pi), 0, -2/9*sqrt(2)/sqrt(pi), 0]
partial sums of sum n^2 |<e_n, v>|^2 for N = 5, 10, 20: [5.862561, 6.029375, 6.155967] ; limit 2 (8/pi)(pi^2/8) = 2 pi = 6.283185
```
::::
:::

In the Fourier picture the domain of the adjoint is a decay condition on the coefficients, decided by a series. The third exercise asks
for the relevant partial sums for two functions on the circle, one with a jump and one with a kink.

::: {#exr-ub-unbounded-norm}
#### Domains in the Fourier picture

For $f(x) = x$ and $g(x) = \pi^2 - x^2$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$, compute the partial sums of $\sum_nn^2|\langle e_n, f\rangle|^2$,
$\sum_nn^2|\langle e_n, g\rangle|^2$ and $\sum_nn^4|\langle e_n, g\rangle|^2$ for $N = 10, 100, 1000$, and decide which of $f, g$ lie in the
domains of the adjoints of $-i\,d/dx$ and of $-d^2/dx^2$ on the trigonometric polynomials.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Integrating by parts, $\langle e_n, f\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\pi}^\pi xe^{-inx}dx = \frac{2\pi i(-1)^n}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,n}$, so
$|\langle e_n, f\rangle|^2 = 2\pi/n^2$ for $n \neq 0$, and $\sum n^2|\langle e_n, f\rangle|^2 = \sum_{n \neq 0}2\pi$ diverges: by
@exr-ub-closed-graph and @exm-ub-laplacian-domain, $f$ is not in the domain of either adjoint. Twice integrating by parts, $|\langle e_n,
g\rangle|^2 = 8\pi/n^4$; then $\sum_{n \neq 0}n^2\cdot8\pi/n^4 = 16\pi\cdot\pi^2/6 = 8\pi^3/3$ converges and $\sum n^4\cdot8\pi/n^4$ diverges. So
$g$ lies in the domain of the adjoint of $-i\,d/dx$ but not in that of the adjoint of $-d^2/dx^2$. The periodic extension of $f$ jumps at
$\pm\pi$, that of $g$ is continuous with a corner there.

## SageMath

The code computes the first coefficients exactly and the three partial sums from the closed forms.

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x")
c = lambda f, n: (integrate(f * exp(-I * n * x), x, -pi, pi) / sqrt(2 * pi)).simplify_full()
f, g = x, pi ** 2 - x ** 2
print("|<e_n, x>|^2, n = 1..3:", [(abs(c(f, n)) ** 2).simplify_full() for n in [1, 2, 3]], "; |<e_n, pi^2 - x^2>|^2:", [(abs(c(g, n)) ** 2).simplify_full() for n in [1, 2, 3]])
for N in [10, 100, 1000]:
    s1 = sum(2 * n ** 2 * 2 * pi / n ** 2 for n in range(1, N + 1)); s2 = sum(2 * n ** 2 * 8 * pi / n ** 4 for n in range(1, N + 1)); s3 = sum(2 * n ** 4 * 8 * pi / n ** 4 for n in range(1, N + 1))
    print("N = %4d: %10.3f  %10.4f  %10.1f" % (N, s1.n(), s2.n(), s3.n()))
k = var("k", domain="integer")
print("limit of the middle series:", 2 * sum(k ** 2 * 8 * pi / k ** 4, k, 1, oo))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
|<e_n, x>|^2, n = 1..3: [2*pi, 1/2*pi, 2/9*pi] ; |<e_n, pi^2 - x^2>|^2: [8*pi, 1/2*pi, 8/81*pi]
N =   10:    125.664     77.8998       502.7
N =  100:   1256.637     82.1833      5026.5
N = 1000:  12566.371     82.6332     50265.5
limit of the middle series: 8/3*pi^3
```
::::
:::

A diagonal operator with real entries on its largest possible domain is the prototype of a self-adjoint operator, and the proof is a
direct computation of the adjoint's domain. The fourth exercise asks for it, the simplest instance of showing $D(A^\dagger) = D(A)$.

::: {#exr-ub-symmetric-adjoint}
#### Self-adjointness of a multiplication operator

Let $(\lambda_n)$ be a real sequence and let $M$ act on $\ell^2$ by $(Ma)_n = \lambda_na_n$ on $D(M) = \{a : \sum\lambda_n^2|a_n|^2 <
\infty\}$. Show that $M$ is densely defined, symmetric and self-adjoint, and that it is bounded if and only if $(\lambda_n)$ is bounded.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$D(M) \supseteq c_{00}$ is dense, and $M$ maps it into $\ell^2$ by definition. Symmetry: $\langle Ma, b\rangle = \sum\lambda_na_n^*b_n =
\langle a, Mb\rangle$, the series converging absolutely by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. So $M \subset M^\dagger$ (part (3)). Let $v
\in D(M^\dagger)$ with $w = M^\dagger v$. Testing with $a = \delta^{(n)} \in D(M)$ gives $\lambda_nv_n^* = \langle v, M\delta^{(n)}\rangle =
\langle w, \delta^{(n)}\rangle = w_n^*$, so $w_n = \lambda_nv_n$, and $\sum\lambda_n^2|v_n|^2 = \|w\|^2 < \infty$: $v \in D(M)$. Hence $D(M^\dagger) = D(M)$ and $M^\dagger
= M$. If $|\lambda_n| \leq C$, then $\|Ma\| \leq C\|a\|$; if not, $\|M\delta^{(n)}\| = |\lambda_n|$ is unbounded on unit vectors.

## SageMath

Check on $\lambda_n = (-1)^nn$ and truncations: the code compares $\langle Ma, b\rangle$ with $\langle a, Mb\rangle$ for random finite
sequences with Gaussian-integer entries.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(1)
N = 8
lam = vector(QQ, [(-1) ** n * n for n in range(1, N + 1)])
M = diagonal_matrix(lam)
a = vector(QQ[I], [ZZ.random_element(-5, 5) + I * ZZ.random_element(-5, 5) for _ in range(N)])
b = vector(QQ[I], [ZZ.random_element(-5, 5) + I * ZZ.random_element(-5, 5) for _ in range(N)])
ip = lambda u, v: sum(conjugate(s) * t for s, t in zip(u, v))
print("<Ma, b> =", ip(M * a, b), "; <a, Mb> =", ip(a, M * b), "; equal:", ip(M * a, b) == ip(a, M * b))
print("||M delta^(n)|| for n = 1..8:", [abs(l) for l in lam])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
<Ma, b> = -157*I - 101 ; <a, Mb> = -157*I - 101 ; equal: True
||M delta^(n)|| for n = 1..8: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
```
::::
:::

An evaluation at a point is not continuous in mean square, and an operator built from it is not closable. The fifth exercise asks for a
variant of @exm-unb-not-closable with the point in the middle and a general target vector.

::: {#exr-unb-not-closable}
#### Evaluation at the midpoint

Fix $g \neq 0$ in $L^2[0, 1]$ and let $Af = f(\tfrac12)\,g$ on $D(A) = C[0, 1]$. Show that $A$ is not closable, compute $D(A^\dagger)$ and
$A^\dagger$, and explain why the answer does not depend on $g$ beyond the condition $v \perp g$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $t_n$ be the tent with $t_n(\tfrac12) = 1$ vanishing outside $(\tfrac12 - \tfrac1n, \tfrac12 + \tfrac1n)$. Then $\|t_n\|^2 = \tfrac{2}{3n}
\to 0$ and $At_n = g \neq 0$, so by @def-closed-operator (4), $A$ is not closable. For $v \in L^2[0, 1]$, $\langle v, Af\rangle =
f(\tfrac12)\langle v, g\rangle$. If $\langle v, g\rangle \neq 0$, the tents give $|\langle v, At_n\rangle| = |\langle v, g\rangle|$ with
$\|t_n\| \to 0$, so the functional is unbounded. If $\langle v, g\rangle = 0$, it is identically $0$. So $D(A^\dagger) = \{g\}^\perp$, a
closed hyperplane which is not dense (@thm-projection (3)), and $A^\dagger = 0$ there; only the line through $g$ matters.

## SageMath

Check on $g = x$: the code computes $\|t_n\|$ and $\langle v, At_n\rangle$ for $v = 1$ and $v = 1 - \tfrac32x$, which is orthogonal to $g$.

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x")
def tent(n):
    return (1 - n * abs(x - 1/2))
g = x
for n in [4, 16, 64]:
    t = tent(n)
    nt = sqrt(2 * integrate(t.subs(x=x) ** 2, x, 1/2, 1/2 + 1/n))
    print("n = %2d: ||t_n|| = %.5f, <1, A t_n> = %s, <1 - 3x/2, A t_n> = %s" % (n, nt.n(), integrate(g, x, 0, 1), integrate((1 - 3 * x / 2) * g, x, 0, 1)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
n =  4: ||t_n|| = 0.40825, <1, A t_n> = 1/2, <1 - 3x/2, A t_n> = 0
n = 16: ||t_n|| = 0.20412, <1, A t_n> = 1/2, <1 - 3x/2, A t_n> = 0
n = 64: ||t_n|| = 0.10206, <1, A t_n> = 1/2, <1 - 3x/2, A t_n> = 0
```
::::
:::

The resolvent set is open because of the Neumann series of part (5), and for a diagonal operator the disc it guarantees can be compared
with the exact distance to the spectrum. The sixth exercise asks for this comparison.

::: {#exr-unb-resolvent-disc}
#### The disc of part (5)

Let $M$ be the operator of @exr-ub-symmetric-adjoint with $\lambda_n = n$, $n \geq 1$. Show that every $z \notin \{1, 2, \dots\}$ lies in
$\rho(M)$, with $R_z(M)$ the diagonal operator with entries $1/(n - z)$ and $\|R_z(M)\| = 1/\operatorname{dist}(z, \{1, 2, \dots\})$, and
that the disc of part (5) around $z$ is exactly the largest disc about $z$ in $\rho(M)$. Compute both for $z = \tfrac52 + i$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $d = \operatorname{dist}(z, \{1, 2, \dots\}) > 0$ and $(Ra)_n = a_n/(n - z)$. Then $\|Ra\| \leq \|a\|/d$, and $Ra \in D(M)$ because
$|n/(n - z)| \leq 1 + |z|/d$ is bounded; $(M - z)Ra = a$ for all $a$ and $R(M - z)a = a$ for $a \in D(M)$. So $z \in \rho(M)$ and $R_z(M) =
R$. Taking $a = \delta^{(n)}$ with $|n - z| = d$ gives $\|R\| = 1/d$. Part (5) gives the disc $|w - z| < 1/\|R_z\| = d$, whose boundary
contains the nearest eigenvalue $n$; a larger disc would contain $n \in \sigma(M)$. For $z = \tfrac52 + i$, $d = |\tfrac12 + i| =
\sqrt5/2$, so $\|R_z\| = 2/\sqrt5$.

## SageMath

The code computes $\max_n 1/|n - z|$ over $n \leq 100$ and the distance.

```{.python .sage}
z = 5/2 + I
vals = [1 / abs(n - z) for n in range(1, 101)]
print("max_n 1/|n - z| =", max(vals), "=", max(vals).n(digits=8), "; 2/sqrt(5) =", (2 / sqrt(5)).n(digits=8))
print("radius of the disc 1/||R_z|| =", 1 / max(vals))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
max_n 1/|n - z| = 2/5*sqrt(5) = 0.89442719 ; 2/sqrt(5) = 0.89442719
radius of the disc 1/||R_z|| = 1/2*sqrt(5)
```
::::
:::

Scalar multiples and bounded perturbations behave as expected under the adjoint, but sums of two unbounded operators do not in general.
The seventh exercise asks for the rules that do hold.

::: {#exr-unb-adjoint-rules}
#### Adjoints of sums and multiples

Let $A$ be an operator on $\mathcal H$, $\alpha \neq 0$ a number and $B \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$. Show that $(\alpha A)^\dagger =
\alpha^*A^\dagger$ and $(A + B)^\dagger = A^\dagger + B^\dagger$ with $D((A + B)^\dagger) = D(A^\dagger)$. Deduce that if $A$ is
self-adjoint and $B$ is bounded and self-adjoint, then $A + B$ is self-adjoint on $D(A)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$u \mapsto \langle v, \alpha Au\rangle = \alpha\langle v, Au\rangle$ is bounded exactly when $u \mapsto \langle v, Au\rangle$ is, and then it
equals $\langle\alpha^*A^\dagger v, u\rangle$. For $A + B$ on $D(A)$, $\langle v, (A + B)u\rangle = \langle v, Au\rangle + \langle B^\dagger
v, u\rangle$, and the second term is always bounded in $u$; so the sum is bounded in $u$ exactly when $\langle v, Au\rangle$ is, and then
it equals $\langle A^\dagger v + B^\dagger v, u\rangle$. If $A = A^\dagger$ and $B = B^\dagger$, then $(A + B)^\dagger = A + B$ on $D(A)$:
$A + B$ is self-adjoint.

## SageMath

Check on a finite truncation: for $4 \times 4$ matrices $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$, the code verifies $(\alpha\mathbf A + \mathbf
B)^\dagger = \alpha^*\mathbf A^\dagger + \mathbf B^\dagger$.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(2)
K = QQ[I]
A = random_matrix(K, 4, 4); B = random_matrix(K, 4, 4); al = 2 - 3 * I
lhs = (al * A + B).conjugate_transpose(); rhs = conjugate(al) * A.conjugate_transpose() + B.conjugate_transpose()
print("(alpha A + B)^dagger = alpha^* A^dagger + B^dagger:", lhs == rhs)
H = diagonal_matrix(K, [1, 2, 3, 4]); S = matrix(K, [[0, 1, 0, 0], [1, 0, I, 0], [0, -I, 0, 1], [0, 0, 1, 0]])
print("H + S is self-adjoint:", (H + S).conjugate_transpose() == H + S)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
(alpha A + B)^dagger = alpha^* A^dagger + B^dagger: True
H + S is self-adjoint: True
```
::::
:::

The closure of the derivative of @exm-unb-closure-derivative was described by the integrals $J\chi$. The eighth exercise asks for the
converse, which identifies the domain of the closure completely.

::: {#exr-unb-closure-derivative}
#### The domain of the closure

With $T_0$ and $J$ as in @exm-unb-closure-derivative, show that $D(\overline{T_0})$ is the set of continuous functions $u = iJ\chi$ with
$\chi \in L^2[0, 1]$ and $\langle 1, \chi\rangle = 0$, and that $\overline{T_0}u = \chi$. Check the description on the tent of
@fig-unb-graph-closure.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

@exm-unb-closure-derivative showed that every $u \in D(\overline{T_0})$ is $iJ\chi$ with $\chi = \overline{T_0}u$ and $\langle 1, \chi\rangle
= -iu(1) = 0$. Conversely let $\chi \in L^2[0, 1]$ with $\langle 1, \chi\rangle = 0$. The orthogonal projection $P$ onto $\{1\}^\perp$ maps a
continuous $c$ to the continuous $c - \langle 1, c\rangle$. Choose continuous $c_n \to \chi$ (@def-lp-space (2)); then $Pc_n \to P\chi =
\chi$, and $u_n = iJ(Pc_n)$ is $C^1$ with $u_n' = iPc_n$, $u_n(0) = 0$ and $u_n(1) = i\langle 1, Pc_n\rangle = 0$. So $u_n \in D(T_0)$,
$T_0u_n = Pc_n \to \chi$, and $u_n \to iJ\chi$ uniformly, hence in $L^2$. By the definition of the closure, $iJ\chi \in D(\overline{T_0})$
with $\overline{T_0}(iJ\chi) = \chi$. For the tent, $\chi = -i$ on $(0, \tfrac12)$, $i$ on $(\tfrac12, 1)$ has $\langle 1, \chi\rangle = 0$
and $iJ\chi(x) = x$ for $x \leq \tfrac12$, $1 - x$ beyond.

## SageMath

Check on the tent: the code integrates $i\chi$ piecewise and compares with $\min(x, 1 - x)$ at several points.

```{.python .sage}
t = var("t")
chi = lambda s: -I if s < 1/2 else I
def u(x):
    return I * (integrate(-I, t, 0, min(x, 1/2)) + (integrate(I, t, 1/2, x) if x > 1/2 else 0))
pts = [0, 1/5, 1/2, 7/10, 1]
print("i J chi at", pts, ":", [u(p) for p in pts])
print("min(x, 1 - x):", [min(p, 1 - p) for p in pts], "; <1, chi> =", integrate(-I, t, 0, 1/2) + integrate(I, t, 1/2, 1))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
i J chi at [0, 1/5, 1/2, 7/10, 1] : [0, 1/5, 1/2, 3/10, 0]
min(x, 1 - x): [0, 1/5, 1/2, 3/10, 0] ; <1, chi> = 0
```
::::
:::

For a closable operator the closure can be recovered from the adjoint, by taking the adjoint once more. The ninth exercise proves this
with orthogonal complements in $\mathcal H \times \mathcal H$ and derives a test for essential self-adjointness.

::: {#exr-unb-double-adjoint}
#### The double adjoint

Give $\mathcal H \times \mathcal H$ the inner product $\langle(u, w), (u', w')\rangle = \langle u, u'\rangle + \langle w, w'\rangle$ and let
$J(u, w) = (-w, u)$. Show that the graph of $A^\dagger$ is $(J\Gamma(A))^\perp$. Deduce that if $A^\dagger$ is densely defined, then $A$
is closable and $\overline A = (A^\dagger)^\dagger$, and that a symmetric $A$ is essentially self-adjoint if and only if $A^\dagger$ is
symmetric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The inner product makes $\mathcal H \times \mathcal H$ a Hilbert space whose norm is equivalent to that of @def-closed-operator, so closures
agree. $(v, y) \perp J\Gamma(A)$ means $-\langle v, Au\rangle + \langle y, u\rangle = 0$ for all $u \in D(A)$, that is $v \in D(A^\dagger)$ and
$y = A^\dagger v$. $J$ is a bijective isometry with $J^2 = -1$, so $J$ maps orthogonal complements to orthogonal complements. Hence $J\Gamma(A^\dagger) =
J\bigl((J\Gamma(A))^\perp\bigr) = (J^2\Gamma(A))^\perp = \Gamma(A)^\perp$, since $J^2\Gamma(A) = -\Gamma(A) = \Gamma(A)$, and
$\Gamma((A^\dagger)^\dagger) = (J\Gamma(A^\dagger))^\perp = (\Gamma(A)^\perp)^\perp = \overline{\Gamma(A)}$ by @thm-projection (3), whenever $A^\dagger$ is densely defined so that its adjoint is
defined. So $\overline{\Gamma(A)}$ is a graph, $A$ is closable, and $\overline A = A^{\dagger\dagger}$. For symmetric $A$, $A^\dagger \supset A$
is densely defined. If $\overline A$ is self-adjoint, $A^\dagger = (\overline A)^\dagger = \overline A$ (part (3)) is symmetric. If
$A^\dagger$ is symmetric, $A^\dagger \subset A^{\dagger\dagger} = \overline A \subset A^\dagger$, so $\overline A = A^\dagger$ and
$(\overline A)^\dagger = A^\dagger = \overline A$.

## SageMath

Check in finite dimensions, where every operator is closed: for a $3 \times 3$ matrix the code verifies that the graph of $\mathbf A^\dagger$
is orthogonal to $J\Gamma(\mathbf A)$ and that the dimensions add up to $6$.

```{.python .sage}
K = QQ[I]
A = matrix(K, [[1, 2 * I, 0], [0, 3, 1 - I], [I, 0, 2]])
G = matrix(K, [list(e) + list(A * e) for e in identity_matrix(K, 3).columns()])
JG = matrix(K, [list(-r[3:]) + list(r[:3]) for r in G.rows()])
Ad = A.conjugate_transpose()
GA = matrix(K, [list(e) + list(Ad * e) for e in identity_matrix(K, 3).columns()])
print("Gamma(A^dagger) is orthogonal to J Gamma(A):", (GA.conjugate() * JG.transpose()).is_zero())
print("dimensions:", GA.rank(), "+", JG.rank(), "=", GA.rank() + JG.rank())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
Gamma(A^dagger) is orthogonal to J Gamma(A): True
dimensions: 3 + 3 = 6
```
::::
:::

The position operator becomes a tridiagonal infinite matrix in the Hermite basis, and its matrix elements show directly that it is
unbounded. The last exercise combines the recurrences of @def-hermite-polynomial with @thm-hermite-basis.

::: {#exr-unb-hermite-position}
#### Position in the Hermite basis

Using $H_{n+1} = 2xH_n - 2nH_{n-1}$, show that $xh_n = \sqrt{n/2}\,h_{n-1} + \sqrt{(n+1)/2}\,h_{n+1}$, deduce $\|xh_n\|^2 = n + \tfrac12$,
and conclude that multiplication by $x$ on the span of the Hermite functions is symmetric and unbounded.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

With $\psi_n = H_ne^{-x^2/2}$ the recurrence gives $x\psi_n = \tfrac12\psi_{n+1} + n\psi_{n-1}$. Since $h_n = \psi_n/c_n$ with $c_n =
(2^nn!\sqrt\pi)^{1/2}$ and $c_{n+1}/c_n = \sqrt{2(n+1)}$, $xh_n = \frac{c_{n+1}}{2c_n}h_{n+1} + \frac{nc_{n-1}}{c_n}h_{n-1} =
\sqrt{\tfrac{n+1}{2}}h_{n+1} + \sqrt{\tfrac n2}h_{n-1}$. The $h_n$ are orthonormal (@thm-hermite-basis), so $\|xh_n\|^2 = \tfrac n2 +
\tfrac{n+1}2 = n + \tfrac12 \to \infty$ with $\|h_n\| = 1$: $x$ is unbounded on the span. Symmetry is $\int(xf)^*g = \int f^*(xg)$ for
the functions $p(x)e^{-x^2/2}$ of the span.

## SageMath

The code checks the three-term formula and $\|xh_n\|^2$ symbolically for $n \leq 5$.

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x")
h = lambda n: hermite(n, x) * exp(-x ** 2 / 2) / sqrt(2 ** n * factorial(n) * sqrt(pi))
print("x h_n = sqrt(n/2) h_{n-1} + sqrt((n+1)/2) h_{n+1} for n = 1..5:", all(bool(((x * h(n) - sqrt(n / 2) * h(n - 1) - sqrt((n + 1) / 2) * h(n + 1)) * exp(x ** 2 / 2)).expand().canonicalize_radical() == 0) for n in srange(1, 6)))
print("||x h_n||^2 for n = 0..5:", [integrate((x * h(n)) ** 2, x, -oo, oo).simplify_full() for n in range(6)])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
x h_n = sqrt(n/2) h_{n-1} + sqrt((n+1)/2) h_{n+1} for n = 1..5: True
||x h_n||^2 for n = 0..5: [1/2, 3/2, 5/2, 7/2, 9/2, 11/2]
```

:::
::::

### Self-adjointness and the spectrum

A symmetric operator is contained in its adjoint, and it is self-adjoint exactly when the two domains coincide. Computing an adjoint
directly is rarely practical, so one needs criteria that can be checked by solving equations. The theorem below proves the basic
criterion, that $A$ is self-adjoint when $A \pm i$ are onto, its version for essential self-adjointness, and the consequence that the
spectrum of a self-adjoint operator is real. It ends with the two ways in which the rest of the section produces self-adjoint
operators: an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, and a compact resolvent.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-unb-self-adjointness}
#### Criteria for self-adjointness

Let $A$ be a symmetric operator on a Hilbert space $\mathcal H$.

1. (**The basic estimate**) $\langle u, Au\rangle$ is real for $u \in D(A)$, and for $z = a + ib$ with $a, b$ real,
   $\|(A - z)u\|^2 = \|(A - a)u\|^2 + b^2\|u\|^2$. If $A$ is closed and $b \neq 0$, $\operatorname{ran}(A - z)$ is closed.
2. (**Basic criterion**) The following are equivalent: (a) $A$ is self-adjoint; (b) $A$ is closed and $\ker(A^\dagger - i) =
   \ker(A^\dagger + i) = \{0\}$; (c) $\operatorname{ran}(A + i) = \operatorname{ran}(A - i) = \mathcal H$. If $\operatorname{ran}(A -
   \mu) = \mathcal H$ for one real $\mu$, then $A$ is self-adjoint and $\mu \in \rho(A)$.
3. (**Essential self-adjointness**) The following are equivalent: (a) $A$ is essentially self-adjoint; (b) $\ker(A^\dagger \mp i) =
   \{0\}$; (c) $\operatorname{ran}(A \pm i)$ are dense. If for one real $\mu$ there is $c > 0$ with $\|(A - \mu)u\| \geq c\|u\|$ on
   $D(A)$ and $\operatorname{ran}(A - \mu)$ is dense, then $A$ is essentially self-adjoint and $\mu \in \rho(\overline A)$. A
   self-adjoint operator has no symmetric extension other than itself, and an essentially self-adjoint $A$ has exactly one
   self-adjoint extension, $\overline A$.
4. (**Real spectrum**) If $A$ is self-adjoint, then $\sigma(A) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is closed; for $\operatorname{Im}z \neq 0$,
   $\|R_z(A)\| \leq 1/|\operatorname{Im}z|$; for $z, w \in \rho(A)$, $R_z(A)^\dagger = R_{z^*}(A)$ and $R_z(A) - R_w(A) = (z -
   w)R_z(A)R_w(A)$. A real $\lambda$ lies in $\sigma(A)$ if and only if there are unit vectors $u_n \in D(A)$ with $\|(A -
   \lambda)u_n\| \to 0$ (**Weyl's criterion**). Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal. If $\langle u, Au\rangle \geq
   m\|u\|^2$ on $D(A)$, then $\sigma(A) \subseteq [m, \infty)$.
5. (**Eigenbases**) Let $(e_k)$ be an orthonormal basis of $\mathcal H$ and $(\lambda_k)$ real numbers. The **diagonal operator**
   $D_\lambda u = \sum_k\lambda_k\langle e_k, u\rangle e_k$ on $D(D_\lambda) = \{u : \sum_k\lambda_k^2|\langle e_k, u\rangle|^2 <
   \infty\}$ is self-adjoint; $\sigma(D_\lambda)$ is the closure of $\{\lambda_k\}$; the eigenvalues are the $\lambda_k$, and the
   eigenspace of $\lambda$ is the closed span of the $e_k$ with $\lambda_k = \lambda$; for $z \in \rho(D_\lambda)$, $R_z(D_\lambda)u
   = \sum_k(\lambda_k - z)^{-1}\langle e_k, u\rangle e_k$ and $\|R_z(D_\lambda)\| = 1/\operatorname{dist}(z, \{\lambda_k\})$. If
   every $e_k$ lies in $D(A)$ with $Ae_k = \lambda_ke_k$, then $A$ is essentially self-adjoint and $\overline A = D_\lambda$.
6. (**Compact resolvent**) Let $A$ be self-adjoint, $\mathcal H$ separable and infinite-dimensional, and suppose $R_\mu(A)$ is compact
   for one real $\mu \in \rho(A)$. Then $\mathcal H$ has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors $e_k$ of $A$, $A = D_\lambda$ for their
   eigenvalues $\lambda_k$, every eigenvalue has finite multiplicity, $|\lambda_k| \to \infty$, $\sigma(A) = \{\lambda_k\}$, and
   $R_z(A)$ is compact for every $z \in \rho(A)$. Conversely, $D_\lambda$ with $|\lambda_k| \to \infty$ has compact resolvents.
:::
::::

*Proof.* (1) $\langle u, Au\rangle = \langle Au, u\rangle = \langle u, Au\rangle^*$. Expanding, $\|(A - a)u - ibu\|^2 = \|(A - a)u\|^2 +
b^2\|u\|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(-ib\langle(A - a)u, u\rangle\bigr)$, and the last term vanishes because $\langle(A - a)u, u\rangle$
is real. If $(A - z)u_n \to w$, then $\|u_n - u_m\| \leq |b|^{-1}\|(A - z)(u_n - u_m)\|$ and $\|A(u_n - u_m)\| \leq \|(A - z)(u_n -
u_m)\| + |z|\|u_n - u_m\|$, so $u_n \to u$ and $Au_n \to y$; if $A$ is closed, $u \in D(A)$, $y = Au$ and $w = (A - z)u$.

(2) (a)$\Rightarrow$(b): $A$ is closed by @def-unbounded-operator (3). If $A^\dagger u = iu$, then $u \in D(A)$ and $Au = iu$, so
$\langle u, Au\rangle = i\|u\|^2$ is real only if $u = 0$; likewise for $-i$. (b)$\Rightarrow$(c): by @def-unbounded-operator (1),
$\operatorname{ran}(A - i)^\perp = \ker(A^\dagger + i) = \{0\}$ and $\operatorname{ran}(A + i)^\perp = \ker(A^\dagger - i) = \{0\}$, so
both ranges are dense (@thm-projection (3)), and they are closed by (1). (c)$\Rightarrow$(a): $A \subset A^\dagger$. Let $v \in
D(A^\dagger)$ and choose $u \in D(A)$ with $(A - i)u = (A^\dagger - i)v$. Then $(A^\dagger - i)(v - u) = 0$, and $\ker(A^\dagger - i) =
\operatorname{ran}(A + i)^\perp = \{0\}$, so $v = u \in D(A)$. For real $\mu$ the same argument with $\mu$ in place of $\pm i$ gives
$D(A^\dagger) = D(A)$, using $\ker(A^\dagger - \mu) = \operatorname{ran}(A - \mu)^\perp = \{0\}$. Then $\ker(A - \mu) \subseteq
\ker(A^\dagger - \mu) = \{0\}$, so $A - \mu$ is a bijection of $D(A)$ onto $\mathcal H$. Its inverse $R$ satisfies $\langle Rf, g\rangle =
\langle Rf, (A - \mu)Rg\rangle = \langle(A - \mu)Rf, Rg\rangle = \langle f, Rg\rangle$ for all $f, g$, so it is bounded by
@thm-sesquilinear-forms (5), and $\mu \in \rho(A)$.

(3) Since $\operatorname{ran}(A \pm i)^\perp = \ker(A^\dagger \mp i)$, (b) and (c) are equivalent. (a)$\Rightarrow$(c): by (2),
$\operatorname{ran}(\overline A \pm i) = \mathcal H$; for $u \in D(\overline A)$ choose $u_n \in D(A)$ with $u_n \to u$ and $Au_n \to
\overline Au$, so $(A \pm i)u_n \to (\overline A \pm i)u$, and $\operatorname{ran}(A \pm i)$ is dense. (c)$\Rightarrow$(a): $\overline
A$ is closed and symmetric (@def-unbounded-operator (3)), so $\operatorname{ran}(\overline A \pm i)$ is closed by (1); it contains the
dense set $\operatorname{ran}(A \pm i)$, so it is $\mathcal H$, and $\overline A$ is self-adjoint by (2). For real $\mu$, the bound
$\|(A - \mu)u\| \geq c\|u\|$ passes to $\overline A$ by taking limits, the argument of (1) shows that $\operatorname{ran}(\overline A -
\mu)$ is closed, so it is $\mathcal H$, and (2) applies to $\overline A$. If $A$ is self-adjoint and $B \supset A$ is symmetric, then $B
\subset B^\dagger \subset A^\dagger = A$ by @def-unbounded-operator (2), (3), so $B = A$. If $A$ is essentially self-adjoint and $B$ is a
self-adjoint extension, $B$ is closed, so $\overline A \subset B$ by @def-closed-operator (4), and $B = \overline A$ by what was just
shown.

(4) Let $z = a + ib$, $b \neq 0$. $\ker(A - z^*) = \{0\}$ by (1), so $\operatorname{ran}(A - z)^\perp = \ker(A^\dagger - z^*) =
\ker(A - z^*) = \{0\}$, and $\operatorname{ran}(A - z)$ is dense and closed (1). So $A - z$ is a bijection, and $\|u\| \leq |b|^{-1}\|(A -
z)u\|$ gives $\|R_z(A)\| \leq 1/|b|$. The spectrum is closed by @def-unbounded-operator (5). For $z, w \in \rho(A)$, $f, g \in
\mathcal H$, $u = R_z(A)f$ and $v = R_{z^*}(A)g$, symmetry gives $\langle f, v\rangle = \langle(A - z)u, v\rangle = \langle u, (A -
z^*)v\rangle = \langle u, g\rangle$, that is $R_{z^*}(A) = R_z(A)^\dagger$; and $R_z(A) - R_w(A) = R_z(A)\bigl((A - w) - (A -
z)\bigr)R_w(A) = (z - w)R_z(A)R_w(A)$. If $\lambda \in \rho(A)$, then $\|u\| \leq \|R_\lambda(A)\|\,\|(A - \lambda)u\|$, so no unit
vectors with $\|(A - \lambda)u_n\| \to 0$ exist. If no such vectors exist, there is $c > 0$ with $\|(A - \lambda)u\| \geq c\|u\|$, so
$\operatorname{ran}(A - \lambda)$ is closed (as in (1)) and $\operatorname{ran}(A - \lambda)^\perp = \ker(A - \lambda) = \{0\}$; by
(2), $\lambda \in \rho(A)$. If $Au = \lambda u$ and $Av = \nu v$ with $\lambda \neq \nu$, both real by (1), then $\lambda\langle u,
v\rangle = \langle Au, v\rangle = \langle u, Av\rangle = \nu\langle u, v\rangle$, so $\langle u, v\rangle = 0$. If $\langle u, Au\rangle
\geq m\|u\|^2$ and $\lambda < m$, then $\|(A - \lambda)u\|\,\|u\| \geq \langle u, (A - \lambda)u\rangle \geq (m - \lambda)\|u\|^2$, and
Weyl's criterion gives $\lambda \in \rho(A)$.

(5) Write $c_k = \langle e_k, u\rangle$. $D(D_\lambda)$ contains the span of the $e_k$, hence is dense, and $D_\lambda u$ converges by
@def-orthonormal-basis (1). Symmetry is $\langle D_\lambda u, v\rangle = \sum\lambda_kc_k^*d_k = \langle u, D_\lambda v\rangle$, by
@def-orthonormal-basis (2)(e). For $f \in \mathcal H$, $u = \sum_k(\lambda_k \pm i)^{-1}\langle e_k, f\rangle e_k$ lies in
$D(D_\lambda)$, since $|\lambda_k/(\lambda_k \pm i)| \leq 1$, and $(D_\lambda \pm i)u = f$; so $D_\lambda$ is self-adjoint by (2). Let
$d = \operatorname{dist}(z, \{\lambda_k\}) > 0$. Then $R = \sum_k(\lambda_k - z)^{-1}\langle e_k, \cdot\rangle e_k$ has $\|R\| \leq 1/d$,
maps into $D(D_\lambda)$ since $|\lambda_k/(\lambda_k - z)| \leq 1 + |z|/d$, and inverts $D_\lambda - z$ on both sides; testing on $e_k$
with $|\lambda_k - z|$ close to $d$ gives $\|R\| = 1/d$. If $z$ is in the closure, there are $e_{k_j}$ with $\|(D_\lambda - z)e_{k_j}\| =
|\lambda_{k_j} - z| \to 0$, so $z \in \sigma(D_\lambda)$ (Weyl's criterion if $z$ is real; $z$ is real, being a limit of real numbers).
$D_\lambda u = \lambda u$ means $(\lambda_k - \lambda)c_k = 0$ for all $k$, which gives the eigenspaces. Finally let $A$ be symmetric with
$Ae_k = \lambda_ke_k$. Then $\operatorname{ran}(A \pm i)$ contains every $e_k = (A \pm i)\bigl(e_k/(\lambda_k \pm i)\bigr)$, so it is dense
and $A$ is essentially self-adjoint by (3). For $u \in D(A)$, $\langle e_k, Au\rangle = \langle Ae_k, u\rangle = \lambda_kc_k$, so $Au =
\sum_k\lambda_kc_ke_k$ with $\sum\lambda_k^2|c_k|^2 = \|Au\|^2 < \infty$: $A \subset D_\lambda$. Hence $\overline A \subset D_\lambda$, and
since $\overline A$ is self-adjoint and $D_\lambda$ symmetric, $\overline A = D_\lambda$ by (3).

(6) $R = R_\mu(A)$ is bounded, compact by assumption, self-adjoint by (4), and injective, being an inverse. By
@thm-spectral-theorem-compact (3), $\overline{\operatorname{ran}R} = (\ker R)^\perp = \mathcal H$ has an orthonormal basis of
eigenvectors $e_k$, $Re_k = \nu_ke_k$ with $\nu_k \neq 0$, infinitely many since $\mathcal H$ is infinite-dimensional, so $\nu_k \to 0$
and each value is repeated finitely often (@thm-spectral-theorem-compact (2)). Then $e_k = R(e_k/\nu_k) \in D(A)$ and $(A - \mu)e_k =
e_k/\nu_k$, so $Ae_k = \lambda_ke_k$ with $\lambda_k = \mu + 1/\nu_k$, and $|\lambda_k| \to \infty$. By (5), the restriction of $A$ to
the span of the $e_k$ has closure $D_\lambda$, so $D_\lambda \subset A$, and $A = D_\lambda$ by the maximality in (3). By (5),
$\sigma(A)$ is the closure of $\{\lambda_k\}$, which is $\{\lambda_k\}$ because the $\lambda_k$ have no finite accumulation point, and the
eigenspace of $\lambda_k$ is spanned by finitely many $e_j$. For $z \in \rho(A)$, $R_z(A) = R + (z - \mu)R_z(A)R$ is compact by
@def-compact-operator (2), (3). Conversely, for $D_\lambda$ with $|\lambda_k| \to \infty$, $R_z(D_\lambda)$ is diagonal with entries
$(\lambda_k - z)^{-1} \to 0$, hence compact by @def-compact-operator (5). $\square$

Part (2) is the basic criterion of @reed1980methods [Vol. I, Thm. VIII.3, pp. 256-257], and part (3) is its corollary there; the version with
a real $\mu$ and the resolvent identities are in @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 7.4, Lemmas 7.6, 7.7, Props. 7.5, 7.6, 7.9 and Cor. 7.3], and Weyl's
criterion for unbounded operators is @hall2013quantum [Prop. 9.18]. Part (6) is the route of @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 7.9.2] to compact
self-adjoint inverses.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In finite dimensions every symmetric operator is self-adjoint, and the criterion holds trivially. The first example records this, so
that every difficulty below is visibly an effect of infinite dimensions.

::: {#exm-unb-matrix-symmetric}
#### Hermitian matrices

On $\mathbb{C}^n$ every subspace is closed, so a densely defined operator has $D(A) = \mathbb{C}^n$, and a symmetric one is a Hermitian
matrix $\mathbf A$. By part (1), $\|(\mathbf A \pm i)\mathbf u\| \geq \|\mathbf u\|$, so $\mathbf A \pm i$ are injective, hence onto by
rank-nullity, and part (2)(c) holds. For $\mathbf A = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, $\|(\mathbf A -
i)\mathbf u\|^2 = \|\mathbf A\mathbf u\|^2 + \|\mathbf u\|^2 = 2\|\mathbf u\|^2$.
:::

The diagonal operator of @exm-unb-diagonal-domain is the model case of part (5). The second example reads off its spectrum and its
resolvent.

::: {#exm-unb-diagonal-spectrum}
#### The diagonal operator

For $(Aa)_n = na_n$ on $c_{00}$, the vectors $\delta^{(n)}$ are eigenvectors in the domain, so by part (5) $A$ is essentially
self-adjoint, $\overline A = D_\lambda$ with $\lambda_n = n$, as found in @exm-unb-diagonal-essential. Its spectrum is $\{1, 2, 3,
\dots\}$, unbounded and closed, every point an eigenvalue of multiplicity one, and $R_z(\overline A)$ multiplies by $1/(n - z)$. By
part (6) the resolvent is compact, since $n \to \infty$.
:::

The Laplacian of the circle is diagonal in the trigonometric basis, with every non-zero eigenvalue repeated twice. The third example applies
parts (5) and (6) to it.

::: {#exm-unb-circle-laplacian-sa}
#### The Laplacian of the circle is essentially self-adjoint

For $A = -d^2/dx^2$ on the trigonometric polynomials of @exm-ub-laplacian-domain, $Ae_n = n^2e_n$ and $(e_n)_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is an
orthonormal basis (@thm-trigonometric-basis). By part (5), $A$ is essentially self-adjoint, $\overline A$ acts by $n^2$ on $\{F :
\sum n^4|\langle e_n, F\rangle|^2 < \infty\}$, and $\sigma(\overline A) = \{0, 1, 4, 9, \dots\}$, with eigenspaces spanned by $e_n,
e_{-n}$; the resolvent is compact by part (6). So the domain of the adjoint found in @exm-ub-laplacian-domain is the domain of the
closure.
:::

The estimate $\|R_z(A)\| \leq 1/|\operatorname{Im}z|$ of part (4) is the only information on the resolvent that self-adjointness gives
without knowing the spectrum. The fourth example compares it with the exact norm for a diagonal operator, and the figure shows both
along a vertical line.

![The norm $\|R_z\| = 1/\operatorname{dist}(z, \sigma)$ for the diagonal operator with eigenvalues $0, 1, 4, 9, \dots$ along the line $z =
2 + iy$ (thick), and the bound $1/|y|$ (thin). The two agree only when the nearest eigenvalue is $\operatorname{Re}z$ itself.
](figures/unb-resolvent-norm.svg){#fig-unb-resolvent-norm width=70%}

::: {#exm-unb-resolvent-norm}
#### The resolvent bound

For the operator of @exm-unb-circle-laplacian-sa, $\|R_z\| = 1/\operatorname{dist}(z, \{n^2\})$ by part (5). At $z = 2 + iy$ the nearest
eigenvalue is $1$, so $\|R_z\| = (1 + y^2)^{-1/2} < 1/|y|$, as in @fig-unb-resolvent-norm; at $z = 4 + iy$ the nearest eigenvalue is
$\operatorname{Re}z$ and $\|R_z\| = 1/|y|$ exactly. The bound of part (4) is attained exactly when $\operatorname{Re}z \in \sigma(A)$.
:::

For differential operators the criterion with a real $\mu$ is often the easiest to check, because a real shift turns the equation $(A -
\mu)u = f$ into a boundary value problem with a Green's function. The fifth example does this for the vibrating string.

::: {#exm-unb-dirichlet-green}
#### The Dirichlet second derivative

Let $A = -d^2/dx^2$ on $\{u \in C^2[0, \pi] : u(0) = u(\pi) = 0\}$, symmetric with $\langle u, Au\rangle = \|u'\|^2$
(@exr-unb-dirichlet-unbounded). Then $\langle u, (A + 1)u\rangle \geq \|u\|^2$, so $\|(A + 1)u\| \geq \|u\|$. By
@thm-fred-sturm-liouville-completeness (2) with $\mu = -1$ and @exm-fred-slc-string, every continuous $f$ is $(A + 1)u$ for $u(x) =
\int_0^\pi g(x, \xi)f(\xi)\,d\xi$, $g(x, \xi) = \sinh x_<\sinh(\pi - x_>)/\sinh\pi$; so $\operatorname{ran}(A + 1) \supseteq C[0, \pi]$ is
dense. By part (3), $A$ is essentially self-adjoint and $-1 \in \rho(\overline A)$. The resolvent $R_{-1}(\overline A)$ agrees with the
integral operator $K$ with kernel $g$ on the dense set $C[0, \pi]$, hence everywhere, and $K$ is compact (@def-compact-operator (7)). By
part (6) and @thm-fred-sturm-liouville-completeness (3), $\overline A$ has the eigenbasis $\sqrt{2/\pi}\sin nx$ and spectrum $\{n^2 : n
\geq 1\}$.
:::

The harmonic oscillator is diagonal in the Hermite basis. The sixth example applies part (5) to its Hamiltonian on the span of the
Hermite functions.

::: {#exm-unb-oscillator-sa}
#### The harmonic oscillator

By @def-hermite-polynomial (3), $H_n'' - 2xH_n' + 2nH_n = 0$, and for $\psi_n = H_ne^{-x^2/2}$ this gives $-\psi_n'' + x^2\psi_n = (2n +
1)\psi_n$. So $H = \tfrac12(-d^2/dx^2 + x^2)$ on the span of the Hermite functions has $Hh_n = (n + \tfrac12)h_n$. It is symmetric, by
integration by parts with Gaussian decay, and the $h_n$ form an orthonormal basis (@thm-hermite-basis). By parts (5) and (6), $H$ is
essentially self-adjoint, $\sigma(\overline H) = \{\tfrac12, \tfrac32, \tfrac52, \dots\}$, and the resolvent is compact: the oscillator
has a purely discrete spectrum of equally spaced levels.
:::

Bound states of hydrogen accumulate at the ionisation threshold. The seventh example models only the bound states by a diagonal operator,
and shows that the accumulation point belongs to the spectrum without being an eigenvalue.

::: {#exm-unb-hydrogen-levels}
#### Accumulating energy levels

On $\ell^2$, with an orthonormal basis grouped so that $n^2$ basis vectors carry the value $E_n = -1/(2n^2)$ (energies in Hartree units,
multiplicity $n^2$ as for hydrogen), the operator $D_E$ of part (5) is bounded and self-adjoint. Its spectrum is the closure of $\{E_n\}$,
which is $\{E_n\} \cup \{0\}$. The point $0$ is not an eigenvalue, since no $E_n$ is $0$, but it lies in the spectrum: the eigenvectors
for $E_n$ are approximate eigenvectors for $0$, with $\|(D_E - 0)e\| = 1/(2n^2) \to 0$.
:::

Symmetry alone does not give the criterion. The eighth example exhibits a vector orthogonal to $\operatorname{ran}(A + i)$ for the
derivative on an interval with both ends fixed.

::: {#exm-unb-momentum-not-esa}
#### A symmetric operator that is not essentially self-adjoint

Let $T_0 = -i\,d/dx$ on $\{u \in C^1[0, 1] : u(0) = u(1) = 0\}$ (@exm-unb-closure-derivative). For such $u$, an integration by parts gives
$$
\langle e^{-x}, (T_0 + i)u\rangle = \int_0^1e^{-x}(-iu' + iu)\,dx = -i\bigl[e^{-x}u\bigr]_0^1 - i\int_0^1e^{-x}u\,dx + i\int_0^1e^{-x}u\,dx =
0 .
$$
So $e^{-x} \perp \operatorname{ran}(T_0 + i)$, the range is not dense, and $T_0$ is not essentially self-adjoint by part (3); $e^{-x}$
lies in $\ker(T_0^\dagger - i)$.
:::

A closed symmetric operator that is not self-adjoint can have non-real spectrum, so part (4) needs self-adjointness. The ninth example
shows that the closure of $T_0$ has every complex number in its spectrum.

::: {#exm-unb-spectrum-symmetric}
#### A closed symmetric operator with spectrum $\mathbb{C}$

For $z \in \mathbb{C}$ let $v_z(x) = e^{iz^*x}$. As in @exm-unb-momentum-not-esa, $\langle v_z, (T_0 - z)u\rangle = \int_0^1e^{-izx}(-iu' -
zu)\,dx = -i[e^{-izx}u]_0^1 + \int_0^1(-z + z)e^{-izx}u\,dx = 0$ for $u \in D(T_0)$. So $\operatorname{ran}(T_0 - z)$ is not dense, and
neither is $\operatorname{ran}(\overline{T_0} - z)$, which lies in its closure. Hence $z \in \sigma(\overline{T_0})$ for every $z$: the
closed symmetric operator $\overline{T_0}$ has $\sigma(\overline{T_0}) = \mathbb{C}$.
:::

A compact resolvent forces the eigenvalues to escape to infinity, so a bounded operator on an infinite-dimensional space never has one. The
last example checks this against part (6) and its converse.

::: {#exm-unb-no-compact-resolvent}
#### When the resolvent is not compact

If $A \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ is self-adjoint and $\mathcal H$ is infinite-dimensional, then $R_z(A)$ has the bounded inverse $A - z$,
so it is not compact (@def-compact-operator (3)). For $D_\lambda$ with $\lambda_k = 1/k$, the resolvent at $z = -1$ is diagonal with
entries $k/(1 + k) \to 1$, not $0$, so it is not compact, in agreement with part (6): the eigenvalues accumulate at $0$ instead of
escaping to infinity.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The identity of part (1) is a Pythagorean decomposition that can be checked directly. The first exercise checks it for a diagonal operator
and a non-real $z$.

::: {#exr-unb-basic-estimate}
#### The basic estimate

For the diagonal operator with entries $\lambda_n = (-1)^nn$ and the finite sequence $u = (1, 2i, -1, 3)$, verify $\|(A - z)u\|^2 = \|(A -
a)u\|^2 + b^2\|u\|^2$ for $z = \tfrac12 + 2i$, and show that the identity fails for the non-symmetric operator $\mathbf N =
\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & 1\\ 0 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ on $\mathbb{C}^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For a diagonal operator with real entries, $\|(A - z)u\|^2 = \sum|\lambda_n - a - ib|^2|u_n|^2 = \sum\bigl((\lambda_n - a)^2 +
b^2\bigr)|u_n|^2$, which is the identity of part (1) term by term. For $\mathbf N$, $\mathbf u = (0, 1)$ and $z = i$: $(\mathbf N -
i)\mathbf u = (1, -i)$ has norm squared $2$, while $\|\mathbf N\mathbf u\|^2 + \|\mathbf u\|^2 = 1 + 1 = 2$ happens to agree; with
$\mathbf u = (1, i)$, $(\mathbf N - i)\mathbf u = (i - i, 1) = (0, 1)$ has norm squared $1$, but $\|\mathbf N\mathbf u\|^2 + \|\mathbf
u\|^2 = 1 + 2 = 3$. The cross term $2\operatorname{Re}(-ib\langle\mathbf N\mathbf u, \mathbf u\rangle)$ does not vanish because
$\langle\mathbf u, \mathbf N\mathbf u\rangle = i$ is not real.

## SageMath

The code evaluates both sides for the diagonal operator and for $\mathbf N$.

```{.python .sage}
K = QQ[I]
lam = [(-1) ** n * n for n in range(1, 5)]
u = vector(K, [1, 2 * I, -1, 3]); a, b = 1/2, 2; z = a + b * I
nrm2 = lambda v: sum(abs(t) ** 2 for t in v)
lhs = nrm2([(l - z) * t for l, t in zip(lam, u)]); rhs = nrm2([(l - a) * t for l, t in zip(lam, u)]) + b ** 2 * nrm2(u)
print("diagonal: ||(A - z)u||^2 =", lhs, "; ||(A - a)u||^2 + b^2 ||u||^2 =", rhs)
N = matrix(K, [[0, 1], [0, 0]]); w = vector(K, [1, I])
print("N: ||(N - i)u||^2 =", nrm2((N - I) * w), "; ||N u||^2 + ||u||^2 =", nrm2(N * w) + nrm2(w))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
diagonal: ||(A - z)u||^2 = 775/4 ; ||(A - a)u||^2 + b^2 ||u||^2 = 775/4
N: ||(N - i)u||^2 = 1 ; ||N u||^2 + ||u||^2 = 3
```
::::
:::

The numbers $\pm i$ in the criterion can be replaced by $\pm i\mu$ for any $\mu > 0$, which is convenient when a scale is present. The
second exercise asks for this version.

::: {#exr-unb-mu-criterion}
#### Scaling the criterion

Let $A$ be symmetric and $\mu > 0$. Show that $A$ is self-adjoint if and only if $\operatorname{ran}(A \pm i\mu) = \mathcal H$, and
essentially self-adjoint if and only if $\operatorname{ran}(A \pm i\mu)$ are dense. Check the first statement for $A = D_\lambda$ with
$\lambda_n = n$ and $\mu = 3$ by solving $(A + 3i)u = \delta^{(2)} + \delta^{(5)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$A/\mu$ is symmetric, with the same domain, and $(A/\mu)^\dagger = A^\dagger/\mu$ (@exr-unb-adjoint-rules). It is self-adjoint exactly
when $A$ is, essentially self-adjoint exactly when $A$ is (its closure is $\overline A/\mu$), and $\operatorname{ran}(A/\mu \pm i) =
\operatorname{ran}(A \pm i\mu)$. Parts (2) and (3) applied to $A/\mu$ give both claims. For the diagonal operator, $u = \delta^{(2)}/(2 +
3i) + \delta^{(5)}/(5 + 3i)$.

## SageMath

The code solves the equation entrywise and checks the result.

```{.python .sage}
K = QQ[I]
N = 6
A = diagonal_matrix(K, list(range(1, N + 1)))
f = vector(K, [0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0])
u = (A + 3 * I).solve_right(f)
print("u =", u)
print("(A + 3i) u = f:", (A + 3 * I) * u == f)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
u = (0, -3/13*I + 2/13, 0, 0, -3/34*I + 5/34, 0)
(A + 3i) u = f: True
```
::::
:::

A self-adjoint operator has two useful bounded companions besides its resolvent. The third exercise asks for the norm bounds on them,
which are used in perturbation theory.

::: {#exr-unb-resolvent-estimates}
#### Two resolvent bounds

Let $A$ be self-adjoint and $\mu$ real, $\mu \neq 0$. Show that $\|f\|^2 = \|AR_{-i\mu}(A)f\|^2 + \mu^2\|R_{-i\mu}(A)f\|^2$ for every
$f$, so that $\|AR_{-i\mu}(A)\| \leq 1$. If moreover $A \geq 0$ and $\lambda > 0$, show that $\|R_{-\lambda}(A)\| \leq 1/\lambda$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$-i\mu \in \rho(A)$ by part (4). With $u = R_{-i\mu}(A)f \in D(A)$, $f = (A + i\mu)u$, and part (1) with $a = 0$, $b = -\mu$ gives $\|f\|^2
= \|Au\|^2 + \mu^2\|u\|^2$, which is the identity; dropping the second term gives $\|AR_{-i\mu}f\| \leq \|f\|$. If $A \geq 0$, then
$\sigma(A) \subseteq [0, \infty)$ by part (4), so $-\lambda \in \rho(A)$, and for $u = R_{-\lambda}(A)f$, $\|f\|\,\|u\| \geq \langle u,
(A + \lambda)u\rangle \geq \lambda\|u\|^2$, so $\|u\| \leq \|f\|/\lambda$.

## SageMath

Check on the diagonal operator with entries $n^2$, $n \leq 50$: the code computes the largest entries of $|\lambda_n/(\lambda_n + i\mu)|$
and $1/(\lambda_n + \lambda)$.

```{.python .sage}
mu, lm = 3, 2
lam = [n ** 2 for n in range(0, 51)]
print("max |lambda_n / (lambda_n + i mu)| =", max(abs(l / (l + I * mu)) for l in lam).n(digits=6), "<= 1")
print("max 1/(lambda_n + lambda) =", max(1 / (l + lm) for l in lam), "= 1/lambda =", 1 / lm)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
max |lambda_n / (lambda_n + i mu)| = 0.999999 <= 1
max 1/(lambda_n + lambda) = 1/2 = 1/lambda = 1/2
```
::::
:::

The spectrum is the closure of the set of eigenvalues for a diagonal operator, and that closure can be an interval even though the
eigenvalues are countable. The fourth exercise asks for an example with $\lambda_k = \sin k$.

::: {#exr-unb-dense-spectrum}
#### A spectrum filling an interval

Show that the numbers $\sin k$, $k = 1, 2, \dots$, are dense in $[-1, 1]$, and conclude that the bounded diagonal operator with these
entries has spectrum $[-1, 1]$, although its eigenvalues are countable. Find the $k \leq 10^4$ for which $\sin k$ is closest to $0.3$, and explain why the
approach is slow.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $N > 2\pi/\varepsilon$. Of the $N + 1$ points $k\bmod 2\pi$, $k = 0, \dots, N$, in $[0, 2\pi)$ two lie within
$2\pi/N < \varepsilon$ of each other (pigeonhole), say for $k_1 < k_2$; then $q = k_2 - k_1$ has $q\bmod 2\pi \in (0, \varepsilon) \cup
(2\pi - \varepsilon, 2\pi)$, and it is not $0$ since $\pi$ is irrational. The multiples $jq\bmod 2\pi$ then step around the circle in steps
shorter than $\varepsilon$, so every point of $[0, 2\pi)$ is within $\varepsilon$ of some $k\bmod 2\pi$, and since $\sin$ is
1-Lipschitz every $s \in [-1, 1]$ is within $\varepsilon$ of some $\sin k$. By part (5) the spectrum is the closure of $\{\sin k\}$,
which is $[-1, 1]$, while the eigenvalues are the countably many values $\sin k$ (all distinct, since $\sin k = \sin k'$ would force $k
\pm k' \in \pi\mathbb{Z}$). The approach is slow because $710 = 226\pi + 0.00006\ldots$: the step $q = 710$ is tiny, so the values
$\sin k$ cluster along slowly drifting families, and $k = 9978$ only gets within about $3 \cdot 10^{-3}$ of $0.3$.

## SageMath

The code searches $k \leq 10^4$.

```{.python .sage}
best = min(range(1, 10001), key=lambda k: abs(RDF(k).sin() - 0.3))
print("k =", best, "; sin k =", sin(best).n(digits=8), "; |sin k - 0.3| = %.5f" % abs(sin(best).n() - 0.3))
print("710 mod 2 pi = %.6f" % (710 - 113 * 2 * pi).n())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
k = 9978 ; sin k = 0.29717460 ; |sin k - 0.3| = 0.00283
710 mod 2 pi = 0.000060
```
::::
:::

The resolvent identity and the relation $R_z^\dagger = R_{z^*}$ are algebraic, and on a diagonal operator they become identities between
fractions. The fifth exercise checks them on a truncation.

::: {#exr-unb-resolvent-identity}
#### The resolvent identity

For $D_\lambda$ with $\lambda_n = n^2$, show directly from part (5) that $R_z - R_w = (z - w)R_zR_w$ and $R_z^\dagger = R_{z^*}$, and
check both on the first ten entries for $z = i$, $w = 2 - i$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

All three operators are diagonal in the same basis, with entries $(\lambda_n - z)^{-1}$, $(\lambda_n - w)^{-1}$, and
$$
\frac{1}{\lambda_n - z} - \frac{1}{\lambda_n - w} = \frac{(\lambda_n - w) - (\lambda_n - z)}{(\lambda_n - z)(\lambda_n - w)} = \frac{z -
w}{(\lambda_n - z)(\lambda_n - w)} .
$$
The adjoint of a bounded diagonal operator has the conjugate entries (@def-adjoint-operator (6)), and $((\lambda_n - z)^{-1})^* =
(\lambda_n - z^*)^{-1}$ because $\lambda_n$ is real.

## SageMath

The code builds the truncated resolvents as matrices over $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ and compares.

```{.python .sage}
K = QQ[I]
z, w = I, 2 - I
R = lambda s: diagonal_matrix(K, [1 / (n ** 2 - s) for n in range(1, 11)])
print("R_z - R_w = (z - w) R_z R_w:", R(z) - R(w) == (z - w) * R(z) * R(w))
print("R_z^dagger = R_{z^*}:", R(z).conjugate_transpose() == R(conjugate(z)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
R_z - R_w = (z - w) R_z R_w: True
R_z^dagger = R_{z^*}: True
```
::::
:::

For a non-negative symmetric operator one real shift suffices to test essential self-adjointness. The sixth exercise proves this
version of part (3), which is the one used for Laplacians.

::: {#exr-unb-positive-criterion}
#### Non-negative operators

Let $A$ be symmetric with $\langle u, Au\rangle \geq 0$ on $D(A)$. Show that $A$ is essentially self-adjoint if and only if
$\operatorname{ran}(A + 1)$ is dense, and that then $\sigma(\overline A) \subseteq [0, \infty)$. Check the bound $\|(A + 1)u\| \geq \|u\|$
on $u = x(\pi - x)$ for the operator of @exr-unb-dirichlet-unbounded.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\|(A + 1)u\|\,\|u\| \geq \langle u, (A + 1)u\rangle \geq \|u\|^2$, so $\|(A + 1)u\| \geq \|u\|$. If $\operatorname{ran}(A + 1)$ is dense,
part (3) with $\mu = -1$, $c = 1$ makes $A$ essentially self-adjoint. Conversely, if $\overline A$ is self-adjoint, $\langle u, \overline
Au\rangle \geq 0$ on $D(\overline A)$ by taking limits, so $\sigma(\overline A) \subseteq [0, \infty)$ by part (4); then $-1 \in
\rho(\overline A)$, $\operatorname{ran}(\overline A + 1) = \mathcal H$, and $\operatorname{ran}(A + 1)$ is dense in it as in the proof of
part (3).

## SageMath

The code computes $\|(A + 1)u\|^2$ and $\|u\|^2$ for $u = x(\pi - x)$.

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x")
u = x * (pi - x); Au1 = -diff(u, x, 2) + u
a = integrate(Au1 ** 2, x, 0, pi); b = integrate(u ** 2, x, 0, pi)
print("||(A + 1)u||^2 =", a.simplify_full(), "=", a.n(digits=6), "; ||u||^2 =", b, "=", b.n(digits=6))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
||(A + 1)u||^2 = 4*pi + 1/30*pi^5 + 2/3*pi^3 = 43.4379 ; ||u||^2 = 1/30*pi^5 = 10.2007
```
::::
:::

A self-adjoint operator is determined by its values on a suitable dense subspace, called a core. The seventh exercise characterises
cores and finds one for the Dirichlet operator.

::: {#exr-unb-core}
#### Cores

Let $A$ be self-adjoint and $D_0 \subseteq D(A)$ a subspace with $A_0 = A|_{D_0}$ densely defined. Show that $A_0$ is essentially
self-adjoint if and only if $\overline{A_0} = A$. Deduce that the span of the functions $\sin nx$ is a core for the closure of the
Dirichlet operator of @exm-unb-dirichlet-green.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$A_0$ is symmetric, since $A$ is. If $\overline{A_0} = A$, it is self-adjoint. Conversely, if $\overline{A_0}$ is self-adjoint, then
$\overline{A_0} \subset A$ because $A$ is closed (@def-closed-operator (4)), and maximality (part (3)) gives $\overline{A_0} = A$. For
the Dirichlet operator, the restriction to the span of the $\sin nx$ is essentially self-adjoint by part (5), since the normalised $\sin nx$
form an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors (@thm-fred-sturm-liouville-completeness (5), @exm-fred-slc-string); so its closure is the
closure of the Dirichlet operator.

## SageMath

Check on $u = x(\pi - x)$: the code computes the partial sums of its sine expansion and of $-u''$, and the errors in $L^2[0, \pi]$, which
tend to $0$ together, as the graph-norm convergence requires.

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x")
u = x * (pi - x)
c = lambda n: 2 / pi * integrate(u * sin(n * x), x, 0, pi)
for N in [1, 5, 25]:
    S = sum(c(n) * sin(n * x) for n in range(1, N + 1)); AS = sum(n ** 2 * c(n) * sin(n * x) for n in range(1, N + 1))
    e1 = numerical_integral((u - S) ** 2, 0, pi)[0]; e2 = numerical_integral((2 - AS) ** 2, 0, pi)[0]
    print("N = %2d: ||u - S_N||^2 = %.2e, ||-u'' - A S_N||^2 = %.4f" % (N, e1, e2))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
N =  1: ||u - S_N||^2 = 1.47e-02, ||-u'' - A S_N||^2 = 2.3805
N =  5: ||u - S_N||^2 = 1.15e-04, ||-u'' - A S_N||^2 = 0.8412
N = 25: ||u - S_N||^2 = 8.51e-08, ||-u'' - A S_N||^2 = 0.1958
```
::::
:::

Part (6) and its converse say that a diagonal operator has a compact resolvent exactly when its entries escape to infinity. The eighth
exercise asks for the proof of this equivalence directly from @def-compact-operator.

::: {#exr-unb-compact-resolvent-iff}
#### Compact resolvent and diagonal operators

For $D_\lambda$ as in part (5), show that $R_z(D_\lambda)$ is compact for one (and then every) $z \in \rho(D_\lambda)$ if and only if
every bounded interval contains only finitely many $\lambda_k$, counted with repetition. Decide this for $\lambda_k = \log k$ and for
$\lambda_k = (-1)^kk$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$R_z$ is diagonal with entries $d_k = (\lambda_k - z)^{-1}$, compact if and only if $d_k \to 0$ (@def-compact-operator (5)), that is,
$|\lambda_k| \to \infty$, which says that each bounded interval contains $\lambda_k$ for finitely many $k$. The condition does not involve
$z$. For $\lambda_k = \log k$, $\lambda_k \to \infty$, so the resolvent is compact although the eigenvalues grow very slowly; for
$(-1)^kk$, $|\lambda_k| = k \to \infty$, compact as well, with spectrum unbounded in both directions.

## SageMath

The code counts the entries of $\log k$ in $[0, 5]$ and computes the largest $|d_k|$ beyond $k = 10^4$ at $z = i$.

```{.python .sage}
print("number of k with log k <= 5:", len([k for k in range(1, 10 ** 4) if RDF(k).log() <= 5]), "= floor(e^5) =", floor(e ** 5))
print("|1/(log k - i)| at k = 10^4:", (1 / abs(log(10 ** 4) - I)).n(digits=6), "; at k = 10^8:", (1 / abs(log(10 ** 8) - I)).n(digits=6))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
number of k with log k <= 5: 148 = floor(e^5) = 148
|1/(log k - i)| at k = 10^4: 0.107939 ; at k = 10^8: 0.0542070
```
::::
:::

Weyl's criterion locates the spectrum through approximate eigenvectors, and for a diagonal operator the best approximate eigenvector is a
basis vector. The ninth exercise makes this quantitative.

::: {#exr-unb-weyl-distance}
#### Distance to the spectrum

For self-adjoint $D_\lambda$ and real $\lambda$, show that $\inf\{\|(D_\lambda - \lambda)u\| : u \in D(D_\lambda), \|u\| = 1\} =
\operatorname{dist}(\lambda, \{\lambda_k\})$. For $\lambda_k = k^2$ compute this distance at $\lambda = 10$ and at $\lambda = 12.5$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\|(D_\lambda - \lambda)u\|^2 = \sum_k(\lambda_k - \lambda)^2|c_k|^2 \geq d^2\sum_k|c_k|^2 = d^2$ for unit $u$, with $d =
\operatorname{dist}(\lambda, \{\lambda_k\})$; and $u = e_k$ gives $|\lambda_k - \lambda|$, arbitrarily close to $d$. For $k^2$: at $10$ the
nearest square is $9$, distance $1$; at $12.5$ it is $16$ or $9$, distances $3.5$, so the infimum is $3.5$.

## SageMath

The code minimises $|k^2 - \lambda|$ over $k \leq 100$.

```{.python .sage}
for lm in [10, 25/2]:
    print("lambda =", lm, ": dist =", min(abs(k ** 2 - lm) for k in range(0, 101)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
lambda = 10 : dist = 1
lambda = 25/2 : dist = 7/2
```
::::
:::

A bounded perturbation moves the spectrum of a self-adjoint diagonal operator by at most its norm. The last exercise proves this with
part (5) and the Neumann series, and checks it on the truncated oscillator.

::: {#exr-unb-perturbation-spectrum}
#### Bounded perturbations move the spectrum a little

Let $A = D_\lambda$ be self-adjoint and $B \in \mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ self-adjoint. Show that $A + B$ is self-adjoint on $D(A)$ and that
every $z$ with $\operatorname{dist}(z, \{\lambda_k\}) > \|B\|$ lies in $\rho(A + B)$. Check this on the $8 \times 8$ truncation of the
oscillator $\lambda_n = n + \tfrac12$ with $\mathbf B$ the tridiagonal matrix with $0.3$ above and below the diagonal.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$A + B$ is self-adjoint on $D(A)$ by @exr-unb-adjoint-rules. Let $d = \operatorname{dist}(z, \{\lambda_k\}) > \|B\|$. Then $z \in \rho(A)$
and $\|BR_z(A)\| \leq \|B\|/d < 1$ by part (5), so $1 + BR_z(A)$ has a bounded inverse (@def-spectrum (1)), and $A + B - z = (1 +
BR_z(A))(A - z)$ on $D(A)$ is a bijection of $D(A)$ onto $\mathcal H$ with the bounded inverse $R_z(A)(1 + BR_z(A))^{-1}$. So $z \in
\rho(A + B)$, and $\sigma(A + B)$ lies within $\|B\|$ of $\{\lambda_k\}$.

## SageMath

Check on the truncation: the code computes $\|\mathbf B\|$ and the distance of each eigenvalue of $\mathbf A + \mathbf B$ to the nearest $n +
\tfrac12$.

```{.python .sage}
N = 8
A = diagonal_matrix(RDF, [n + 0.5 for n in range(N)])
B = matrix(RDF, N, N, lambda i, j: 0.3 if abs(i - j) == 1 else 0)
nB = B.norm(2)
ev = sorted((A + B).eigenvalues())
print("||B|| = %.4f" % nB)
print("max distance of an eigenvalue of A + B to {n + 1/2}: %.4f" % max(min(abs(e - (n + 0.5)) for n in range(N)) for e in ev), "<= ||B||:", max(min(abs(e - (n + 0.5)) for n in range(N)) for e in ev) <= nB)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
||B|| = 0.5638
max distance of an eigenvalue of A + B to {n + 1/2}: 0.0863 <= ||B||: True
```

:::
::::

### Self-adjoint extensions

A symmetric operator on a small domain can often be enlarged to a self-adjoint operator in several ways, each with its own spectrum; for
differential operators on an interval these ways are boundary conditions. @thm-unb-self-adjointness (3) detected the failure of essential
self-adjointness by the kernels of $A^\dagger \mp i$. The definition below names them, and proves von Neumann's description of all
self-adjoint extensions in terms of them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-self-adjoint-extension}
#### Self-adjoint extension

Let $A$ be a symmetric operator on $\mathcal H$. A **self-adjoint extension** of $A$ is a self-adjoint operator $B$ with $A \subset B$.
The **deficiency subspaces** of $A$ are $\mathcal K_+ = \ker(A^\dagger - i)$ and $\mathcal K_- = \ker(A^\dagger + i)$, and its
**deficiency indices** are $n_\pm = \dim\mathcal K_\pm \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots, \infty\}$. Then:

1. (**Deficiency subspaces**) $\mathcal K_\pm = \operatorname{ran}(A \pm i)^\perp$ are closed, and they are the same for $A$ and
   $\overline A$. $A$ is essentially self-adjoint if and only if $n_+ = n_- = 0$, and then $\overline A$ is its only self-adjoint
   extension. Every self-adjoint extension $B$ satisfies $\overline A \subset B \subset A^\dagger$.
2. (**Von Neumann's formula**) If $A$ is closed, every $v \in D(A^\dagger)$ is uniquely $v = u + k_+ + k_-$ with $u \in D(A)$, $k_\pm
   \in \mathcal K_\pm$, and $A^\dagger v = Au + ik_+ - ik_-$. For $v = u + k_+ + k_-$ and $w = u' + l_+ + l_-$,
   $$
   \langle A^\dagger v, w\rangle - \langle v, A^\dagger w\rangle = 2i\bigl(\langle k_-, l_-\rangle - \langle k_+, l_+\rangle\bigr) .
   $$
3. (**Von Neumann's theorem**) Let $A$ be closed. For every linear bijection $U : \mathcal K_+ \to \mathcal K_-$ preserving norms, the
   restriction $A_U$ of $A^\dagger$ to $D(A_U) = \{u + k + Uk : u \in D(A), k \in \mathcal K_+\}$ is a self-adjoint extension of $A$,
   and every self-adjoint extension of $A$ is $A_U$ for exactly one such $U$. In particular, if $n_+$ and $n_-$ are finite, $A$ has
   self-adjoint extensions if and only if $n_+ = n_-$; if $n_+ = n_- = 1$, with $\mathcal K_\pm$ spanned by unit vectors $k_\pm$, the
   extensions are indexed by the phases $\gamma$, $|\gamma| = 1$, through $Uk_+ = \gamma k_-$.
:::
::::

*Proof.* (1) $\operatorname{ran}(A \pm i)^\perp = \ker(A^\dagger \mp i)$ by @def-unbounded-operator (1), and orthogonal complements are
closed (@thm-projection (3)); $(\overline A)^\dagger = A^\dagger$ (@def-unbounded-operator (3)) gives the same subspaces for $\overline
A$. The characterisation of essential self-adjointness and the uniqueness of the extension are @thm-unb-self-adjointness (3). If $B$ is a
self-adjoint extension, $B$ is closed, so $\overline A \subset B$ (@def-closed-operator (4)), and $B = B^\dagger \subset A^\dagger$ by
@def-unbounded-operator (2).

(2) $\operatorname{ran}(A - i)$ is closed (@thm-unb-self-adjointness (1)), so $\mathcal H = \operatorname{ran}(A - i) \oplus \mathcal
K_-$ (@thm-projection (2)). Let $v \in D(A^\dagger)$ and write $(A^\dagger - i)v = (A - i)u + k$ with $u \in D(A)$, $k \in \mathcal K_-$.
Put $k_- = ik/2$; since $A^\dagger k_- = -ik_-$, $(A^\dagger - i)k_- = -2ik_- = k$. Then $(A^\dagger - i)(v - u - k_-) = 0$, because $A
\subset A^\dagger$, so $k_+ = v - u - k_- \in \mathcal K_+$. For uniqueness let $u + k_+ + k_- = 0$. Applying $A^\dagger - i$ gives $(A -
i)u - 2ik_- = 0$, and since the two terms lie in the orthogonal subspaces $\operatorname{ran}(A - i)$ and $\mathcal K_-$, both vanish; $A
- i$ is injective (@thm-unb-self-adjointness (1)), so $u = 0$, and then $k_+ = 0$. The formula for $A^\dagger v$ follows from $A^\dagger k_\pm
= \pm ik_\pm$. For the boundary form, terms involving $u$ or $u'$ cancel, since $\langle Au, w\rangle = \langle u, A^\dagger w\rangle$ and
$\langle A^\dagger v, u'\rangle = \langle v, Au'\rangle$. What remains is
$$
\langle ik_+ - ik_-, l_+ + l_-\rangle - \langle k_+ + k_-, il_+ - il_-\rangle = -2i\langle k_+, l_+\rangle + 2i\langle k_-, l_-\rangle ,
$$
the mixed terms $\mp i\langle k_\pm, l_\mp\rangle$ cancelling in pairs.

(3) Let $U$ be given. $D(A_U)$ is a subspace containing $D(A)$, and $A \subset A_U$. For $v = u + k + Uk$ and $w = u' + l + Ul$ in
$D(A_U)$, the boundary form of (2) is $2i(\langle Uk, Ul\rangle - \langle k, l\rangle) = 0$, because a linear map that preserves norms
preserves inner products, by polarisation (@thm-sesquilinear-forms (1)); so $A_U$ is symmetric. By (2), $(A_U - i)(u + k + Uk) = (A - i)u
- 2iUk$ and $(A_U + i)(u + k + Uk) = (A + i)u + 2ik$. Since $U$ is onto $\mathcal K_-$ and $\mathcal H = \operatorname{ran}(A - i) \oplus
\mathcal K_- = \operatorname{ran}(A + i) \oplus \mathcal K_+$, both ranges are $\mathcal H$, and $A_U$ is self-adjoint by
@thm-unb-self-adjointness (2). Conversely let $B$ be a self-adjoint extension. By (1), $B \subset A^\dagger$, so every $v \in D(B)$ is $u +
k_+ + k_-$ as in (2), and $B$ acts by $A^\dagger$. Symmetry of $B$ and the boundary form give $\|k_+\| = \|k_-\|$. Hence $k_+ = 0$ forces
$k_- = 0$, so $Uk_+ = k_-$ defines a norm-preserving linear map on $P_+ = \{k_+ : v \in D(B)\} \subseteq \mathcal K_+$ onto $P_- =
\{k_- : v \in D(B)\}$. Since $\operatorname{ran}(B - i) = \mathcal H$ and $(B - i)v = (A - i)u - 2ik_-$, every element of $\mathcal K_-$
is some $-2ik_-$, so $P_- = \mathcal K_-$; likewise $(B + i)v = (A + i)u + 2ik_+$ gives $P_+ = \mathcal K_+$. So $U : \mathcal K_+ \to
\mathcal K_-$ is a norm-preserving bijection, $D(B) \subseteq D(A_U)$, and $B = A_U$ by the maximality of @thm-unb-self-adjointness (3).
$U$ is determined by $B$ because the decomposition of (2) is unique. A linear bijection between spaces of finite dimensions $n_+$, $n_-$
exists only if $n_+ = n_-$, and then a norm-preserving one exists (map an orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis). If $n_\pm = 1$, the
norm-preserving maps are $k_+ \mapsto \gamma k_-$ with $|\gamma| = 1$. $\square$

The deficiency indices and both results of von Neumann are @reed1980methods [Vol. II, Sec. X.1, Thm. X.2 and its corollary, pp. 138-141];
the momentum operator on an interval, the model case below, is Example 1 there [pp. 141-143] and @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 7.5.2]; the
half-line is @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 7.5.2.5] and @hall2013quantum [Exercise 9.11]. Physical discussions are in @galitski2013exploring
[Problem 1.29].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
An essentially self-adjoint operator has nothing to choose. The first example records the deficiency indices of the diagonal operator,
the simplest such case.

::: {#exm-unb-sae-diagonal}
#### No choice for the diagonal operator

For $(Aa)_n = na_n$ on $c_{00}$, @exm-unb-diagonal-essential showed that $\overline A = A^\dagger$ is self-adjoint. So $\mathcal K_\pm =
\ker(A^\dagger \mp i) = \ker(\overline A \mp i) = \{0\}$, since $\pm i$ are not eigenvalues of a self-adjoint operator
(@thm-unb-self-adjointness (4)): $n_+ = n_- = 0$, and by part (1) $\overline A$ is the only self-adjoint extension. Directly, $(A^\dagger \mp
i)v = 0$ means $(n \mp i)v_n = 0$ for all $n$.
:::

The deficiency subspaces of the momentum operator on an interval are found by solving a first-order equation. The second example computes
them, using only continuous functions.
